# rustc_serialize - Rust

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc-serialize/

## Expand description

Support code for encoding and decoding types.

NOTE: This crate is deprecated in favor of[. No new feature development will happen in this crate, although bug fixes proposed through PRs will still be merged. It is very highly recommended by the Rust Library Team that you use](https://serde.rs)`serde`[, not this crate.](https://serde.rs)`serde`

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#usage)Usage

This crate is [on crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/rustc-serialize) and
can be used by adding `rustc-serialize` to the dependencies in your
project’s `Cargo.toml`.

```
[dependencies]
rustc-serialize = "0.3"
```
and this to your crate root:

`extern crate rustc_serialize;`## Modules[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#modules)

- [base64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/base64/index.html)
- Base64 binary-to-text encoding
- [hex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/hex/index.html)
- Hex binary-to-text encoding
- [json](https://doc.rust-lang.org/json/index.html)
- JSON parsing and serialization

## Traits[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#traits)

- [Decodable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/trait.Decodable.html)
- Trait for deserializing a type.
- [Decoder](https://doc.rust-lang.org/trait.Decoder.html)
- Trait for reading in an encoding for deserialization.
- [Decoder](https://doc.rust-lang.org/trait.DecoderHelpers.html)- Helpers
- Trait with helper functions for implementing `Decodable`.
- [Encodable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/trait.Encodable.html)
- Trait for serializing a type.
- [Encoder](https://doc.rust-lang.org/trait.Encoder.html)
- Trait for writing out an encoding when serializing.
- [Encoder](https://doc.rust-lang.org/trait.EncoderHelpers.html)- Helpers
- Trait with helper functions for implementing `Encodable`.

# Rust Documentation

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/

Welcome to an overview of the documentation provided by the [Rust
project](https://www.rust-lang.org). This page contains links to various helpful references,
most of which are available offline (if opened with `rustup doc`). Many of these
resources take the form of “books”; we collectively call these “The Rust
Bookshelf.” Some are large, some are small.

All of these books are managed by the Rust Organization, but other unofficial documentation resources are included here as well!

If you’re just looking for the standard library reference, here it is:
[Rust API documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/index.html)

If you’d like to learn Rust, this is the section for you! All of these resources assume that you have programmed before, but not in any specific language:

Affectionately nicknamed “the book,” [The Rust Programming Language](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/index.html)
will give you an overview of the language from first principles. You’ll build a
few projects along the way, and by the end, you’ll have a solid grasp of how to
use the language.

If reading multiple hundreds of pages about a language isn’t your style, then
[Rust By Example](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust-by-example/index.html) has you covered. RBE shows off a
bunch of code without using a lot of words. It also includes exercises!

[Rustlings](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustlings) guides you
through downloading and setting up the Rust toolchain, then provides an
interactive tool that teaches you how to solve coding challenges in Rust.

The [Rust Playground](https://play.rust-lang.org) is a great place
to try out and share small bits of code, or experiment with some of the most
popular crates.

Once you’ve gotten familiar with the language, these resources can help you put it to work.

Rust’s standard library has [extensive API documentation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/index.html), with
explanations of how to use various things, as well as example code for
accomplishing various tasks. Code examples have a “Run” button on hover that
opens the sample in the playground.

Whenever you are working in a crate, `cargo doc --open` will generate
documentation for your project *and* all its dependencies in their correct
version, and open it in your browser. Add the flag `--document-private-items` to
also show items not marked `pub`.

[The Release Notes](https://doc.rust-lang.org/releases.html) describes the change history of the Rust
toolchain and language.

[The Edition Guide](https://doc.rust-lang.org/edition-guide/index.html) describes the Rust editions and
their differences. The latest version of the toolchain supports all
historical editions.

`rustc` Book[The  rustc Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/index.html) describes the Rust compiler,

`rustc`.[The Cargo Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/index.html) is a guide to Cargo, Rust’s build tool and
dependency manager.

[The Rustdoc Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/index.html) describes our documentation tool, `rustdoc`.

[The Clippy Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/clippy/index.html) describes our static analyzer, Clippy.

Many of Rust’s errors come with error codes, and you can request extended
diagnostics from the compiler on those errors (with `rustc --explain`). You can
also read them here if you prefer: [rustc error codes](https://doc.rust-lang.org/error_codes/index.html)

Once you’re quite familiar with the language, you may find these advanced resources useful.

[The Reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/index.html) is not a formal spec, but is more detailed
and comprehensive than the book.

[The Rust Style Guide](https://doc.rust-lang.org/style-guide/index.html) describes the standard formatting
of Rust code. Most developers use `cargo fmt` to invoke `rustfmt` and format the
code automatically (the result matches this style guide).

[The Rustonomicon](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/index.html) is your guidebook to the dark arts of
unsafe Rust. It’s also sometimes called “the ’nomicon.”

[The Unstable Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/unstable-book/index.html) has documentation for unstable
features.

`rustc` Development Guide[The  rustc-dev-guide](https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/)
documents how the compiler works and how to contribute to it. This is useful if
you want to build or modify the Rust compiler from source (e.g. to target
something non-standard).

When using Rust in specific domains, consider using the following resources tailored to each area.

When developing for Bare Metal or Embedded Linux systems, you may find these
resources maintained by the [Embedded Working Group](https://github.com/rust-embedded) useful.

[The Embedded Rust Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/embedded-book/index.html) is targeted at developers who are familiar with embedded
development and Rust, but who have not used Rust for embedded development.

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rand/^0.3/

Utilities for random number generation

This release is a compatibility wrapper around `rand` version 0.4. Please
upgrade.

| [chacha](https://doc.rust-lang.org/chacha/index.html) | The ChaCha random number generator. |
| [distributions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/distributions/index.html) | Sampling from random distributions. |
| [isaac](https://doc.rust-lang.org/isaac/index.html) | The ISAAC random number generator. |
| [os](https://doc.rust-lang.org/os/index.html) | Interfaces to the operating system provided random number generators. |
| [read](https://doc.rust-lang.org/read/index.html) | A wrapper around any Read to treat it as an RNG. |
| [reseeding](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reseeding/index.html) | A wrapper around another RNG that reseeds it after it generates a certain number of random bytes. |

| [AsciiGenerator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.AsciiGenerator.html) | Iterator which will continuously generate random ascii characters. |
| [ChaChaRng](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.ChaChaRng.html) | A random number generator that uses the ChaCha20 algorithm [1]. |
| [Closed01](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Closed01.html) | A wrapper for generating floating point numbers uniformly in the
closed interval  |
| [Generator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Generator.html) | Iterator which will generate a stream of random items. |
| [Isaac64Rng](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Isaac64Rng.html) | A random number generator that uses ISAAC-64[1], the 64-bit variant of the ISAAC algorithm. |
| [IsaacRng](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.IsaacRng.html) | A random number generator that uses the ISAAC algorithm[1]. |
| [Open01](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Open01.html) | A wrapper for generating floating point numbers uniformly in the
open interval  |
| [OsRng](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.OsRng.html) | A random number generator that retrieves randomness straight from the operating system. Platform sources: |
| [StdRng](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.StdRng.html) | The standard RNG. This is designed to be efficient on the current platform. |
| [ThreadRng](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.ThreadRng.html) | The thread-local RNG. |
| [XorShiftRng](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.XorShiftRng.html) | An Xorshift[1] random number generator. |

| [Rand](https://doc.rust-lang.org/trait.Rand.html) | A type that can be randomly generated using an  |
| [Rng](https://doc.rust-lang.org/trait.Rng.html) | A random number generator. |
| [SeedableRng](https://doc.rust-lang.org/trait.SeedableRng.html) | A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded to produce the same stream of randomness multiple times. |

# std - Rust

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/

## Expand description

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#the-rust-standard-library)The Rust Standard Library

The Rust Standard Library is the foundation of portable Rust software, a
set of minimal and battle-tested shared abstractions for the [broader Rust
ecosystem](https://crates.io). It offers core types, like [ Vec<T>](https://doc.rust-lang.org/vec/struct.Vec.html) and

[, library-defined](https://doc.rust-lang.org/option/enum.Option.html)

`Option<T>`[operations on language primitives](https://doc.rust-lang.org#primitives),

[standard macros](https://doc.rust-lang.org#macros),

[I/O](https://doc.rust-lang.org/io/index.html)and

[multithreading](https://doc.rust-lang.org/thread/index.html), among

[many other things](https://doc.rust-lang.org#what-is-in-the-standard-library-documentation).

`std` is available to all Rust crates by default. Therefore, the
standard library can be accessed in [ use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch07-02-defining-modules-to-control-scope-and-privacy.html) statements through the path

`std`, as in [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/env/index.html)

`use std::env`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#how-to-read-this-documentation)How to read this documentation

If you already know the name of what you are looking for, the fastest way to
find it is to use the [search
button](https://doc.rust-lang.org) at the top of the page.

Otherwise, you may want to jump to one of these useful sections:

If this is your first time, the documentation for the standard library is written to be casually perused. Clicking on interesting things should generally lead you to interesting places. Still, there are important bits you don’t want to miss, so read on for a tour of the standard library and its documentation!

Once you are familiar with the contents of the standard library you may begin to find the verbosity of the prose distracting. At this stage in your development you may want to press the “ Summary” button near the top of the page to collapse it into a more skimmable view.

While you are looking at the top of the page, also notice the “Source” link. Rust’s API documentation comes with the source code and you are encouraged to read it. The standard library source is generally high quality and a peek behind the curtains is often enlightening.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#what-is-in-the-standard-library-documentation)What is in the standard library documentation?

First of all, The Rust Standard Library is divided into a number of focused
modules, [all listed further down this page](https://doc.rust-lang.org#modules). These modules are
the bedrock upon which all of Rust is forged, and they have mighty names
like [ std::slice](https://doc.rust-lang.org/slice/index.html) and

[. Modules’ documentation typically includes an overview of the module along with examples, and are a smart place to start familiarizing yourself with the library.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cmp/index.html)

`std::cmp`Second, implicit methods on [primitive types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch03-02-data-types.html) are documented here. This can
be a source of confusion for two reasons:

- While primitives are implemented by the compiler, the standard library
implements methods directly on the primitive types (and it is the only
library that does so), which are [documented in the section on primitives](https://doc.rust-lang.org#primitives).
- The standard library exports many modules *with the same name as primitive types*. These define additional items related to the primitive type, but not the all-important methods.

So for example there is a [page for the primitive type
 char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.char.html) that lists all the methods that can be called on
characters (very useful), and there is a

[page for the module](https://doc.rust-lang.org/char/index.html)that documents iterator and error types created by these methods (rarely useful).

`std::char`Note the documentation for the primitives [ str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html) and

[(also called ‘slice’). Many method calls on](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html)

`[T]`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/string/struct.String.html)

`String`[are actually calls to methods on](https://doc.rust-lang.org/vec/struct.Vec.html)

`Vec<T>`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html)

`str`[respectively, via](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html)

`[T]`[deref coercions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch15-02-deref.html#implicit-deref-coercions-with-functions-and-methods).

Third, the standard library defines [The Rust Prelude](https://doc.rust-lang.org/prelude/index.html), a small collection
of items - mostly traits - that are imported into every module of every
crate. The traits in the prelude are pervasive, making the prelude
documentation a good entry point to learning about the library.

And finally, the standard library exports a number of standard macros, and
[lists them on this page](https://doc.rust-lang.org#macros) (technically, not all of the standard
macros are defined by the standard library - some are defined by the
compiler - but they are documented here the same). Like the prelude, the
standard macros are imported by default into all crates.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#contributing-changes-to-the-documentation)Contributing changes to the documentation

Check out the Rust contribution guidelines [here](https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/contributing.html#writing-documentation).
The source for this documentation can be found on
[GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust) in the ‘library/std/’ directory.
To contribute changes, make sure you read the guidelines first, then submit
pull-requests for your suggested changes.

Contributions are appreciated! If you see a part of the docs that can be
improved, submit a PR, or chat with us first on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/219381-t-libs/)
#t-libs.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#a-tour-of-the-rust-standard-library)A Tour of The Rust Standard Library

The rest of this crate documentation is dedicated to pointing out notable features of The Rust Standard Library.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#containers-and-collections)Containers and collections

The [ option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/option/index.html) and

[modules define optional and error-handling types,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/result/index.html)

`result`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/option/enum.Option.html)

`Option<T>`[. The](https://doc.rust-lang.org/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result<T, E>`[module defines Rust’s iterator trait,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/iter/index.html)

`iter`[, which works with the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/iter/trait.Iterator.html)

`Iterator`[loop to access collections.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch03-05-control-flow.html#looping-through-a-collection-with-for)

`for`The standard library exposes three common ways to deal with contiguous regions of memory:

- `Vec<T>`- *vector*that is resizable at runtime.
- `[T; N]`- *array*with a fixed size at compile time.
- `[T]`- *slice*into any other kind of contiguous storage, whether heap-allocated or not.

Slices can only be handled through some kind of *pointer*, and as such come
in many flavors such as:

- `&[T]`-- *shared slice*
- `&mut [T]`-- *mutable slice*
- `Box<[T]>`- *owned slice*

[ str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html), a UTF-8 string slice, is a primitive type, and the standard library
defines many methods for it. Rust

[s are typically accessed as immutable references:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html)

`str``&str`. Use the owned [for building and mutating strings.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/string/struct.String.html)

`String`For converting to strings use the [ format!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.format.html) macro, and for converting from
strings use the

[trait.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/str/trait.FromStr.html)

`FromStr`Data may be shared by placing it in a reference-counted box or the [ Rc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rc/struct.Rc.html)
type, and if further contained in a

[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cell/struct.Cell.html)

`Cell`[, may be mutated as well as shared. Likewise, in a concurrent setting it is common to pair an atomically-reference-counted box,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cell/struct.RefCell.html)

`RefCell`[, with a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/sync/struct.Arc.html)

`Arc`[to get the same effect.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/sync/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex`The [ collections](https://doc.rust-lang.org/collections/index.html) module defines maps, sets, linked lists and other
typical collection types, including the common

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/collections/struct.HashMap.html)

`HashMap<K, V>`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#platform-abstractions-and-io)Platform abstractions and I/O

Besides basic data types, the standard library is largely concerned with abstracting over differences in common platforms, most notably Windows and Unix derivatives.

Common types of I/O, including [files](https://doc.rust-lang.org/fs/struct.File.html), [TCP](https://doc.rust-lang.org/net/struct.TcpStream.html), and [UDP](https://doc.rust-lang.org/net/struct.UdpSocket.html), are defined in
the [ io](https://doc.rust-lang.org/io/index.html),

[, and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/fs/index.html)

`fs`[modules.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/net/index.html)

`net`The [ thread](https://doc.rust-lang.org/thread/index.html) module contains Rust’s threading abstractions.

[contains further primitive shared memory types, including](https://doc.rust-lang.org/sync/index.html)

`sync`[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/sync/atomic/index.html)

`atomic`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/sync/mpmc/index.html)

`mpmc`[, which contains the channel types for message passing.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/sync/mpsc/index.html)

`mpsc`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#use-before-and-after-main)Use before and after `main()`

Many parts of the standard library are expected to work before and after `main()`;
but this is not guaranteed or ensured by tests. It is recommended that you write your own tests
and run them on each platform you wish to support.
This means that use of `std` before/after main, especially of features that interact with the
OS or global state, is exempted from stability and portability guarantees and instead only
provided on a best-effort basis. Nevertheless bug reports are appreciated.

On the other hand `core` and `alloc` are most likely to work in such environments with
the caveat that any hookable behavior such as panics, oom handling or allocators will also
depend on the compatibility of the hooks.

Some features may also behave differently outside main, e.g. stdio could become unbuffered, some panics might turn into aborts, backtraces might not get symbolicated or similar.

Non-exhaustive list of known limitations:

- after-main use of thread-locals, which also affects additional features:
- under UNIX, before main, file descriptors 0, 1, and 2 may be unchanged (they are guaranteed to be open during main, and are opened to /dev/null O_RDWR if they weren’t open on program start)

## Primitive Types[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#primitives)

- [array](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.array.html)
- A fixed-size array, denoted `[T; N]`, for the element type,`T`, and the non-negative compile-time constant size,`N`.
- [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html)
- The boolean type.
- [char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.char.html)
- A character type.
- [f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.f32.html)
- A 32-bit floating-point type (specifically, the “binary32” type defined in IEEE 754-2008).
- [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.f64.html)

- [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html)
- String slices.
- [tuple](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.tuple.html)
- A finite heterogeneous sequence, `(T, U, ..)`.

- [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)

- [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)

- The `()`type, also called “unit”.
- [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html)
- The pointer-sized unsigned integer type.

- [f128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.f128.html)- Experimental
- A 128-bit floating-point type (specifically, the “binary128” type defined in IEEE 754-2008).

## Macros[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#macros)

- [assert](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.assert.html)
- Asserts that a boolean expression is `true`at runtime.
- [assert_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.assert_eq.html)- eq
- Asserts that two expressions are equal to each other (using `PartialEq`
- [assert_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.assert_matches.html)- matches
- Asserts that an expression matches the provided pattern.
- [assert_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.assert_ne.html)- ne
- Asserts that two expressions are not equal to each other (using `PartialEq`
- [cfg](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.cfg.html)
- Evaluates boolean combinations of configuration flags at compile-time.
- [cfg_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.cfg_select.html)- select
- Selects code at compile-time based on `cfg`predicates.
- [column](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.column.html)
- Expands to the column number at which it was invoked.
- [compile_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.compile_error.html)- error
- Causes compilation to fail with the given error message when encountered.
- [concat](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.concat.html)
- Concatenates literals into a static string slice.
- [dbg](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.dbg.html)
- Prints and returns the value of a given expression for quick and dirty debugging.
- [debug_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.debug_assert.html)- assert
- Asserts that a boolean expression is `true`at runtime.
- [debug_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.debug_assert_eq.html)- assert_ - eq
- Asserts that two expressions are equal to each other.
- [debug_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.debug_assert_matches.html)- assert_ - matches
- Asserts that an expression matches the provided pattern.
- [debug_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.debug_assert_ne.html)- assert_ - ne
- Asserts that two expressions are not equal to each other.
- [env](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.env.html)
- Inspects an environment variable at compile time.
- [eprint](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.eprint.html)
- Prints to the standard error.
- [eprintln](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.eprintln.html)
- Prints to the standard error, with a newline.
- [file](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.file.html)
- Expands to the file name in which it was invoked.
- [format](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.format.html)
- Creates a `String`using interpolation of runtime expressions.
- [format_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.format_args.html)- args
- Constructs parameters for the other string-formatting macros.
- [include](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.include.html)
- Parses a file as an expression or an item according to the context.
- [include_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.include_bytes.html)- bytes
- Includes a file as a reference to a byte array.
- [include_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.include_str.html)- str
- Includes a UTF-8 encoded file as a string.
- [is_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.is_x86_feature_detected.html)- x86_ - feature_ - detected
- Check for the presence of a CPU feature at runtime.
- [line](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.line.html)
- Expands to the line number on which it was invoked.
- [matches](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.matches.html)
- Returns whether the given expression matches the provided pattern.
- [module_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.module_path.html)- path
- Expands to a string that represents the current module path.
- [option_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.option_env.html)- env
- Optionally inspects an environment variable at compile time.
- [panic](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.panic.html)
- Panics the current thread.
- [print](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.print.html)
- Prints to the standard output.
- [println](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.println.html)
- Prints to the standard output, with a newline.
- [stringify](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.stringify.html)
- Stringifies its arguments.
- [thread_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.thread_local.html)- local
- Declare a new thread local storage key of type `std::thread::LocalKey`
- [todo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.todo.html)
- Indicates unfinished code.
- [try](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.try.html)- Deprecated
- Unwraps a result or propagates its error.
- [unimplemented](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.unimplemented.html)
- Indicates unimplemented code by panicking with a message of “not implemented”.
- [unreachable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.unreachable.html)
- Indicates unreachable code.
- [vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.vec.html)
- Creates a `Vec`
- [write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.write.html)
- Writes formatted data into a buffer.
- [writeln](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.writeln.html)
- Writes formatted data into a buffer, with a newline appended.
- [concat_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.concat_bytes.html)- bytes - Experimental
- Concatenates literals into a byte slice.
- [const_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.const_format_args.html)- format_ - args - Experimental
- Same as `format_args`
- [hash_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.hash_map.html)- map - Experimental
- Creates a `HashMap`
- [log_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.log_syntax.html)- syntax - Experimental
- Prints passed tokens into the standard output.
- [trace_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.trace_macros.html)- macros - Experimental
- Enables or disables tracing functionality used for debugging other macros.

## Keywords[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#keywords)

- [SelfTy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.SelfTy.html)
- The implementing type within a `trait``impl`
- [as](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.as.html)
- Cast between types, rename an import, or qualify paths to associated items.
- [async](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.async.html)
- Returns a `Future`
- [await](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.await.html)
- Suspend execution until the result of a `Future`
- [become](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.become.html)
- Perform a tail-call of a function.
- [break](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.break.html)
- Exit early from a loop or labelled block.
- [const](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.const.html)
- Compile-time constants, compile-time blocks, compile-time evaluable functions, and raw pointers.
- [continue](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.continue.html)
- Skip to the next iteration of a loop.
- [crate](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.crate.html)
- A Rust binary or library.
- [dyn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.dyn.html)
- `dyn`is a prefix of a- [trait object](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch17-02-trait-objects.html)’s type.
- [else](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.else.html)
- What expression to evaluate when an `if``false`
- [enum](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.enum.html)
- A type that can be any one of several variants.
- [extern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.extern.html)
- Link to or import external code.
- [false](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.false.html)
- A value of type `bool`**false**.
- [fn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.fn.html)
- A function or function pointer.
- [for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.for.html)
- Iteration with `in``impl`[higher-ranked trait bounds](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/trait-bounds.html#higher-ranked-trait-bounds)(`for<'a>`).
- [if](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.if.html)
- Evaluate a block if a condition holds.
- [impl](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.impl.html)
- Implementations of functionality for a type, or a type implementing some functionality.
- [in](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.in.html)
- Iterate over a series of values with `for`
- [let](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.let.html)
- Bind a value to a variable.
- [loop](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.loop.html)
- Loop indefinitely.
- [match](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.match.html)
- Control flow based on pattern matching.
- [mod](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.mod.html)
- Organize code into [modules](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/modules.html).
- [move](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.move.html)
- Capture a [closure](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch13-01-closures.html)’s environment by value.
- [mut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.mut.html)
- A mutable variable, reference, or pointer.
- [pub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.pub.html)
- Make an item visible to others.
- [ref](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.ref.html)
- Bind by reference during pattern matching.
- [return](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.return.html)
- Returns a value from a function.
- [self](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.self.html)
- The receiver of a method, or the current module.
- [static](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.static.html)
- A static item is a value which is valid for the entire duration of your
program (a `'static`lifetime).
- [struct](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.struct.html)
- A type that is composed of other types.
- [super](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.super.html)
- The parent of the current [module](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/modules.html).
- [trait](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.trait.html)
- A common interface for a group of types.
- [true](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.true.html)
- A value of type `bool`**true**.
- [type](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.type.html)
- Define an [alias](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/type-aliases.html)for an existing type.
- [union](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.union.html)
- The [Rust equivalent of a C-style union](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/unions.html).
- [unsafe](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.unsafe.html)
- Code or interfaces whose [memory safety](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch19-01-unsafe-rust.html)cannot be verified by the type system.
- [use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.use.html)
- Import or rename items from other crates or modules, use values under ergonomic clones
semantic, or specify precise capturing with `use<..>`.
- [where](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.where.html)
- Add constraints that must be upheld to use an item.
- [while](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.while.html)
- Loop while a condition is upheld.

# Introduction - Rust By Example

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust-by-example/

[Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org/) is a modern systems programming language focusing on safety, speed,
and concurrency. It accomplishes these goals by being memory safe without using
garbage collection.

Rust by Example (RBE) is a collection of runnable examples that illustrate various Rust
concepts and standard libraries. To get even more out of these examples, don’t forget
to [install Rust locally](https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install) and check out the [official docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/).
Additionally for the curious, you can also [check out the source code for this site](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-by-example).

Now let’s begin!

-
[Hello World](https://doc.rust-lang.org/hello.html)- Start with a traditional Hello World program.
-
[Primitives](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitives.html)- Learn about signed integers, unsigned integers and other primitives.
-
[Custom Types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/custom_types.html)-`struct`and`enum`.
-
[Variable Bindings](https://doc.rust-lang.org/variable_bindings.html)- mutable bindings, scope, shadowing.
-
[Types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/types.html)- Learn about changing and defining types.
-
[Conversion](https://doc.rust-lang.org/conversion.html)- Convert between different types, such as strings, integers, and floats.
-
[Expressions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/expression.html)- Learn about Expressions & how to use them.
-
[Flow of Control](https://doc.rust-lang.org/flow_control.html)-`if`/`else`,`for`, and others.
-
[Functions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/fn.html)- Learn about Methods, Closures and Higher Order Functions.
-
[Modules](https://doc.rust-lang.org/mod.html)- Organize code using modules
-
[Crates](https://doc.rust-lang.org/crates.html)- A crate is a compilation unit in Rust. Learn to create a library.
-
[Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo.html)- Go through some basic features of the official Rust package management tool.
-
[Attributes](https://doc.rust-lang.org/attribute.html)- An attribute is metadata applied to some module, crate or item.
-
[Generics](https://doc.rust-lang.org/generics.html)- Learn about writing a function or data type which can work for multiple types of arguments.
-
[Scoping rules](https://doc.rust-lang.org/scope.html)- Scopes play an important part in ownership, borrowing, and lifetimes.
-
[Traits](https://doc.rust-lang.org/trait.html)- A trait is a collection of methods defined for an unknown type:`Self`
-
[Macros](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macros.html)- Macros are a way of writing code that writes other code, which is known as metaprogramming.
-
[Error handling](https://doc.rust-lang.org/error.html)- Learn Rust way of handling failures.
-
[Std library types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std.html)- Learn about some custom types provided by`std`library.
-

# Introduction - Clippy Documentation

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/clippy

A collection of lints to catch common mistakes and improve your
[Rust](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust) code.

Lints are divided into categories, each with a default [lint
level](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/lints/levels.html). You can choose how
much Clippy is supposed to ~~annoy~~ help you by changing the lint level by
category.

| Category | Description | Default level |
|---|---|---|
| `clippy::all` | all lints that are on by default (correctness, suspicious, style, complexity, perf) | warn/deny |
| `clippy::correctness` | code that is outright wrong or useless | deny |
| `clippy::suspicious` | code that is most likely wrong or useless | warn |
| `clippy::style` | code that should be written in a more idiomatic way | warn |
| `clippy::complexity` | code that does something simple but in a complex way | warn |
| `clippy::perf` | code that can be written to run faster | warn |
| `clippy::pedantic` | lints which are rather strict or have occasional false positives | allow |
| `clippy::restriction` | lints which prevent the use of language and library features [1](https://doc.rust-lang.org#footnote-restrict) | allow |
| `clippy::nursery` | new lints that are still under development | allow |
| `clippy::cargo` | lints for the cargo manifest | allow |

More to come, please [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-clippy/issues) if you have ideas!

The `restriction` category should, *emphatically*, not be enabled as a whole. The contained
lints may lint against perfectly reasonable code, may not have an alternative suggestion,
and may contradict any other lints (including other categories). Lints should be considered
on a case-by-case basis before enabling.

-
Some use cases for `restriction`lints include:- Strict coding styles (e.g. `clippy::else_if_without_else`
- Additional restrictions on CI (e.g. `clippy::todo`
- Preventing panicking in certain functions (e.g. `clippy::unwrap_used`
- Running a lint only on a subset of code (e.g. `#[forbid(clippy::float_arithmetic)]`on a module).
 [↩](https://doc.rust-lang.org#fr-restrict-1)
- Strict coding styles (e.g.

# std - Rust

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#the-rust-standard-library)The Rust Standard Library

The Rust Standard Library is the foundation of portable Rust software, a
set of minimal and battle-tested shared abstractions for the [broader Rust
ecosystem](https://crates.io). It offers core types, like [ Vec<T>](https://doc.rust-lang.org/vec/struct.Vec.html) and

[, library-defined](https://doc.rust-lang.org/option/enum.Option.html)

`Option<T>`[operations on language primitives](https://doc.rust-lang.org#primitives),

[standard macros](https://doc.rust-lang.org#macros),

[I/O](https://doc.rust-lang.org/io/index.html)and

[multithreading](https://doc.rust-lang.org/thread/index.html), among

[many other things](https://doc.rust-lang.org#what-is-in-the-standard-library-documentation).

`std` is available to all Rust crates by default. Therefore, the
standard library can be accessed in [ use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch07-02-defining-modules-to-control-scope-and-privacy.html) statements through the path

`std`, as in [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/env/index.html)

`use std::env`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#how-to-read-this-documentation)How to read this documentation

If you already know the name of what you are looking for, the fastest way to
find it is to use the [search
button](https://doc.rust-lang.org) at the top of the page.

Otherwise, you may want to jump to one of these useful sections:

If this is your first time, the documentation for the standard library is written to be casually perused. Clicking on interesting things should generally lead you to interesting places. Still, there are important bits you don’t want to miss, so read on for a tour of the standard library and its documentation!

Once you are familiar with the contents of the standard library you may begin to find the verbosity of the prose distracting. At this stage in your development you may want to press the “ Summary” button near the top of the page to collapse it into a more skimmable view.

While you are looking at the top of the page, also notice the “Source” link. Rust’s API documentation comes with the source code and you are encouraged to read it. The standard library source is generally high quality and a peek behind the curtains is often enlightening.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#what-is-in-the-standard-library-documentation)What is in the standard library documentation?

First of all, The Rust Standard Library is divided into a number of focused
modules, [all listed further down this page](https://doc.rust-lang.org#modules). These modules are
the bedrock upon which all of Rust is forged, and they have mighty names
like [ std::slice](https://doc.rust-lang.org/slice/index.html) and

[. Modules’ documentation typically includes an overview of the module along with examples, and are a smart place to start familiarizing yourself with the library.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cmp/index.html)

`std::cmp`Second, implicit methods on [primitive types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch03-02-data-types.html) are documented here. This can
be a source of confusion for two reasons:

- While primitives are implemented by the compiler, the standard library
implements methods directly on the primitive types (and it is the only
library that does so), which are [documented in the section on primitives](https://doc.rust-lang.org#primitives).
- The standard library exports many modules *with the same name as primitive types*. These define additional items related to the primitive type, but not the all-important methods.

So for example there is a [page for the primitive type
 char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.char.html) that lists all the methods that can be called on
characters (very useful), and there is a

[page for the module](https://doc.rust-lang.org/char/index.html)that documents iterator and error types created by these methods (rarely useful).

`std::char`Note the documentation for the primitives [ str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html) and

[(also called ‘slice’). Many method calls on](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html)

`[T]`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/string/struct.String.html)

`String`[are actually calls to methods on](https://doc.rust-lang.org/vec/struct.Vec.html)

`Vec<T>`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html)

`str`[respectively, via](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html)

`[T]`[deref coercions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch15-02-deref.html#implicit-deref-coercions-with-functions-and-methods).

Third, the standard library defines [The Rust Prelude](https://doc.rust-lang.org/prelude/index.html), a small collection
of items - mostly traits - that are imported into every module of every
crate. The traits in the prelude are pervasive, making the prelude
documentation a good entry point to learning about the library.

And finally, the standard library exports a number of standard macros, and
[lists them on this page](https://doc.rust-lang.org#macros) (technically, not all of the standard
macros are defined by the standard library - some are defined by the
compiler - but they are documented here the same). Like the prelude, the
standard macros are imported by default into all crates.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#contributing-changes-to-the-documentation)Contributing changes to the documentation

Check out the Rust contribution guidelines [here](https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/contributing.html#writing-documentation).
The source for this documentation can be found on
[GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust) in the ‘library/std/’ directory.
To contribute changes, make sure you read the guidelines first, then submit
pull-requests for your suggested changes.

Contributions are appreciated! If you see a part of the docs that can be
improved, submit a PR, or chat with us first on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/219381-t-libs/)
#t-libs.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#a-tour-of-the-rust-standard-library)A Tour of The Rust Standard Library

The rest of this crate documentation is dedicated to pointing out notable features of The Rust Standard Library.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#containers-and-collections)Containers and collections

The [ option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/option/index.html) and

[modules define optional and error-handling types,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/result/index.html)

`result`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/option/enum.Option.html)

`Option<T>`[. The](https://doc.rust-lang.org/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result<T, E>`[module defines Rust’s iterator trait,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/iter/index.html)

`iter`[, which works with the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/iter/trait.Iterator.html)

`Iterator`[loop to access collections.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch03-05-control-flow.html#looping-through-a-collection-with-for)

`for`The standard library exposes three common ways to deal with contiguous regions of memory:

- `Vec<T>`- *vector*that is resizable at runtime.
- `[T; N]`- *array*with a fixed size at compile time.
- `[T]`- *slice*into any other kind of contiguous storage, whether heap-allocated or not.

Slices can only be handled through some kind of *pointer*, and as such come
in many flavors such as:

- `&[T]`-- *shared slice*
- `&mut [T]`-- *mutable slice*
- `Box<[T]>`- *owned slice*

[ str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html), a UTF-8 string slice, is a primitive type, and the standard library
defines many methods for it. Rust

[s are typically accessed as immutable references:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html)

`str``&str`. Use the owned [for building and mutating strings.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/string/struct.String.html)

`String`For converting to strings use the [ format!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.format.html) macro, and for converting from
strings use the

[trait.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/str/trait.FromStr.html)

`FromStr`Data may be shared by placing it in a reference-counted box or the [ Rc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rc/struct.Rc.html)
type, and if further contained in a

[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cell/struct.Cell.html)

`Cell`[, may be mutated as well as shared. Likewise, in a concurrent setting it is common to pair an atomically-reference-counted box,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cell/struct.RefCell.html)

`RefCell`[, with a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/sync/struct.Arc.html)

`Arc`[to get the same effect.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/sync/struct.Mutex.html)

`Mutex`The [ collections](https://doc.rust-lang.org/collections/index.html) module defines maps, sets, linked lists and other
typical collection types, including the common

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/collections/struct.HashMap.html)

`HashMap<K, V>`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#platform-abstractions-and-io)Platform abstractions and I/O

Besides basic data types, the standard library is largely concerned with abstracting over differences in common platforms, most notably Windows and Unix derivatives.

Common types of I/O, including [files](https://doc.rust-lang.org/fs/struct.File.html), [TCP](https://doc.rust-lang.org/net/struct.TcpStream.html), and [UDP](https://doc.rust-lang.org/net/struct.UdpSocket.html), are defined in
the [ io](https://doc.rust-lang.org/io/index.html),

[, and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/fs/index.html)

`fs`[modules.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/net/index.html)

`net`The [ thread](https://doc.rust-lang.org/thread/index.html) module contains Rust’s threading abstractions.

[contains further primitive shared memory types, including](https://doc.rust-lang.org/sync/index.html)

`sync`[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/sync/atomic/index.html)

`atomic`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/sync/mpmc/index.html)

`mpmc`[, which contains the channel types for message passing.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/sync/mpsc/index.html)

`mpsc`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#use-before-and-after-main)Use before and after `main()`

Many parts of the standard library are expected to work before and after `main()`;
but this is not guaranteed or ensured by tests. It is recommended that you write your own tests
and run them on each platform you wish to support.
This means that use of `std` before/after main, especially of features that interact with the
OS or global state, is exempted from stability and portability guarantees and instead only
provided on a best-effort basis. Nevertheless bug reports are appreciated.

On the other hand `core` and `alloc` are most likely to work in such environments with
the caveat that any hookable behavior such as panics, oom handling or allocators will also
depend on the compatibility of the hooks.

Some features may also behave differently outside main, e.g. stdio could become unbuffered, some panics might turn into aborts, backtraces might not get symbolicated or similar.

Non-exhaustive list of known limitations:

- after-main use of thread-locals, which also affects additional features:
- under UNIX, before main, file descriptors 0, 1, and 2 may be unchanged (they are guaranteed to be open during main, and are opened to /dev/null O_RDWR if they weren’t open on program start)

## Primitive Types[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#primitives)

- [array](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.array.html)
- A fixed-size array, denoted `[T; N]`, for the element type,`T`, and the non-negative compile-time constant size,`N`.
- [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html)
- The boolean type.
- [char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.char.html)
- A character type.
- [f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.f32.html)
- A 32-bit floating-point type (specifically, the “binary32” type defined in IEEE 754-2008).
- [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.f64.html)
- A 64-bit floating-point type (specifically, the “binary64” type defined in IEEE 754-2008).
- [fn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.fn.html)
- Function pointers, like `fn(usize) -> bool`.
- [i8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i8.html)
- The 8-bit signed integer type.
- [i16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i16.html)
- The 16-bit signed integer type.
- [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html)
- The 32-bit signed integer type.
- [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)
- The 64-bit signed integer type.
- [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)
- The 128-bit signed integer type.
- [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)
- The pointer-sized signed integer type.
- [pointer](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html)
- Raw, unsafe pointers, `*const T`, and`*mut T`.
- [reference](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.reference.html)
- References, `&T`and`&mut T`.
- [slice](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html)
- A dynamically-sized view into a contiguous sequence, `[T]`.
- [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html)
- String slices.
- [tuple](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.tuple.html)
- A finite heterogeneous sequence, `(T, U, ..)`.
- [u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u8.html)
- The 8-bit unsigned integer type.
- [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)
- The 16-bit unsigned integer type.
- [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)
- The 32-bit unsigned integer type.
- [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)
- The 64-bit unsigned integer type.
- [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)
- The 128-bit unsigned integer type.
- [unit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.unit.html)
- The `()`type, also called “unit”.
- [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html)
- The pointer-sized unsigned integer type.
- [f16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.f16.html)- Experimental
- A 16-bit floating-point type (specifically, the “binary16” type defined in IEEE 754-2008).
- [f128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.f128.html)- Experimental
- A 128-bit floating-point type (specifically, the “binary128” type defined in IEEE 754-2008).
- [never](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.never.html)- Experimental
- The `!`type, also called “never”.

- Portable SIMD module.
- [unsafe_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/unsafe_binder/index.html)- binder - Experimental
- Operators used to turn types into unsafe binders and back.

## Macros[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#macros)

- [assert](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.assert.html)
- Asserts that a boolean expression is `true`at runtime.
- [assert_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.assert_eq.html)- eq
- Asserts that two expressions are equal to each other (using `PartialEq`
- [assert_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.assert_matches.html)- matches
- Asserts that an expression matches the provided pattern.
- [assert_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.assert_ne.html)- ne
- Asserts that two expressions are not equal to each other (using `PartialEq`
- [cfg](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.cfg.html)
- Evaluates boolean combinations of configuration flags at compile-time.
- [cfg_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.cfg_select.html)- select
- Selects code at compile-time based on `cfg`predicates.
- [column](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.column.html)
- Expands to the column number at which it was invoked.
- [compile_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.compile_error.html)- error
- Causes compilation to fail with the given error message when encountered.
- [concat](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.concat.html)
- Concatenates literals into a static string slice.
- [dbg](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.dbg.html)
- Prints and returns the value of a given expression for quick and dirty debugging.
- [debug_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.debug_assert.html)- assert
- Asserts that a boolean expression is `true`at runtime.
- [debug_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.debug_assert_eq.html)- assert_ - eq
- Asserts that two expressions are equal to each other.
- [debug_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.debug_assert_matches.html)- assert_ - matches
- Asserts that an expression matches the provided pattern.
- [debug_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.debug_assert_ne.html)- assert_ - ne
- Asserts that two expressions are not equal to each other.
- [env](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.env.html)
- Inspects an environment variable at compile time.
- [eprint](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.eprint.html)
- Prints to the standard error.
- [eprintln](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.eprintln.html)
- Prints to the standard error, with a newline.
- [file](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.file.html)
- Expands to the file name in which it was invoked.
- [format](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.format.html)
- Creates a `String`using interpolation of runtime expressions.
- [format_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.format_args.html)- args
- Constructs parameters for the other string-formatting macros.
- [include](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.include.html)
- Parses a file as an expression or an item according to the context.
- [include_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.include_bytes.html)- bytes
- Includes a file as a reference to a byte array.
- [include_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.include_str.html)- str
- Includes a UTF-8 encoded file as a string.
- [is_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.is_x86_feature_detected.html)- x86_ - feature_ - detected
- Check for the presence of a CPU feature at runtime.
- [line](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.line.html)
- Expands to the line number on which it was invoked.
- [matches](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.matches.html)
- Returns whether the given expression matches the provided pattern.
- [module_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.module_path.html)- path
- Expands to a string that represents the current module path.
- [option_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.option_env.html)- env
- Optionally inspects an environment variable at compile time.
- [panic](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.panic.html)
- Panics the current thread.
- [print](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.print.html)
- Prints to the standard output.
- [println](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.println.html)
- Prints to the standard output, with a newline.
- [stringify](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.stringify.html)
- Stringifies its arguments.
- [thread_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.thread_local.html)- local
- Declare a new thread local storage key of type `std::thread::LocalKey`
- [todo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.todo.html)
- Indicates unfinished code.
- [try](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.try.html)- Deprecated
- Unwraps a result or propagates its error.
- [unimplemented](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.unimplemented.html)
- Indicates unimplemented code by panicking with a message of “not implemented”.
- [unreachable](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.unreachable.html)
- Indicates unreachable code.
- [vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.vec.html)
- Creates a `Vec`
- [write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.write.html)
- Writes formatted data into a buffer.
- [writeln](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.writeln.html)
- Writes formatted data into a buffer, with a newline appended.
- [concat_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.concat_bytes.html)- bytes - Experimental
- Concatenates literals into a byte slice.
- [const_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.const_format_args.html)- format_ - args - Experimental
- Same as `format_args`
- [hash_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.hash_map.html)- map - Experimental
- Creates a `HashMap`
- [log_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.log_syntax.html)- syntax - Experimental
- Prints passed tokens into the standard output.
- [trace_](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.trace_macros.html)- macros - Experimental
- Enables or disables tracing functionality used for debugging other macros.

## Keywords[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#keywords)

- [SelfTy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.SelfTy.html)
- The implementing type within a `trait``impl`
- [as](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.as.html)
- Cast between types, rename an import, or qualify paths to associated items.
- [async](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.async.html)
- Returns a `Future`
- [await](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.await.html)
- Suspend execution until the result of a `Future`
- [become](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.become.html)
- Perform a tail-call of a function.
- [break](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.break.html)
- Exit early from a loop or labelled block.
- [const](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.const.html)
- Compile-time constants, compile-time blocks, compile-time evaluable functions, and raw pointers.
- [continue](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.continue.html)
- Skip to the next iteration of a loop.
- [crate](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.crate.html)
- A Rust binary or library.
- [dyn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.dyn.html)
- `dyn`is a prefix of a- [trait object](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch17-02-trait-objects.html)’s type.
- [else](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.else.html)
- What expression to evaluate when an `if``false`
- [enum](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.enum.html)
- A type that can be any one of several variants.
- [extern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.extern.html)
- Link to or import external code.
- [false](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.false.html)
- A value of type `bool`**false**.
- [fn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.fn.html)
- A function or function pointer.
- [for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.for.html)
- Iteration with `in``impl`[higher-ranked trait bounds](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/trait-bounds.html#higher-ranked-trait-bounds)(`for<'a>`).
- [if](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.if.html)
- Evaluate a block if a condition holds.
- [impl](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.impl.html)
- Implementations of functionality for a type, or a type implementing some functionality.
- [in](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.in.html)
- Iterate over a series of values with `for`
- [let](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.let.html)
- Bind a value to a variable.
- [loop](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.loop.html)
- Loop indefinitely.
- [match](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.match.html)
- Control flow based on pattern matching.
- [mod](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.mod.html)
- Organize code into [modules](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/modules.html).
- [move](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.move.html)
- Capture a [closure](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch13-01-closures.html)’s environment by value.
- [mut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.mut.html)
- A mutable variable, reference, or pointer.
- [pub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.pub.html)
- Make an item visible to others.
- [ref](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.ref.html)
- Bind by reference during pattern matching.
- [return](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.return.html)
- Returns a value from a function.
- [self](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.self.html)
- The receiver of a method, or the current module.
- [static](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.static.html)
- A static item is a value which is valid for the entire duration of your
program (a `'static`lifetime).
- [struct](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.struct.html)
- A type that is composed of other types.
- [super](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.super.html)
- The parent of the current [module](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/modules.html).
- [trait](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.trait.html)
- A common interface for a group of types.
- [true](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.true.html)
- A value of type `bool`**true**.
- [type](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.type.html)
- Define an [alias](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/type-aliases.html)for an existing type.
- [union](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.union.html)
- The [Rust equivalent of a C-style union](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/unions.html).
- [unsafe](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.unsafe.html)
- Code or interfaces whose [memory safety](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch19-01-unsafe-rust.html)cannot be verified by the type system.
- [use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.use.html)
- Import or rename items from other crates or modules, use values under ergonomic clones
semantic, or specify precise capturing with `use<..>`.
- [where](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.where.html)
- Add constraints that must be upheld to use an item.
- [while](https://doc.rust-lang.org/keyword.while.html)
- Loop while a condition is upheld.

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/index.html

*by Steve Klabnik, Carol Nichols, and Chris Krycho, with contributions from the
Rust Community*

This version of the text assumes you’re using Rust 1.90.0 (released 2025-09-18)
or later with `edition = "2024"` in the *Cargo.toml* file of all projects to
configure them to use Rust 2024 Edition idioms. See the [“Installation” section
of Chapter 1](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ch01-01-installation.html) for instructions on installing or
updating Rust, and see [Appendix E](https://doc.rust-lang.org/appendix-05-editions.html) for information
on editions.

The HTML format is available online at
[https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/book/](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/book/)
and offline with installations of Rust made with `rustup`; run `rustup doc --book` to open.

Several community [translations](https://doc.rust-lang.org/appendix-06-translation.html) are also available.

This text is available in [paperback and ebook format from No Starch
Press](https://nostarch.com/rust-programming-language-3rd-edition).

# Introduction - Rust By Example

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rust-by-example/index.html

[Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org/) is a modern systems programming language focusing on safety, speed,
and concurrency. It accomplishes these goals by being memory safe without using
garbage collection.

Rust by Example (RBE) is a collection of runnable examples that illustrate various Rust
concepts and standard libraries. To get even more out of these examples, don’t forget
to [install Rust locally](https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install) and check out the [official docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/).
Additionally for the curious, you can also [check out the source code for this site](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-by-example).

Now let’s begin!

-
[Hello World](https://doc.rust-lang.org/hello.html)- Start with a traditional Hello World program.
-
[Primitives](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitives.html)- Learn about signed integers, unsigned integers and other primitives.
-
[Custom Types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/custom_types.html)-`struct`and`enum`.
-
[Variable Bindings](https://doc.rust-lang.org/variable_bindings.html)- mutable bindings, scope, shadowing.
-
[Types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/types.html)- Learn about changing and defining types.
-
[Conversion](https://doc.rust-lang.org/conversion.html)- Convert between different types, such as strings, integers, and floats.
-
[Expressions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/expression.html)- Learn about Expressions & how to use them.
-
[Flow of Control](https://doc.rust-lang.org/flow_control.html)-`if`/`else`,`for`, and others.
-
[Functions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/fn.html)- Learn about Methods, Closures and Higher Order Functions.
-
[Modules](https://doc.rust-lang.org/mod.html)- Organize code using modules
-
[Crates](https://doc.rust-lang.org/crates.html)- A crate is a compilation unit in Rust. Learn to create a library.
-
[Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo.html)- Go through some basic features of the official Rust package management tool.
-
[Attributes](https://doc.rust-lang.org/attribute.html)- An attribute is metadata applied to some module, crate or item.
-
[Generics](https://doc.rust-lang.org/generics.html)- Learn about writing a function or data type which can work for multiple types of arguments.
-
[Scoping rules](https://doc.rust-lang.org/scope.html)- Scopes play an important part in ownership, borrowing, and lifetimes.
-
[Traits](https://doc.rust-lang.org/trait.html)- A trait is a collection of methods defined for an unknown type:`Self`
-
[Macros](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macros.html)- Macros are a way of writing code that writes other code, which is known as metaprogramming.
-
[Error handling](https://doc.rust-lang.org/error.html)- Learn Rust way of handling failures.
-
[Std library types](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std.html)- Learn about some custom types provided by`std`library.
-
[Std misc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std_misc.html)- More custom types for file handling, threads.
-
[Testing](https://doc.rust-lang.org/testing.html)- All sorts of testing in Rust.
-
[Unsafe Operations](https://doc.rust-lang.org/unsafe.html)- Learn about entering a block of unsafe operations.
-
[Compatibility](https://doc.rust-lang.org/compatibility.html)- Handling Rust’s evolution and potential compatibility issues.
-
[Meta](https://doc.rust-lang.org/meta.html)- Documentation, Benchmarking.

`std::env::home_dir()` has been deprecated for years, because it can give surprising results in some Windows configurations if the `HOME` environment variable is set (which is not the normal configuration on Windows). We had previously avoided changing its behavior, out of concern for compatibility with code depending on this non-standard configuration. Given how long this function has been deprecated, we’re now fixing its behavior as a bugfix. A subsequent release will remove the deprecation for this function.

This changed `c_char` from an `i8` to `u8` or vice versa on many Tier 2 and 3
targets (mostly Arm and RISC-V embedded targets). The new definition may
result in compilation failures but fixes compatibility issues with C.

The `libc` crate matches this change as of its 0.2.169 release.

These changes do not affect any public interfaces of Rust, but they represent significant improvements to the performance or internals of rustc and related tools.

Linking on macOS now correctly includes Rust’s default deployment target. Due to a linker bug, you might have to pass `MACOSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET` or fix your `#[link]` attributes to point to the correct frameworks. See [https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/129369](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/129369).

The future incompatibility lint `deprecated_cfg_attr_crate_type_name` [has been made into a hard error](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/129670). It was used to deny usage of `#![crate_type]` and `#![crate_name]` attributes in `#![cfg_attr]`, which required a hack in the compiler to be able to change the used crate type and crate name after cfg expansion.
Users can use `--crate-type` instead of `#![cfg_attr(..., crate_type = "...")]` and `--crate-name` instead of `#![cfg_attr(..., crate_name = "...")]` when running `rustc`/`cargo rustc` on the command line.
Use of those two attributes outside of `#![cfg_attr]` continue to be fully supported.

Until now, paths into the sysroot were always prefixed with `/rustc/$hash` in diagnostics, codegen, backtrace, e.g.

```
thread 'main' panicked at 'hello world', map-panic.rs:2:50
stack backtrace:
   0: std::panicking::begin_panic
             at /rustc/a55dd71d5fb0ec5a6a3a9e8c27b2127ba491ce52/library/std/src/panicking.rs:616:12
   1: map_panic::main::{{closure}}
             at ./map-panic.rs:2:50
   2: core::option::Option<T>::map
             at /rustc/a55dd71d5fb0ec5a6a3a9e8c27b2127ba491ce52/library/core/src/option.rs:929:29
   3: map_panic::main
             at ./map-panic.rs:2:30
   4: core::ops::function::FnOnce::call_once
             at /rustc/a55dd71d5fb0ec5a6a3a9e8c27b2127ba491ce52/library/core/src/ops/function.rs:248:5
note: Some details are omitted, run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=full` for a verbose backtrace.
```
We want to change this behaviour such that, when

`rust-src`source files can be discovered, the virtual path is discarded and therefore the local path will be embedded, unless there is a`--remap-path-prefix`that causes this local path to be remapped in the usual way.

[#129687](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/129687) implements this behaviour, when `rust-src` is present at compile time, `rustc` replaces `/rustc/$hash` with a real path into the local `rust-src` component with best effort.
To sanitize this, users must explicitly supply `--remap-path-prefix=<path to rust-src>=foo` or not have the `rust-src` component installed.

The allow-by-default `missing_docs` lint used to disable itself when invoked through `rustc --test`/`cargo test`, resulting in `#[expect(missing_docs)]` emitting false positives due to the expectation being wrongly unfulfilled. This behavior [has now been removed](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/130025), which allows `#[expect(missing_docs)]` to be fulfilled in all scenarios, but will also report new `missing_docs` diagnostics for publicly reachable `#[cfg(test)]` items, [integration test](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/cargo-targets.html#integration-tests) crate-level documentation, and publicly reachable items in integration tests.

a function with multiple returns in WebAssembly from Rust source code. For the
`reference-types` feature the encoding of immediates in the `call_indirect`, a
commonly used instruction by the WebAssembly backend, has changed. Validators
and parsers which don’t understand the `reference-types` proposal will no
longer accept modules produced by LLVM due to this change in encoding of
immediates. Additionally these features being enabled are encoded in the
`target_features` custom section and may affect downstream tooling such as
`wasm-opt` consuming the module. Generating a WebAssembly module that disables

We have renamed `std::panic::PanicInfo` to `std::panic::PanicHookInfo`. The old name will continue to work as an alias, but will result in a deprecation warning starting in Rust 1.82.0.

`core::panic::PanicInfo` will remain unchanged, however, as this is now a *different type*.

The reason is that these types have different roles: `std::panic::PanicHookInfo` is the argument to the [panic hook](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/panic/fn.set_hook.html) in std context (where panics can have an arbitrary payload), while `core::panic::PanicInfo` is the argument to the [ #[panic_handler]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nomicon/panic-handler.html) in no_std context (where panics always carry a formatted

`std::panic::PanicHookInfo::payload_as_str()` and `core::panic::PanicInfo::message()`.The new sort implementations may panic if a type’s implementation of [ Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/cmp/trait.Ord.html) (or the given comparison function) does not implement a

`Ord`’s supertraits (`PartialOrd`, `Eq`, and `PartialEq`) must also be consistent. The previous implementations would not “notice” any problem, but the new implementations have a good chance of detecting inconsistencies, throwing a panic rather than returning knowingly unsorted data.These changes do not affect any public interfaces of Rust, but they represent significant improvements to the performance or internals of rustc and related tools.

`std::sys::windows::alloc` implementation.`get_blanket_impls`This release disables incremental compilation, unless the user has explicitly opted in via the newly added RUSTC_FORCE_INCREMENTAL=1 environment variable.

This is due to the widespread, and frequently occurring, breakage encountered by
Rust users due to newly enabled incremental verification in 1.52.0. Notably,
Rust users **should** upgrade to 1.52.0 or 1.52.1: the bugs that are detected by
newly added incremental verification are still present in past stable versions,
and are not yet fixed on any channel. These bugs can lead to miscompilation of
Rust binaries.

These problems only affect incremental builds, so release builds with Cargo should not be affected unless the user has explicitly opted into incremental. Debug and check builds are affected.

See [84970](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/84970) for more details.

    let array: Box<[u8; 4]> = Box::new([1, 2, 3, 4]);
    match array {
        nums
//      ---- `nums` is bound by move.
            if nums.iter().sum::<u8>() == 10
//                 ^------ `.iter()` implicitly takes a reference to `nums`.
        => {
            drop(nums);
//          ----------- Legal as `nums` was bound by move and so we have ownership.
        }
        _ => unreachable!(),
    }
}
```

In this guide, we’ll discuss:

- What editions are
- Which changes are contained in each edition
- How to migrate your code from one edition to another

# What is rustc? - The rustc book

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/index.html

Welcome to “The rustc book”! `rustc` is the compiler for the Rust programming
language, provided by the project itself. Compilers take your source code and
produce binary code, either as a library or executable.

Most Rust programmers don’t invoke `rustc` directly, but instead do it through
[Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/index.html). It’s all in service of `rustc` though! If you
want to see how Cargo calls `rustc`, you can

```
$ cargo build --verbose
```
And it will print out each `rustc` invocation. This book can help you
understand what each of these options does. Additionally, while most
Rustaceans use Cargo, not all do: sometimes they integrate `rustc` into other
build systems. This book should provide a guide to all of the options you’d
need to do so.

Let’s say you’ve got a little hello world program in a file `hello.rs`:

```
fn main() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}
```
To turn this source code into an executable, you can use `rustc`:

```
$ rustc hello.rs
$ ./hello # on a *NIX
$ .\hello.exe # on Windows
```
Note that we only ever pass `rustc` the *crate root*, not every file we wish
to compile. For example, if we had a `main.rs` that looked like this:

```
mod foo;
fn main() {
    foo::hello();
}
```
And a `foo.rs` that had this:

```
pub fn hello() {
    println!("Hello, world!");
}
```
To compile this, we’d run this command:

```
$ rustc main.rs
```
No need to tell `rustc` about `foo.rs`; the `mod` statements give it
everything that it needs. This is different than how you would use a C
compiler, where you invoke the compiler on each file, and then link
everything together. In other words, the *crate* is a translation unit, not a
particular module.

# What is rustdoc? - The rustdoc book

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/index.html

The standard Rust distribution ships with a tool called `rustdoc`. Its job is
to generate documentation for Rust projects. On a fundamental level, Rustdoc
takes as an argument either a crate root or a Markdown file, and produces HTML,
CSS, and JavaScript.

Let’s give it a try! Create a new project with Cargo:

```
$ cargo new docs --lib
$ cd docs
```
In `src/lib.rs`, Cargo has generated some sample code. Delete
it and replace it with this:

```
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
/// foo is a function
fn foo() {}
}
```
Let’s run `rustdoc` on our code. To do so, we can call it with the path to
our crate root like this:

```
$ rustdoc src/lib.rs
```
This will create a new directory, `doc`, with a website inside! In our case,
the main page is located in `doc/lib/index.html`. If you open that up in
a web browser, you will see a page with a search bar, and “Crate lib” at the
top, with no contents.

You can also use `cargo doc` to generate documentation for the whole project.
See [Using rustdoc with Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org#using-rustdoc-with-cargo).

There are two problems with this: first, why does it think that our crate is named “lib”? Second, why does it not have any contents?

The first problem is due to `rustdoc` trying to be helpful; like `rustc`,
it assumes that our crate’s name is the name of the file for the crate
root. To fix this, we can pass in a command-line flag:

```
$ rustdoc src/lib.rs --crate-name docs
```
Now, `doc/docs/index.html` will be generated, and the page says “Crate docs.”

For the second issue, it is because our function `foo` is not public; `rustdoc`
defaults to generating documentation for only public functions. If we change
our code…

```
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
/// foo is a function
pub fn foo() {}
}
```
… and then re-run `rustdoc`:

```
$ rustdoc src/lib.rs --crate-name docs
```
We now have some generated documentation. Open up `doc/docs/index.html` and
check it out! It should show a link to the `foo` function’s page, which
is located at `doc/docs/fn.foo.html`. On that page, you’ll see the “foo is
a function” we put inside the documentation comment in our crate.

Cargo also has integration with `rustdoc` to make it easier to generate
docs. Instead of the `rustdoc` command, we could have done this:

```
$ cargo doc
```
If you want `cargo` to automatically open the generated documentation, you can use:

```
$ cargo doc --open
```
Internally, `cargo doc` calls out to `rustdoc` like this:

```
$ rustdoc --crate-name docs src/lib.rs -o <path>/docs/target/doc -L
dependency=<path>/docs/target/debug/deps
```
You can see this with `cargo doc --verbose`.

It generates the correct `--crate-name` for us, as well as pointing to
`src/lib.rs`. But what about those other arguments?

- `-o`controls the- *o*utput of our docs. Instead of a top-level- `doc`directory, notice that Cargo puts generated documentation under- `target`. That is the idiomatic place for generated files in Cargo projects.
- `-L`flag helps rustdoc find the dependencies your code relies on. If our project used dependencies, we would get documentation for them as well!

The `///` syntax is used to document the item present after it.
That’s why it is called an outer documentation.
There is another syntax: `//!`, which is used to document the
item it is present inside. It is called an inner documentation.
It is often used when documenting the entire crate,
because nothing comes before it: it is the root of the crate.
So in order to document an entire crate, you need to use `//!` syntax.
For example:

```
#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
//! This is my first rust crate
}
```
When used in the crate root, it documents the item it is inside, which is the crate itself.

For more information about the `//!` syntax, see [the Book](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch14-02-publishing-to-crates-io.html#commenting-contained-items).

`rustdoc` can also generate HTML from standalone Markdown files. Let’ s
give it a try: create a `README.md` file with these contents:

```
# Docs
This is a project to test out `rustdoc`.
[Here is a link!](https://www.rust-lang.org)
## Example
```rust
fn foo() -> i32 {
    1 + 1
}
```
```
And call `rustdoc` on it:

```
$ rustdoc README.md
```
You will find an HTML file in `docs/doc/README.html` generated from its
Markdown contents.

Cargo currently does not understand standalone Markdown files, unfortunately.

This covers the simplest use-cases of `rustdoc`. The rest of this book will
explain all of the options that `rustdoc` has, and how to use them.
