# std/lib.rs

[1](https://doc.rust-lang.org#1)//! # The Rust Standard Library
[2](https://doc.rust-lang.org#2)//!
[3](https://doc.rust-lang.org#3)//! The Rust Standard Library is the foundation of portable Rust software, a
[4](https://doc.rust-lang.org#4)//! set of minimal and battle-tested shared abstractions for the [broader Rust
[5](https://doc.rust-lang.org#5)//! ecosystem][crates.io]. It offers core types, like [`Vec<T>`] and
[6](https://doc.rust-lang.org#6)//! [`Option<T>`], library-defined [operations on language
[7](https://doc.rust-lang.org#7)//! primitives](#primitives), [standard macros](#macros), [I/O] and
[8](https://doc.rust-lang.org#8)//! [multithreading], among [many other things][other].
[9](https://doc.rust-lang.org#9)//!
[10](https://doc.rust-lang.org#10)//! `std` is available to all Rust crates by default. Therefore, the
[11](https://doc.rust-lang.org#11)//! standard library can be accessed in [`use`] statements through the path
[12](https://doc.rust-lang.org#12)//! `std`, as in [`use std::env`].
[13](https://doc.rust-lang.org#13)//!
[14](https://doc.rust-lang.org#14)//! # How to read this documentation
[15](https://doc.rust-lang.org#15)//!
[16](https://doc.rust-lang.org#16)//! If you already know the name of what you are looking for, the fastest way to
[17](https://doc.rust-lang.org#17)//! find it is to use the <a href="#" onclick="window.searchState.focus();">search
[18](https://doc.rust-lang.org#18)//! button</a> at the top of the page.
[19](https://doc.rust-lang.org#19)//!
[20](https://doc.rust-lang.org#20)//! Otherwise, you may want to jump to one of these useful sections:
[21](https://doc.rust-lang.org#21)//!
[22](https://doc.rust-lang.org#22)//! * [`std::*` modules](#modules)
[23](https://doc.rust-lang.org#23)//! * [Primitive types](#primitives)
[24](https://doc.rust-lang.org#24)//! * [Standard macros](#macros)
[25](https://doc.rust-lang.org#25)//! * [The Rust Prelude]
[26](https://doc.rust-lang.org#26)//!
[27](https://doc.rust-lang.org#27)//! If this is your first time, the documentation for the standard library is
[28](https://doc.rust-lang.org#28)//! written to be casually perused. Clicking on interesting things should
[29](https://doc.rust-lang.org#29)//! generally lead you to interesting places. Still, there are important bits
[30](https://doc.rust-lang.org#30)//! you don't want to miss, so read on for a tour of the standard library and
[31](https://doc.rust-lang.org#31)//! its documentation!
[32](https://doc.rust-lang.org#32)//!
[33](https://doc.rust-lang.org#33)//! Once you are familiar with the contents of the standard library you may
[34](https://doc.rust-lang.org#34)//! begin to find the verbosity of the prose distracting. At this stage in your
[35](https://doc.rust-lang.org#35)//! development you may want to press the
[36](https://doc.rust-lang.org#36)//! "<svg style="width:0.75rem;height:0.75rem" viewBox="0 0 12 12" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><path d="M2,2l4,4l4,-4M2,6l4,4l4,-4"/></svg> Summary"
[37](https://doc.rust-lang.org#37)//! button near the top of the page to collapse it into a more skimmable view.
[38](https://doc.rust-lang.org#38)//!
[39](https://doc.rust-lang.org#39)//! While you are looking at the top of the page, also notice the
[40](https://doc.rust-lang.org#40)//! "Source" link. Rust's API documentation comes with the source
[41](https://doc.rust-lang.org#41)//! code and you are encouraged to read it. The standard library source is
[42](https://doc.rust-lang.org#42)//! generally high quality and a peek behind the curtains is
[43](https://doc.rust-lang.org#43)//! often enlightening.
[44](https://doc.rust-lang.org#44)//!
[45](https://doc.rust-lang.org#45)//! # What is in the standard library documentation?
[46](https://doc.rust-lang.org#46)//!
[47](https://doc.rust-lang.org#47)//! First of all, The Rust Standard Library is divided into a number of focused
[48](https://doc.rust-lang.org#48)//! modules, [all listed further down this page](#modules). These modules are
[49](https://doc.rust-lang.org#49)//! the bedrock upon which all of Rust is forged, and they have mighty names
[50](https://doc.rust-lang.org#50)//! like [`std::slice`] and [`std::cmp`]. Modules' documentation typically
[51](https://doc.rust-lang.org#51)//! includes an overview of the module along with examples, and are a smart
[52](https://doc.rust-lang.org#52)//! place to start familiarizing yourself with the library.
[53](https://doc.rust-lang.org#53)//!
[54](https://doc.rust-lang.org#54)//! Second, implicit methods on [primitive types] are documented here. This can
[55](https://doc.rust-lang.org#55)//! be a source of confusion for two reasons:
[56](https://doc.rust-lang.org#56)//!
[57](https://doc.rust-lang.org#57)//! 1. While primitives are implemented by the compiler, the standard library
[58](https://doc.rust-lang.org#58)//!    implements methods directly on the primitive types (and it is the only
[59](https://doc.rust-lang.org#59)//!    library that does so), which are [documented in the section on
[60](https://doc.rust-lang.org#60)//!    primitives](#primitives).
[61](https://doc.rust-lang.org#61)//! 2. The standard library exports many modules *with the same name as
[62](https://doc.rust-lang.org#62)//!    primitive types*. These define additional items related to the primitive
[63](https://doc.rust-lang.org#63)//!    type, but not the all-important methods.
[64](https://doc.rust-lang.org#64)//!
[65](https://doc.rust-lang.org#65)//! So for example there is a [page for the primitive type
[66](https://doc.rust-lang.org#66)//! `char`](primitive::char) that lists all the methods that can be called on
[67](https://doc.rust-lang.org#67)//! characters (very useful), and there is a [page for the module
[68](https://doc.rust-lang.org#68)//! `std::char`](crate::char) that documents iterator and error types created by these methods
[69](https://doc.rust-lang.org#69)//! (rarely useful).
[70](https://doc.rust-lang.org#70)//!
[71](https://doc.rust-lang.org#71)//! Note the documentation for the primitives [`str`] and [`[T]`][prim@slice] (also
[72](https://doc.rust-lang.org#72)//! called 'slice'). Many method calls on [`String`] and [`Vec<T>`] are actually
[73](https://doc.rust-lang.org#73)//! calls to methods on [`str`] and [`[T]`][prim@slice] respectively, via [deref
[74](https://doc.rust-lang.org#74)//! coercions][deref-coercions].
[75](https://doc.rust-lang.org#75)//!
[76](https://doc.rust-lang.org#76)//! Third, the standard library defines [The Rust Prelude], a small collection
[77](https://doc.rust-lang.org#77)//! of items - mostly traits - that are imported into every module of every
[78](https://doc.rust-lang.org#78)//! crate. The traits in the prelude are pervasive, making the prelude
[79](https://doc.rust-lang.org#79)//! documentation a good entry point to learning about the library.
[80](https://doc.rust-lang.org#80)//!
[81](https://doc.rust-lang.org#81)//! And finally, the standard library exports a number of standard macros, and
[82](https://doc.rust-lang.org#82)//! [lists them on this page](#macros) (technically, not all of the standard
[83](https://doc.rust-lang.org#83)//! macros are defined by the standard library - some are defined by the
[84](https://doc.rust-lang.org#84)//! compiler - but they are documented here the same). Like the prelude, the
[85](https://doc.rust-lang.org#85)//! standard macros are imported by default into all crates.
[86](https://doc.rust-lang.org#86)//!
[87](https://doc.rust-lang.org#87)//! # Contributing changes to the documentation
[88](https://doc.rust-lang.org#88)//!
[89](https://doc.rust-lang.org#89)//! Check out the Rust contribution guidelines [here](
[90](https://doc.rust-lang.org#90)//! https://rustc-dev-guide.rust-lang.org/contributing.html#writing-documentation).
[91](https://doc.rust-lang.org#91)//! The source for this documentation can be found on
[92](https://doc.rust-lang.org#92)//! [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust) in the 'library/std/' directory.
[93](https://doc.rust-lang.org#93)//! To contribute changes, make sure you read the guidelines first, then submit
[94](https://doc.rust-lang.org#94)//! pull-requests for your suggested changes.
[95](https://doc.rust-lang.org#95)//!
[96](https://doc.rust-lang.org#96)//! Contributions are appreciated! If you see a part of the docs that can be
[97](https://doc.rust-lang.org#97)//! improved, submit a PR, or chat with us first on [Zulip][t-libs-zulip]
[98](https://doc.rust-lang.org#98)//! #t-libs.
[99](https://doc.rust-lang.org#99)//!
[100](https://doc.rust-lang.org#100)//! # A Tour of The Rust Standard Library
[101](https://doc.rust-lang.org#101)//!
[102](https://doc.rust-lang.org#102)//! The rest of this crate documentation is dedicated to pointing out notable
[103](https://doc.rust-lang.org#103)//! features of The Rust Standard Library.
[104](https://doc.rust-lang.org#104)//!
[105](https://doc.rust-lang.org#105)//! ## Containers and collections
[106](https://doc.rust-lang.org#106)//!
[107](https://doc.rust-lang.org#107)//! The [`option`] and [`result`] modules define optional and error-handling
[108](https://doc.rust-lang.org#108)//! types, [`Option<T>`] and [`Result<T, E>`]. The [`iter`] module defines
[109](https://doc.rust-lang.org#109)//! Rust's iterator trait, [`Iterator`], which works with the [`for`] loop to
[110](https://doc.rust-lang.org#110)//! access collections.
[111](https://doc.rust-lang.org#111)//!
[112](https://doc.rust-lang.org#112)//! The standard library exposes three common ways to deal with contiguous
[113](https://doc.rust-lang.org#113)//! regions of memory:
[114](https://doc.rust-lang.org#114)//!
[115](https://doc.rust-lang.org#115)//! * [`Vec<T>`] - A heap-allocated *vector* that is resizable at runtime.
[116](https://doc.rust-lang.org#116)//! * [`[T; N]`][prim@array] - An inline *array* with a fixed size at compile time.
[117](https://doc.rust-lang.org#117)//! * [`[T]`][prim@slice] - A dynamically sized *slice* into any other kind of contiguous
[118](https://doc.rust-lang.org#118)//!   storage, whether heap-allocated or not.
[119](https://doc.rust-lang.org#119)//!
[120](https://doc.rust-lang.org#120)//! Slices can only be handled through some kind of *pointer*, and as such come
[121](https://doc.rust-lang.org#121)//! in many flavors such as:
[122](https://doc.rust-lang.org#122)//!
[123](https://doc.rust-lang.org#123)//! * `&[T]` - *shared slice*
[124](https://doc.rust-lang.org#124)//! * `&mut [T]` - *mutable slice*
[125](https://doc.rust-lang.org#125)//! * [`Box<[T]>`][owned slice] - *owned slice*
[126](https://doc.rust-lang.org#126)//!
[127](https://doc.rust-lang.org#127)//! [`str`], a UTF-8 string slice, is a primitive type, and the standard library
[128](https://doc.rust-lang.org#128)//! defines many methods for it. Rust [`str`]s are typically accessed as
[129](https://doc.rust-lang.org#129)//! immutable references: `&str`. Use the owned [`String`] for building and
[130](https://doc.rust-lang.org#130)//! mutating strings.
[131](https://doc.rust-lang.org#131)//!
[132](https://doc.rust-lang.org#132)//! For converting to strings use the [`format!`] macro, and for converting from
[133](https://doc.rust-lang.org#133)//! strings use the [`FromStr`] trait.
[134](https://doc.rust-lang.org#134)//!
[135](https://doc.rust-lang.org#135)//! Data may be shared by placing it in a reference-counted box or the [`Rc`]
[136](https://doc.rust-lang.org#136)//! type, and if further contained in a [`Cell`] or [`RefCell`], may be mutated
[137](https://doc.rust-lang.org#137)//! as well as shared. Likewise, in a concurrent setting it is common to pair an
[138](https://doc.rust-lang.org#138)//! atomically-reference-counted box, [`Arc`], with a [`Mutex`] to get the same
[139](https://doc.rust-lang.org#139)//! effect.
[140](https://doc.rust-lang.org#140)//!
[141](https://doc.rust-lang.org#141)//! The [`collections`] module defines maps, sets, linked lists and other
[142](https://doc.rust-lang.org#142)//! typical collection types, including the common [`HashMap<K, V>`].
[143](https://doc.rust-lang.org#143)//!
[144](https://doc.rust-lang.org#144)//! ## Platform abstractions and I/O
[145](https://doc.rust-lang.org#145)//!
[146](https://doc.rust-lang.org#146)//! Besides basic data types, the standard library is largely concerned with
[147](https://doc.rust-lang.org#147)//! abstracting over differences in common platforms, most notably Windows and
[148](https://doc.rust-lang.org#148)//! Unix derivatives.
[149](https://doc.rust-lang.org#149)//!
[150](https://doc.rust-lang.org#150)//! Common types of I/O, including [files], [TCP], and [UDP], are defined in
[151](https://doc.rust-lang.org#151)//! the [`io`], [`fs`], and [`net`] modules.
[152](https://doc.rust-lang.org#152)//!
[153](https://doc.rust-lang.org#153)//! The [`thread`] module contains Rust's threading abstractions. [`sync`]
[154](https://doc.rust-lang.org#154)//! contains further primitive shared memory types, including [`atomic`], [`mpmc`] and
[155](https://doc.rust-lang.org#155)//! [`mpsc`], which contains the channel types for message passing.
[156](https://doc.rust-lang.org#156)//!
[157](https://doc.rust-lang.org#157)//! # Use before and after `main()`
[158](https://doc.rust-lang.org#158)//!
[159](https://doc.rust-lang.org#159)//! Many parts of the standard library are expected to work before and after `main()`;
[160](https://doc.rust-lang.org#160)//! but this is not guaranteed or ensured by tests. It is recommended that you write your own tests
[161](https://doc.rust-lang.org#161)//! and run them on each platform you wish to support.
[162](https://doc.rust-lang.org#162)//! This means that use of `std` before/after main, especially of features that interact with the
[163](https://doc.rust-lang.org#163)//! OS or global state, is exempted from stability and portability guarantees and instead only
[164](https://doc.rust-lang.org#164)//! provided on a best-effort basis. Nevertheless bug reports are appreciated.
[165](https://doc.rust-lang.org#165)//!
[166](https://doc.rust-lang.org#166)//! On the other hand `core` and `alloc` are most likely to work in such environments with
[167](https://doc.rust-lang.org#167)//! the caveat that any hookable behavior such as panics, oom handling or allocators will also
[168](https://doc.rust-lang.org#168)//! depend on the compatibility of the hooks.
[169](https://doc.rust-lang.org#169)//!
[170](https://doc.rust-lang.org#170)//! Some features may also behave differently outside main, e.g. stdio could become unbuffered,
[171](https://doc.rust-lang.org#171)//! some panics might turn into aborts, backtraces might not get symbolicated or similar.
[172](https://doc.rust-lang.org#172)//!
[173](https://doc.rust-lang.org#173)//! Non-exhaustive list of known limitations:
[174](https://doc.rust-lang.org#174)//!
[175](https://doc.rust-lang.org#175)//! - after-main use of thread-locals, which also affects additional features:
[176](https://doc.rust-lang.org#176)//!   - [`thread::current()`]
[177](https://doc.rust-lang.org#177)//! - under UNIX, before main, file descriptors 0, 1, and 2 may be unchanged
[178](https://doc.rust-lang.org#178)//!   (they are guaranteed to be open during main,
[179](https://doc.rust-lang.org#179)//!    and are opened to /dev/null O_RDWR if they weren't open on program start)
[180](https://doc.rust-lang.org#180)//!
[181](https://doc.rust-lang.org#181)//!

[429](https://doc.rust-lang.org#429)// Explicitly import the prelude. The compiler uses this same unstable attribute
[430](https://doc.rust-lang.org#430)// to import the prelude implicitly when building crates that depend on std.
[431](https://doc.rust-lang.org#431)#[prelude_import]

[455](https://doc.rust-lang.org#455)// FIXME: #94122 this extern crate definition only exist here to stop
[456](https://doc.rust-lang.org#456)// miniz_oxide docs leaking into std docs. Find better way to do it.
[457](https://doc.rust-lang.org#457)// Remove exclusion from tidy platform check when this removed.

[459](https://doc.rust-lang.org#459)#[allow(unused_extern_crates)]
[460](https://doc.rust-lang.org#460)#[cfg(all(
[461](https://doc.rust-lang.org#461)    not(all(windows, target_env = "msvc", not(target_vendor = "uwp"))),
[462](https://doc.rust-lang.org#462)    feature = "miniz_oxide"
[463](https://doc.rust-lang.org#463)))]
[464](https://doc.rust-lang.org#464)extern crate miniz_oxide;
[465](https://doc.rust-lang.org#465)
[466](https://doc.rust-lang.org#466)// During testing, this crate is not actually the "real" std library, but rather
[467](https://doc.rust-lang.org#467)// it links to the real std library, which was compiled from this same source
[468](https://doc.rust-lang.org#468)// code. So any lang items std defines are conditionally excluded (or else they
[469](https://doc.rust-lang.org#469)// would generate duplicate lang item errors), and any globals it defines are
[470](https://doc.rust-lang.org#470)// _not_ the globals used by "real" std. So this import, defined only during
[471](https://doc.rust-lang.org#471)// testing gives test-std access to real-std lang items and globals. See #2912
[472](https://doc.rust-lang.org#472)#[cfg(test)]
[473](https://doc.rust-lang.org#473)extern crate std as realstd;

# Vec in std::vec - Rust

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/vec/struct.Vec.html

`pub struct Vec<T, A = `[Global](https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/struct.Global.html)>{ /* private fields */ }## Expand description

A contiguous growable array type, written as `Vec<T>`, short for ‘vector’.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples)Examples

```
let mut vec = Vec::new();
vec.push(1);
vec.push(2);
assert_eq!(vec.len(), 2);
assert_eq!(vec[0], 1);
assert_eq!(vec.pop(), Some(2));
assert_eq!(vec.len(), 1);
vec[0] = 7;
assert_eq!(vec[0], 7);
vec.extend([1, 2, 3]);
for x in &vec {
    println!("{x}");
}
assert_eq!(vec, [7, 1, 2, 3]);
```
The [ vec!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.vec.html) macro is provided for convenient initialization:

```
let mut vec1 = vec![1, 2, 3];
vec1.push(4);
let vec2 = Vec::from([1, 2, 3, 4]);
assert_eq!(vec1, vec2);
```
It can also initialize each element of a `Vec<T>` with a given value.
This may be more efficient than performing allocation and initialization
in separate steps, especially when initializing a vector of zeros:

```
let vec = vec![0; 5];
assert_eq!(vec, [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]);
// The following is equivalent, but potentially slower:
let mut vec = Vec::with_capacity(5);
vec.resize(5, 0);
assert_eq!(vec, [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]);
```
For more information, see
[Capacity and Reallocation](https://doc.rust-lang.org#capacity-and-reallocation).

Use a `Vec<T>` as an efficient stack:

```
let mut stack = Vec::new();
stack.push(1);
stack.push(2);
stack.push(3);
while let Some(top) = stack.pop() {
    // Prints 3, 2, 1
    println!("{top}");
}
```
[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#indexing)Indexing

The `Vec` type allows access to values by index, because it implements the
[ Index](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ops/trait.Index.html) trait. An example will be more explicit:

However be careful: if you try to access an index which isn’t in the `Vec`,
your software will panic! You cannot do this:

Use [ get](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html#method.get) and

[if you want to check whether the index is in the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html#method.get_mut)

`get_mut``Vec`.[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#slicing)Slicing

A `Vec` can be mutable. On the other hand, slices are read-only objects.
To get a [slice](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html), use [ &](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.reference.html). Example:

```
fn read_slice(slice: &[usize]) {
    // ...
}
let v = vec![0, 1];
read_slice(&v);
// ... and that's all!
// you can also do it like this:
let u: &[usize] = &v;
// or like this:
let u: &[_] = &v;
```
In Rust, it’s more common to pass slices as arguments rather than vectors
when you just want to provide read access. The same goes for [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/string/struct.String.html) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html)

`&str`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#capacity-and-reallocation)Capacity and reallocation

The capacity of a vector is the amount of space allocated for any future
elements that will be added onto the vector. This is not to be confused with
the *length* of a vector, which specifies the number of actual elements
within the vector. If a vector’s length exceeds its capacity, its capacity
will automatically be increased, but its elements will have to be
reallocated.

For example, a vector with capacity 10 and length 0 would be an empty vector
with space for 10 more elements. Pushing 10 or fewer elements onto the
vector will not change its capacity or cause reallocation to occur. However,
if the vector’s length is increased to 11, it will have to reallocate, which
can be slow. For this reason, it is recommended to use [ Vec::with_capacity](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.with_capacity)
whenever possible to specify how big the vector is expected to get.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#guarantees)Guarantees

Due to its incredibly fundamental nature, `Vec` makes a lot of guarantees
about its design. This ensures that it’s as low-overhead as possible in
the general case, and can be correctly manipulated in primitive ways
by unsafe code. Note that these guarantees refer to an unqualified `Vec<T>`.
If additional type parameters are added (e.g., to support custom allocators),
overriding their defaults may change the behavior.

Most fundamentally, `Vec` is and always will be a (pointer, capacity, length)
triplet. No more, no less. The order of these fields is completely
unspecified, and you should use the appropriate methods to modify these.
The pointer will never be null, so this type is null-pointer-optimized.

However, the pointer might not actually point to allocated memory. In particular,
if you construct a `Vec` with capacity 0 via [ Vec::new](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.new),

[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/macro.vec.html)

`vec![]`[, or by calling](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.with_capacity)

`Vec::with_capacity(0)`[on an empty Vec, it will not allocate memory. Similarly, if you store zero-sized types inside a](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.shrink_to_fit)

`shrink_to_fit``Vec`, it will not allocate space for them. *Note that in this case the*.

`Vec` might not report a [of 0](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.capacity)`capacity``Vec` will allocate if and only
if [size_of::<T>](https://doc.rust-lang.org/mem/fn.size_of.html)() * [capacity](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.capacity)() > 0`Vec`’s allocation
details are very subtle — if you intend to allocate memory using a `Vec`
and use it for something else (either to pass to unsafe code, or to build your
own memory-backed collection), be sure to deallocate this memory by using
`from_raw_parts` to recover the `Vec` and then dropping it.If a `Vec` *has* allocated memory, then the memory it points to is on the heap
(as defined by the allocator Rust is configured to use by default), and its
pointer points to [ len](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.len) initialized, contiguous elements in order (what
you would see if you coerced it to a slice), followed by

[capacity](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.capacity) - [len](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.len)A vector containing the elements `'a'` and `'b'` with capacity 4 can be
visualized as below. The top part is the `Vec` struct, it contains a
pointer to the head of the allocation in the heap, length and capacity.
The bottom part is the allocation on the heap, a contiguous memory block.

```
            ptr      len  capacity
       +--------+--------+--------+
       | 0x0123 |      2 |      4 |
       +--------+--------+--------+
            |
            v
Heap   +--------+--------+--------+--------+
       |    'a' |    'b' | uninit | uninit |
       +--------+--------+--------+--------+
```
- **uninit**represents memory that is not initialized, see- `MaybeUninit`
- Note: the ABI is not stable and `Vec`makes no guarantees about its memory layout (including the order of fields).

`Vec` will never perform a “small optimization” where elements are actually
stored on the stack for two reasons:

-
It would make it more difficult for unsafe code to correctly manipulate a `Vec`. The contents of a`Vec`wouldn’t have a stable address if it were only moved, and it would be more difficult to determine if a`Vec`had actually allocated memory.
-
It would penalize the general case, incurring an additional branch on every access.

`Vec` will never automatically shrink itself, even if completely empty. This
ensures no unnecessary allocations or deallocations occur. Emptying a `Vec`
and then filling it back up to the same [ len](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.len) should incur no calls to
the allocator. If you wish to free up unused memory, use

[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.shrink_to_fit)

`shrink_to_fit`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.shrink_to)

`shrink_to`[ push](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.push) and

[will never (re)allocate if the reported capacity is sufficient.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.insert)

`insert`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.push)

`push`

`insert`*will*(re)allocate if

[len](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.len) == [capacity](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.capacity)`Vec` if desired. Bulk insertion methods *may*reallocate, even when not necessary.

`Vec` does not guarantee any particular growth strategy when reallocating
when full, nor when [ reserve](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.reserve) is called. The current strategy is basic
and it may prove desirable to use a non-constant growth factor. Whatever
strategy is used will of course guarantee

*O*(1) amortized

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.push)

`push`It is guaranteed, in order to respect the intentions of the programmer, that
all of `vec![e_1, e_2, ..., e_n]`, `vec![x; n]`, and [ Vec::with_capacity(n)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.with_capacity) produce a

`Vec`
that requests an allocation of the exact size needed for precisely `n` elements from the allocator,
and no other size (such as, for example: a size rounded up to the nearest power of 2).
The allocator will return an allocation that is at least as large as requested, but it may be larger.It is guaranteed that the [ Vec::capacity](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.capacity) method returns a value that is at least the requested capacity
and not more than the allocated capacity.

The method [ Vec::shrink_to_fit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.shrink_to_fit) will attempt to discard excess capacity an allocator has given to a

`Vec`.
If [len](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.len) == [capacity](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.capacity)`Vec<T>` can be converted
to and from a [without reallocating or moving the elements.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/boxed/struct.Box.html)

`Box<[T]>``Vec` exploits this fact as much as reasonable when implementing common conversions
such as [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.into_boxed_slice)

`into_boxed_slice``Vec` will not specifically overwrite any data that is removed from it,
but also won’t specifically preserve it. Its uninitialized memory is
scratch space that it may use however it wants. It will generally just do
whatever is most efficient or otherwise easy to implement. Do not rely on
removed data to be erased for security purposes. Even if you drop a `Vec`, its
buffer may simply be reused by another allocation. Even if you zero a `Vec`’s memory
first, that might not actually happen because the optimizer does not consider
this a side-effect that must be preserved. There is one case which we will
not break, however: using `unsafe` code to write to the excess capacity,
and then increasing the length to match, is always valid.

Currently, `Vec` does not guarantee the order in which elements are dropped.
The order has changed in the past and may change again.

1.0.0 (const: [unstable](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/79597)) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#523)#### pub fn [with_capacity](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.with_capacity)(capacity: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html)<T>

[unstable](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/79597)) ·

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#523)

#### pub fn [with_capacity](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.with_capacity)(capacity: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html)<T>

Constructs a new, empty `Vec<T>` with at least the specified capacity.

The vector will be able to hold at least `capacity` elements without
reallocating. This method is allowed to allocate for more elements than
`capacity`. If `capacity` is zero, the vector will not allocate.

It is important to note that although the returned vector has the
minimum *capacity* specified, the vector will have a zero *length*. For
an explanation of the difference between length and capacity, see
* Capacity and reallocation*.

If it is important to know the exact allocated capacity of a `Vec`,
always use the [ capacity](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.capacity) method after construction.

For `Vec<T>` where `T` is a zero-sized type, there will be no allocation
and the capacity will always be `usize::MAX`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics)Panics

Panics if the new capacity exceeds `isize::MAX` *bytes*.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-2)Examples

```
let mut vec = Vec::with_capacity(10);
// The vector contains no items, even though it has capacity for more
assert_eq!(vec.len(), 0);
assert!(vec.capacity() >= 10);
// These are all done without reallocating...
for i in 0..10 {
    vec.push(i);
}
assert_eq!(vec.len(), 10);
assert!(vec.capacity() >= 10);
// ...but this may make the vector reallocate
vec.push(11);
assert_eq!(vec.len(), 11);
assert!(vec.capacity() >= 11);
// A vector of a zero-sized type will always over-allocate, since no
// allocation is necessary
let vec_units = Vec::<()>::with_capacity(10);
assert_eq!(vec_units.capacity(), usize::MAX);
```

#### pub unsafe fn [from_raw_parts](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.from_raw_parts)(
    ptr: [*mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html),
    length: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html),
    capacity: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html),
) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html)<T>

Creates a `Vec<T>` directly from a pointer, a length, and a capacity.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety)Safety

This is highly unsafe, due to the number of invariants that aren’t checked:

- If `T`is not a zero-sized type and the capacity is nonzero,`ptr`must have been allocated using the global allocator, such as via the`alloc::alloc``T`is a zero-sized type or the capacity is zero,`ptr`need only be non-null and aligned.
- `T`needs to have the same alignment as what- `ptr`was allocated with, if the pointer is required to be allocated. (- `T`having a less strict alignment is not sufficient, the alignment really needs to be equal to satisfy the- `dealloc`
- The size of `T`times the`capacity`(i.e. the allocated size in bytes), if nonzero, needs to be the same size as the pointer was allocated with. (Because similar to alignment,`dealloc``size`.)
- `length`needs to be less than or equal to- `capacity`.
- The first `length`values must be properly initialized values of type`T`.
- `capacity`needs to be the capacity that the pointer was allocated with, if the pointer is required to be allocated.
- The allocated size in bytes must be no larger than `isize::MAX`. See the safety documentation of`pointer::offset`

These requirements are always upheld by any `ptr` that has been allocated
via `Vec<T>`. Other allocation sources are allowed if the invariants are
upheld.

Violating these may cause problems like corrupting the allocator’s
internal data structures. For example it is normally **not** safe
to build a `Vec<u8>` from a pointer to a C `char` array with length
`size_t`, doing so is only safe if the array was initially allocated by
a `Vec` or `String`.
It’s also not safe to build one from a `Vec<u16>` and its length, because
the allocator cares about the alignment, and these two types have different
alignments. The buffer was allocated with alignment 2 (for `u16`), but after
turning it into a `Vec<u8>` it’ll be deallocated with alignment 1. To avoid
these issues, it is often preferable to do casting/transmuting using
[ slice::from_raw_parts](https://doc.rust-lang.org/slice/fn.from_raw_parts.html) instead.

The ownership of `ptr` is effectively transferred to the
`Vec<T>` which may then deallocate, reallocate or change the
contents of memory pointed to by the pointer at will. Ensure
that nothing else uses the pointer after calling this
function.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-3)Examples

```
use std::ptr;
let v = vec![1, 2, 3];
// Deconstruct the vector into parts.
let (p, len, cap) = v.into_raw_parts();
unsafe {
    // Overwrite memory with 4, 5, 6
    for i in 0..len {
        ptr::write(p.add(i), 4 + i);
    }
    // Put everything back together into a Vec
    let rebuilt = Vec::from_raw_parts(p, len, cap);
    assert_eq!(rebuilt, [4, 5, 6]);
}
```
Using memory that was allocated elsewhere:

```
use std::alloc::{alloc, Layout};
fn main() {
    let layout = Layout::array::<u32>(16).expect("overflow cannot happen");
    let vec = unsafe {
        let mem = alloc(layout).cast::<u32>();
        if mem.is_null() {
            return;
        }
        mem.write(1_000_000);
        Vec::from_raw_parts(mem, 1, 16)
    };
    assert_eq!(vec, &[1_000_000]);
    assert_eq!(vec.capacity(), 16);
}
```
Creates a `Vec<T>` directly from a `NonNull` pointer, a length, and a capacity.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety-1)Safety

This is highly unsafe, due to the number of invariants that aren’t checked:

- `ptr`must have been allocated using the global allocator, such as via the- `alloc::alloc`
- `T`needs to have the same alignment as what- `ptr`was allocated with. (- `T`having a less strict alignment is not sufficient, the alignment really needs to be equal to satisfy the- `dealloc`
- The size of `T`times the`capacity`(i.e. the allocated size in bytes) needs to be the same size as the pointer was allocated with. (Because similar to alignment,`dealloc``size`.)
- `length`needs to be less than or equal to- `capacity`.
- The first `length`values must be properly initialized values of type`T`.
- `capacity`needs to be the capacity that the pointer was allocated with.
- The allocated size in bytes must be no larger than `isize::MAX`. See the safety documentation of`pointer::offset`

These requirements are always upheld by any `ptr` that has been allocated
via `Vec<T>`. Other allocation sources are allowed if the invariants are
upheld.

Violating these may cause problems like corrupting the allocator’s
internal data structures. For example it is normally **not** safe
to build a `Vec<u8>` from a pointer to a C `char` array with length
`size_t`, doing so is only safe if the array was initially allocated by
a `Vec` or `String`.
It’s also not safe to build one from a `Vec<u16>` and its length, because
the allocator cares about the alignment, and these two types have different
alignments. The buffer was allocated with alignment 2 (for `u16`), but after
turning it into a `Vec<u8>` it’ll be deallocated with alignment 1. To avoid
these issues, it is often preferable to do casting/transmuting using
[ NonNull::slice_from_raw_parts](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/struct.NonNull.html#method.slice_from_raw_parts) instead.

The ownership of `ptr` is effectively transferred to the
`Vec<T>` which may then deallocate, reallocate or change the
contents of memory pointed to by the pointer at will. Ensure
that nothing else uses the pointer after calling this
function.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-4)Examples

```
#![feature(box_vec_non_null)]
let v = vec![1, 2, 3];
// Deconstruct the vector into parts.
let (p, len, cap) = v.into_parts();
unsafe {
    // Overwrite memory with 4, 5, 6
    for i in 0..len {
        p.add(i).write(4 + i);
    }
    // Put everything back together into a Vec
    let rebuilt = Vec::from_parts(p, len, cap);
    assert_eq!(rebuilt, [4, 5, 6]);
}
```
Using memory that was allocated elsewhere:

```
#![feature(box_vec_non_null)]
use std::alloc::{alloc, Layout};
use std::ptr::NonNull;
fn main() {
    let layout = Layout::array::<u32>(16).expect("overflow cannot happen");
    let vec = unsafe {
        let Some(mem) = NonNull::new(alloc(layout).cast::<u32>()) else {
            return;
        };
        mem.write(1_000_000);
        Vec::from_parts(mem, 1, 16)
    };
    assert_eq!(vec, &[1_000_000]);
    assert_eq!(vec.capacity(), 16);
}
```
Creates a `Vec<T>` where each element is produced by calling `f` with
that element’s index while walking forward through the `Vec<T>`.

This is essentially the same as writing

`vec![f(0), f(1), f(2), …, f(length - 2), f(length - 1)]`and is similar to `(0..i).map(f)`, just for `Vec<T>`s not iterators.

If `length == 0`, this produces an empty `Vec<T>` without ever calling `f`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#example)Example

```
#![feature(vec_from_fn)]
let vec = Vec::from_fn(5, |i| i);
// indexes are:  0  1  2  3  4
assert_eq!(vec, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]);
let vec2 = Vec::from_fn(8, |i| i * 2);
// indexes are:   0  1  2  3  4  5   6   7
assert_eq!(vec2, [0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14]);
let bool_vec = Vec::from_fn(5, |i| i % 2 == 0);
// indexes are:       0     1      2     3      4
assert_eq!(bool_vec, [true, false, true, false, true]);
```
The `Vec<T>` is generated in ascending index order, starting from the front
and going towards the back, so you can use closures with mutable state:

Decomposes a `Vec<T>` into its raw components: `(pointer, length, capacity)`.

Returns the raw pointer to the underlying data, the length of
the vector (in elements), and the allocated capacity of the
data (in elements). These are the same arguments in the same
order as the arguments to [ from_raw_parts](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.from_raw_parts).

After calling this function, the caller is responsible for the
memory previously managed by the `Vec`. Most often, one does
this by converting the raw pointer, length, and capacity back
into a `Vec` with the [ from_raw_parts](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.from_raw_parts) function; more generally,
if

`T` is non-zero-sized and the capacity is nonzero, one may use
any method that calls [with a layout of](https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html#tymethod.dealloc)

`dealloc``Layout::array::<T>(capacity)`; if `T` is zero-sized or the
capacity is zero, nothing needs to be done.[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-5)Examples

```
let v: Vec<i32> = vec![-1, 0, 1];
let (ptr, len, cap) = v.into_raw_parts();
let rebuilt = unsafe {
    // We can now make changes to the components, such as
    // transmuting the raw pointer to a compatible type.
    let ptr = ptr as *mut u32;
    Vec::from_raw_parts(ptr, len, cap)
};
assert_eq!(rebuilt, [4294967295, 0, 1]);
```

// These are all done without reallocating...
for i in 0..10 {
    vec.push(i);
}
assert_eq!(vec.len(), 10);
assert!(vec.capacity() >= 10);
// ...but this may make the vector reallocate
vec.push(11);
assert_eq!(vec.len(), 11);
assert!(vec.capacity() >= 11);
// A vector of a zero-sized type will always over-allocate, since no
// allocation is necessary
let vec_units = Vec::<(), System>::with_capacity_in(10, System);
assert_eq!(vec_units.capacity(), usize::MAX);
```
Appends an element to the back of a collection.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-2)Panics

Panics if the new capacity exceeds `isize::MAX` *bytes*.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-8)Examples

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#time-complexity)Time complexity

Takes amortized *O*(1) time. If the vector’s length would exceed its
capacity after the push, *O*(*capacity*) time is taken to copy the
vector’s elements to a larger allocation. This expensive operation is
offset by the *capacity* *O*(1) insertions it allows.

Appends an element to the back of a collection, returning a reference to it.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-3)Panics

Panics if the new capacity exceeds `isize::MAX` *bytes*.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-9)Examples

```
let mut vec = vec![1, 2];
let last = vec.push_mut(3);
assert_eq!(*last, 3);
assert_eq!(vec, [1, 2, 3]);
let last = vec.push_mut(3);
*last += 1;
assert_eq!(vec, [1, 2, 3, 4]);
```

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#1193-1198)#### pub const unsafe fn [from_raw_parts_in](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.from_raw_parts_in)(

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#1193-1198)

#### pub const unsafe fn [from_raw_parts_in](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.from_raw_parts_in)(
    ptr: [*mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html),
    length: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html),
    capacity: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html),
    alloc: A,
) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html)<T, A>

Creates a `Vec<T, A>` directly from a pointer, a length, a capacity,
and an allocator.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety-2)Safety

This is highly unsafe, due to the number of invariants that aren’t checked:

- `ptr`must be- *currently allocated*- `alloc`.
- `T`needs to have the same alignment as what- `ptr`was allocated with. (- `T`having a less strict alignment is not sufficient, the alignment really needs to be equal to satisfy the- `dealloc`
- The size of `T`times the`capacity`(i.e. the allocated size in bytes) needs to be the same size as the pointer was allocated with. (Because similar to alignment,`dealloc``size`.)
- `length`needs to be less than or equal to- `capacity`.
- The first `length`values must be properly initialized values of type`T`.
- `capacity`needs to- *fit*
- The allocated size in bytes must be no larger than `isize::MAX`. See the safety documentation of`pointer::offset`

These requirements are always upheld by any `ptr` that has been allocated
via `Vec<T, A>`. Other allocation sources are allowed if the invariants are
upheld.

Violating these may cause problems like corrupting the allocator’s
internal data structures. For example it is **not** safe
to build a `Vec<u8>` from a pointer to a C `char` array with length `size_t`.
It’s also not safe to build one from a `Vec<u16>` and its length, because
the allocator cares about the alignment, and these two types have different
alignments. The buffer was allocated with alignment 2 (for `u16`), but after
turning it into a `Vec<u8>` it’ll be deallocated with alignment 1.

The ownership of `ptr` is effectively transferred to the
`Vec<T>` which may then deallocate, reallocate or change the
contents of memory pointed to by the pointer at will. Ensure
that nothing else uses the pointer after calling this
function.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-11)Examples

```
#![feature(allocator_api)]
use std::alloc::System;
use std::ptr;
let mut v = Vec::with_capacity_in(3, System);
v.push(1);
v.push(2);
v.push(3);
// Deconstruct the vector into parts.
let (p, len, cap, alloc) = v.into_raw_parts_with_alloc();
unsafe {
    // Overwrite memory with 4, 5, 6
    for i in 0..len {
        ptr::write(p.add(i), 4 + i);
    }
    // Put everything back together into a Vec
    let rebuilt = Vec::from_raw_parts_in(p, len, cap, alloc.clone());
    assert_eq!(rebuilt, [4, 5, 6]);
}
```
Using memory that was allocated elsewhere:

```
#![feature(allocator_api)]
use std::alloc::{AllocError, Allocator, Global, Layout};
fn main() {
    let layout = Layout::array::<u32>(16).expect("overflow cannot happen");
    let vec = unsafe {
        let mem = match Global.allocate(layout) {
            Ok(mem) => mem.cast::<u32>().as_ptr(),
            Err(AllocError) => return,
        };
        mem.write(1_000_000);
        Vec::from_raw_parts_in(mem, 1, 16, Global)
    };
    assert_eq!(vec, &[1_000_000]);
    assert_eq!(vec.capacity(), 16);
}
```

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#1363)#### pub const fn [into_raw_parts_with_alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.into_raw_parts_with_alloc)(self) -> ([*mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html), [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html), [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html), A)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#1363)

#### pub const fn [into_raw_parts_with_alloc](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.into_raw_parts_with_alloc)(self) -> ([*mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html), [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html), [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html), A)

Decomposes a `Vec<T>` into its raw components: `(pointer, length, capacity, allocator)`.

Returns the raw pointer to the underlying data, the length of the vector (in elements),
the allocated capacity of the data (in elements), and the allocator. These are the same
arguments in the same order as the arguments to [ from_raw_parts_in](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.from_raw_parts_in).

After calling this function, the caller is responsible for the
memory previously managed by the `Vec`. The only way to do
this is to convert the raw pointer, length, and capacity back
into a `Vec` with the [ from_raw_parts_in](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.from_raw_parts_in) function, allowing
the destructor to perform the cleanup.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-13)Examples

```
#![feature(allocator_api)]
use std::alloc::System;
let mut v: Vec<i32, System> = Vec::new_in(System);
v.push(-1);
v.push(0);
v.push(1);
let (ptr, len, cap, alloc) = v.into_raw_parts_with_alloc();
let rebuilt = unsafe {
    // We can now make changes to the components, such as
    // transmuting the raw pointer to a compatible type.
    let ptr = ptr as *mut u32;
    Vec::from_raw_parts_in(ptr, len, cap, alloc)
};
assert_eq!(rebuilt, [4294967295, 0, 1]);
```

#### pub fn [reserve_exact](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.reserve_exact)(&mut self, additional: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html))

Reserves the minimum capacity for at least `additional` more elements to
be inserted in the given `Vec<T>`. Unlike [ reserve](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.reserve), this will not
deliberately over-allocate to speculatively avoid frequent allocations.
After calling

`reserve_exact`, capacity will be greater than or equal to
`self.len() + additional`. Does nothing if the capacity is already
sufficient.Note that the allocator may give the collection more space than it
requests. Therefore, capacity can not be relied upon to be precisely
minimal. Prefer [ reserve](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.reserve) if future insertions are expected.

1.57.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#1537)#### pub fn [try_reserve](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.try_reserve)(&mut self, additional: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.unit.html), [TryReserveError](https://doc.rust-lang.org/collections/struct.TryReserveError.html)>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#1537)

#### pub fn [try_reserve](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.try_reserve)(&mut self, additional: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.unit.html), [TryReserveError](https://doc.rust-lang.org/collections/struct.TryReserveError.html)>

Tries to reserve capacity for at least `additional` more elements to be inserted
in the given `Vec<T>`. The collection may reserve more space to speculatively avoid
frequent reallocations. After calling `try_reserve`, capacity will be
greater than or equal to `self.len() + additional` if it returns
`Ok(())`. Does nothing if capacity is already sufficient. This method
preserves the contents even if an error occurs.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#errors-2)Errors

If the capacity overflows, or the allocator reports a failure, then an error is returned.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-18)Examples

```
use std::collections::TryReserveError;
fn process_data(data: &[u32]) -> Result<Vec<u32>, TryReserveError> {
    let mut output = Vec::new();
    // Pre-reserve the memory, exiting if we can't
    output.try_reserve(data.len())?;
    // Now we know this can't OOM in the middle of our complex work
    output.extend(data.iter().map(|&val| {
        val * 2 + 5 // very complicated
    }));
    Ok(output)
}
```

#### pub fn [shrink_to_fit](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.shrink_to_fit)(&mut self)

Shrinks the capacity of the vector as much as possible.

The behavior of this method depends on the allocator, which may either shrink the vector
in-place or reallocate. The resulting vector might still have some excess capacity, just as
is the case for [ with_capacity](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.with_capacity). See

[for more details.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/trait.Allocator.html#method.shrink)

`Allocator::shrink`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-20)Examples

Shrinks the capacity of the vector with a lower bound.

The capacity will remain at least as large as both the length and the supplied value.

If the current capacity is less than the lower limit, this is a no-op.

) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.unit.html), [TryReserveError](https://doc.rust-lang.org/collections/struct.TryReserveError.html)>

Shrinks the capacity of the vector with a lower bound.

The capacity will remain at least as large as both the length and the supplied value.

If the current capacity is less than the lower limit, this is a no-op.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#errors-5)Errors

This function returns an error if the allocator fails to shrink the allocation,
the vector thereafter is still safe to use, the capacity remains unchanged
however. See [ Allocator::shrink](https://doc.rust-lang.org/alloc/trait.Allocator.html#method.shrink).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-23)Examples

```
#![feature(vec_fallible_shrink)]
let mut vec = Vec::with_capacity(10);
vec.extend([1, 2, 3]);
assert!(vec.capacity() >= 10);
vec.try_shrink_to(4).expect("why is the test harness failing to shrink to 12 bytes");
assert!(vec.capacity() >= 4);
vec.try_shrink_to(0).expect("this is a no-op and thus the allocator isn't involved.");
assert!(vec.capacity() >= 3);
```

Returns a raw pointer to the vector’s buffer, or a dangling raw pointer valid for zero sized reads if the vector didn’t allocate.

The caller must ensure that the vector outlives the pointer this function returns, or else it will end up dangling. Modifying the vector may cause its buffer to be reallocated, which would also make any pointers to it invalid.

The caller must also ensure that the memory the pointer (non-transitively) points to
is never written to (except inside an `UnsafeCell`) using this pointer or any pointer
derived from it. If you need to mutate the contents of the slice, use [ as_mut_ptr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.as_mut_ptr).

Forces the length of the vector to `new_len`.

This is a low-level operation that maintains none of the normal
invariants of the type. Normally changing the length of a vector
is done using one of the safe operations instead, such as
[ truncate](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.truncate),

[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.resize)

`resize`[, or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/iter/trait.Extend.html#tymethod.extend)

`extend`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.clear)

`clear`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety-4)Safety

- `new_len`must be less than or equal to- `capacity()`
- The elements at `old_len..new_len`must be initialized.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-31)Examples

See [ spare_capacity_mut()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.spare_capacity_mut) for an example with safe
initialization of capacity elements and use of this method.

`set_len()` can be useful for situations in which the vector
is serving as a buffer for other code, particularly over FFI:

```
pub fn get_dictionary(&self) -> Option<Vec<u8>> {
    // Per the FFI method's docs, "32768 bytes is always enough".
    let mut dict = Vec::with_capacity(32_768);
    let mut dict_length = 0;
    // SAFETY: When `deflateGetDictionary` returns `Z_OK`, it holds that:
    // 1. `dict_length` elements were initialized.
    // 2. `dict_length` <= the capacity (32_768)
    // which makes `set_len` safe to call.
    unsafe {
        // Make the FFI call...
        let r = deflateGetDictionary(self.strm, dict.as_mut_ptr(), &mut dict_length);
        if r == Z_OK {
            // ...and update the length to what was initialized.
            dict.set_len(dict_length);
            Some(dict)
        } else {
            None
        }
    }
}
```
While the following example is sound, there is a memory leak since
the inner vectors were not freed prior to the `set_len` call:

```
let mut vec = vec![vec![1, 0, 0],
                   vec![0, 1, 0],
                   vec![0, 0, 1]];
// SAFETY:
// 1. `old_len..0` is empty so no elements need to be initialized.
// 2. `0 <= capacity` always holds whatever `capacity` is.
unsafe {
    vec.set_len(0);
}
```
Normally, here, one would use [ clear](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.clear) instead to correctly drop
the contents and thus not leak memory.

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#2779)#### pub fn [push_within_capacity](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.push_within_capacity)(&mut self, value: T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/result/enum.Result.html)<[&mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.reference.html), T>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#2779)

#### pub fn [push_within_capacity](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.push_within_capacity)(&mut self, value: T) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/result/enum.Result.html)<[&mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.reference.html), T>

Appends an element and returns a reference to it if there is sufficient spare capacity, otherwise an error is returned with the element.

Unlike [ push](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.push) this method will not reallocate when there’s insufficient capacity.
The caller should use

[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.reserve)

`reserve`[to ensure that there is enough capacity.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.try_reserve)

`try_reserve`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-41)Examples

A manual, panic-free alternative to [ FromIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/iter/trait.FromIterator.html):

```
#![feature(vec_push_within_capacity)]
use std::collections::TryReserveError;
fn from_iter_fallible<T>(iter: impl Iterator<Item=T>) -> Result<Vec<T>, TryReserveError> {
    let mut vec = Vec::new();
    for value in iter {
        if let Err(value) = vec.push_within_capacity(value) {
            vec.try_reserve(1)?;
            // this cannot fail, the previous line either returned or added at least 1 free slot
            let _ = vec.push_within_capacity(value);
        }
    }
    Ok(vec)
}
assert_eq!(from_iter_fallible(0..100), Ok(Vec::from_iter(0..100)));
```
[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#time-complexity-4)Time complexity

Takes *O*(1) time.

Removes the last element from a vector and returns it, or [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) if it
is empty.

If you’d like to pop the first element, consider using
[ VecDeque::pop_front](https://doc.rust-lang.org/collections/struct.VecDeque.html#method.pop_front) instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-42)Examples

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#time-complexity-5)Time complexity

Removes the subslice indicated by the given range from the vector, returning a double-ended iterator over the removed subslice.

If the iterator is dropped before being fully consumed, it drops the remaining removed elements.

The returned iterator keeps a mutable borrow on the vector to optimize its implementation.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-11)Panics

Panics if the range has `start_bound > end_bound`, or, if the range is
bounded on either end and past the length of the vector.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#leaking)Leaking

If the returned iterator goes out of scope without being dropped (due to
[ mem::forget](https://doc.rust-lang.org/mem/fn.forget.html), for example), the vector may have lost and leaked
elements arbitrarily, including elements outside the range.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-46)Examples

Splits the collection into two at the given index.

Returns a newly allocated vector containing the elements in the range
`[at, len)`. After the call, the original vector will be left containing
the elements `[0, at)` with its previous capacity unchanged.

- If you want to take ownership of the entire contents and capacity of
the vector, see `mem::take``mem::replace`
- If you don’t need the returned vector at all, see `Vec::truncate`
- If you want to take ownership of an arbitrary subslice, or you don’t
necessarily want to store the removed items in a vector, see `Vec::drain`

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-12)Panics

Panics if `at > len`.

1.33.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#3141-3143)#### pub fn [resize_with](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.resize_with)<F>(&mut self, new_len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html), f: F)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#3141-3143)

#### pub fn [resize_with](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.resize_with)<F>(&mut self, new_len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html), f: F)

Resizes the `Vec` in-place so that `len` is equal to `new_len`.

If `new_len` is greater than `len`, the `Vec` is extended by the
difference, with each additional slot filled with the result of
calling the closure `f`. The return values from `f` will end up
in the `Vec` in the order they have been generated.

If `new_len` is less than `len`, the `Vec` is simply truncated.

This method uses a closure to create new values on every push. If
you’d rather [ Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/clone/trait.Clone.html) a given value, use

[. If you want to use the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.resize)

`Vec::resize`[trait to generate values, you can pass](https://doc.rust-lang.org/default/trait.Default.html)

`Default`[as the second argument.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/default/trait.Default.html#tymethod.default)

`Default::default`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-13)Panics

Panics if the new capacity exceeds `isize::MAX` *bytes*.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-51)Examples

Consumes and leaks the `Vec`, returning a mutable reference to the contents,
`&'a mut [T]`.

Note that the type `T` must outlive the chosen lifetime `'a`. If the type
has only static references, or none at all, then this may be chosen to be
`'static`.

As of Rust 1.57, this method does not reallocate or shrink the `Vec`,
so the leaked allocation may include unused capacity that is not part
of the returned slice.

This function is mainly useful for data that lives for the remainder of the program’s life. Dropping the returned reference will cause a memory leak.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-52)Examples

Simple usage:

1.60.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#3221)#### pub fn [spare_capacity_mut](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.spare_capacity_mut)(&mut self) -> &mut [[MaybeUninit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/mem/union.MaybeUninit.html)<T>]

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#3221)

#### pub fn [spare_capacity_mut](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.spare_capacity_mut)(&mut self) -> &mut [[MaybeUninit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/mem/union.MaybeUninit.html)<T>]

Returns the remaining spare capacity of the vector as a slice of
`MaybeUninit<T>`.

The returned slice can be used to fill the vector with data (e.g. by
reading from a file) before marking the data as initialized using the
[ set_len](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.set_len) method.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-53)Examples

```
// Allocate vector big enough for 10 elements.
let mut v = Vec::with_capacity(10);
// Fill in the first 3 elements.
let uninit = v.spare_capacity_mut();
uninit[0].write(0);
uninit[1].write(1);
uninit[2].write(2);
// Mark the first 3 elements of the vector as being initialized.
unsafe {
    v.set_len(3);
}
assert_eq!(&v, &[0, 1, 2]);
```
[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#3286)#### pub fn [split_at_spare_mut](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.split_at_spare_mut)(&mut self) -> (&mut [[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html), &mut [[MaybeUninit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/mem/union.MaybeUninit.html)<T>])

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#3286)

#### pub fn [split_at_spare_mut](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.split_at_spare_mut)(&mut self) -> (&mut [[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html), &mut [[MaybeUninit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/mem/union.MaybeUninit.html)<T>])

Returns vector content as a slice of `T`, along with the remaining spare
capacity of the vector as a slice of `MaybeUninit<T>`.

The returned spare capacity slice can be used to fill the vector with data
(e.g. by reading from a file) before marking the data as initialized using
the [ set_len](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.set_len) method.

Note that this is a low-level API, which should be used with care for
optimization purposes. If you need to append data to a `Vec`
you can use [ push](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.push),

[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.extend)

`extend`[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.extend_from_slice)

`extend_from_slice`[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.extend_from_within)

`extend_from_within`[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.insert)

`insert`[,](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.append)

`append`[or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.resize)

`resize`[, depending on your exact needs.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.resize_with)

`resize_with`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-54)Examples

```
#![feature(vec_split_at_spare)]
let mut v = vec![1, 1, 2];
// Reserve additional space big enough for 10 elements.
v.reserve(10);
let (init, uninit) = v.split_at_spare_mut();
let sum = init.iter().copied().sum::<u32>();
// Fill in the next 4 elements.
uninit[0].write(sum);
uninit[1].write(sum * 2);
uninit[2].write(sum * 3);
uninit[3].write(sum * 4);
// Mark the 4 elements of the vector as being initialized.
unsafe {
    let len = v.len();
    v.set_len(len + 4);
}
assert_eq!(&v, &[1, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16]);
```
[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#3345)#### pub fn [into_chunks](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.into_chunks)<const N: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html)>(self) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html)<[[T; N]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.array.html), A>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#3345)

#### pub fn [into_chunks](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.into_chunks)<const N: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html)>(self) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html)<[[T; N]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.array.html), A>

Groups every `N` elements in the `Vec<T>` into chunks to produce a `Vec<[T; N]>`, dropping
elements in the remainder. `N` must be greater than zero.

If the capacity is not a multiple of the chunk size, the buffer will shrink down to the nearest multiple with a reallocation or deallocation.

This function can be used to reverse [ Vec::into_flattened](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.into_flattened).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-55)Examples

```
#![feature(vec_into_chunks)]
let vec = vec![0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7];
assert_eq!(vec.into_chunks::<3>(), [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]);
let vec = vec![0, 1, 2, 3];
let chunks: Vec<[u8; 10]> = vec.into_chunks();
assert!(chunks.is_empty());
let flat = vec![0; 8 * 8 * 8];
let reshaped: Vec<[[[u8; 8]; 8]; 8]> = flat.into_chunks().into_chunks().into_chunks();
assert_eq!(reshaped.len(), 1);
```
This clears out this `Vec` and recycles the allocation into a new `Vec`.
The item type of the resulting `Vec` needs to have the same size and
alignment as the item type of the original `Vec`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-56)Examples

```
#![feature(vec_recycle, transmutability)]
let a: Vec<u8> = vec![0; 100];
let capacity = a.capacity();
let addr = a.as_ptr().addr();
let b: Vec<i8> = a.recycle();
assert_eq!(b.len(), 0);
assert_eq!(b.capacity(), capacity);
assert_eq!(b.as_ptr().addr(), addr);
```
The `Recyclable` bound prevents this method from being called when `T` and `U` have different sizes; e.g.:

[ⓘ](https://doc.rust-lang.org)

```
#![feature(vec_recycle, transmutability)]
let vec: Vec<[u8; 2]> = Vec::new();
let _: Vec<[u8; 1]> = vec.recycle();
```
…or different alignments:

[ⓘ](https://doc.rust-lang.org)

```
#![feature(vec_recycle, transmutability)]
let vec: Vec<[u16; 0]> = Vec::new();
let _: Vec<[u8; 0]> = vec.recycle();
```
However, due to temporary implementation limitations of `Recyclable`,
this method is not yet callable when `T` or `U` are slices, trait objects,
or other exotic types; e.g.:

[ⓘ](https://doc.rust-lang.org)

```
#![feature(vec_recycle, transmutability)]
let mut storage: Vec<&[&str]> = Vec::new();
for input in inputs {
    let mut buffer: Vec<&str> = storage.recycle();
    buffer.extend(input.split(" "));
    process(&buffer);
    storage = buffer.recycle();
}
```
Resizes the `Vec` in-place so that `len` is equal to `new_len`.

If `new_len` is greater than `len`, the `Vec` is extended by the
difference, with each additional slot filled with `value`.
If `new_len` is less than `len`, the `Vec` is simply truncated.

This method requires `T` to implement [ Clone](https://doc.rust-lang.org/clone/trait.Clone.html),
in order to be able to clone the passed value.
If you need more flexibility (or want to rely on

[instead of](https://doc.rust-lang.org/default/trait.Default.html)

`Default`[), use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/clone/trait.Clone.html)

`Clone`[. If you only need to resize to a smaller size, use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.resize_with)

`Vec::resize_with`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.truncate)

`Vec::truncate`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-14)Panics

Panics if the new capacity exceeds `isize::MAX` *bytes*.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-57)Examples

1.6.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#3525)#### pub fn [extend_from_slice](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.extend_from_slice)(&mut self, other: &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html))

#### pub fn [extend_from_slice](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.extend_from_slice)(&mut self, other: &[[T]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html))

Clones and appends all elements in a slice to the `Vec`.

Iterates over the slice `other`, clones each element, and then appends
it to this `Vec`. The `other` slice is traversed in-order.

Note that this function is the same as [ extend](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.extend),
except that it also works with slice elements that are Clone but not Copy.
If Rust gets specialization this function may be deprecated.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-15)Panics

Panics if the new capacity exceeds `isize::MAX` *bytes*.

1.53.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#3556-3558)#### pub fn [extend_from_within](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.extend_from_within)<R>(&mut self, src: R)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#3556-3558)

#### pub fn [extend_from_within](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.extend_from_within)<R>(&mut self, src: R)

Given a range `src`, clones a slice of elements in that range and appends it to the end.

`src` must be a range that can form a valid subslice of the `Vec`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-16)Panics

Panics if starting index is greater than the end index, if the index is
greater than the length of the vector, or if the new capacity exceeds
`isize::MAX` *bytes*.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-59)Examples

```
let mut characters = vec!['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e'];
characters.extend_from_within(2..);
assert_eq!(characters, ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'c', 'd', 'e']);
let mut numbers = vec![0, 1, 2, 3, 4];
numbers.extend_from_within(..2);
assert_eq!(numbers, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 0, 1]);
let mut strings = vec![String::from("hello"), String::from("world"), String::from("!")];
strings.extend_from_within(1..=2);
assert_eq!(strings, ["hello", "world", "!", "world", "!"]);
```

1.21.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#4091-4094)#### pub fn [splice](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.splice)<R, I>(
    &mut self,
    range: R,
    replace_with: I,
) -> [Splice](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Splice.html)<'_, <I as [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/iter/trait.IntoIterator.html)>::[IntoIter](https://doc.rust-lang.org/iter/trait.IntoIterator.html#associatedtype.IntoIter), A> [ⓘ](https://doc.rust-lang.org)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#4091-4094)

#### pub fn [splice](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.splice)<R, I>(
    &mut self,
    range: R,
    replace_with: I,
) -> [Splice](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Splice.html)<'_, <I as [IntoIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/iter/trait.IntoIterator.html)>::[IntoIter](https://doc.rust-lang.org/iter/trait.IntoIterator.html#associatedtype.IntoIter), A> [ⓘ](https://doc.rust-lang.org)

Creates a splicing iterator that replaces the specified range in the vector
with the given `replace_with` iterator and yields the removed items.
`replace_with` does not need to be the same length as `range`.

`range` is removed even if the `Splice` iterator is not consumed before it is dropped.

It is unspecified how many elements are removed from the vector
if the `Splice` value is leaked.

The input iterator `replace_with` is only consumed when the `Splice` value is dropped.

This is optimal if:

- The tail (elements in the vector after `range`) is empty,
- or `replace_with`yields fewer or equal elements than`range`’s length
- or the lower bound of its `size_hint()`is exact.

Otherwise, a temporary vector is allocated and the tail is moved twice.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-18)Panics

Panics if the range has `start_bound > end_bound`, or, if the range is
bounded on either end and past the length of the vector.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-62)Examples

```
let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4];
let new = [7, 8, 9];
let u: Vec<_> = v.splice(1..3, new).collect();
assert_eq!(v, [1, 7, 8, 9, 4]);
assert_eq!(u, [2, 3]);
```
Using `splice` to insert new items into a vector efficiently at a specific position
indicated by an empty range:

1.87.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#4174-4177)#### pub fn [extract_if](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.extract_if)<F, R>(
    &mut self,
    range: R,
    filter: F,
) -> [ExtractIf](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.ExtractIf.html)<'_, T, F, A> [ⓘ](https://doc.rust-lang.org)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#4174-4177)

#### pub fn [extract_if](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.extract_if)<F, R>(
    &mut self,
    range: R,
    filter: F,
) -> [ExtractIf](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.ExtractIf.html)<'_, T, F, A> [ⓘ](https://doc.rust-lang.org)

Creates an iterator which uses a closure to determine if an element in the range should be removed.

If the closure returns `true`, the element is removed from the vector
and yielded. If the closure returns `false`, or panics, the element
remains in the vector and will not be yielded.

Only elements that fall in the provided range are considered for extraction, but any elements after the range will still have to be moved if any element has been extracted.

If the returned `ExtractIf` is not exhausted, e.g. because it is dropped without iterating
or the iteration short-circuits, then the remaining elements will be retained.
Use `extract_if().for_each(drop)` if you do not need the returned iterator,
or [ retain_mut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/struct.Vec.html#method.retain_mut) with a negated predicate if you also do not need to restrict the range.

Using this method is equivalent to the following code:

```
let mut i = range.start;
let end_items = vec.len() - range.end;
while i < vec.len() - end_items {
    if some_predicate(&mut vec[i]) {
        let val = vec.remove(i);
        // your code here
    } else {
        i += 1;
    }
}
```
But `extract_if` is easier to use. `extract_if` is also more efficient,
because it can backshift the elements of the array in bulk.

The iterator also lets you mutate the value of each element in the closure, regardless of whether you choose to keep or remove it.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-19)Panics

If `range` is out of bounds.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-63)Examples

Splitting a vector into even and odd values, reusing the original vector:

```
let mut numbers = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, 15];
let evens = numbers.extract_if(.., |x| *x % 2 == 0).collect::<Vec<_>>();
let odds = numbers;
assert_eq!(evens, vec![2, 4, 6, 8, 14]);
assert_eq!(odds, vec![1, 3, 5, 9, 11, 13, 15]);
```

For a safe alternative see [ get](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html#method.get).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety-5)Safety

Calling this method with an out-of-bounds index is * undefined behavior*
even if the resulting reference is not used.

You can think of this like `.get(index).unwrap_unchecked()`.  It’s UB
to call `.get_unchecked(len)`, even if you immediately convert to a
pointer.  And it’s UB to call `.get_unchecked(..len + 1)`,
`.get_unchecked(..=len)`, or similar.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-84)Examples

Returns a raw pointer to the slice’s buffer.

The caller must ensure that the slice outlives the pointer this function returns, or else it will end up dangling.

The caller must also ensure that the memory the pointer (non-transitively) points to
is never written to (except inside an `UnsafeCell`) using this pointer or any pointer
derived from it. If you need to mutate the contents of the slice, use [ as_mut_ptr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html#method.as_mut_ptr).

Modifying the container referenced by this slice may cause its buffer to be reallocated, which would also make any pointers to it invalid.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-86)Examples

#### pub fn [as_ptr_range](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.as_ptr_range)(&self) -> [Range](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ops/struct.Range.html)<[*const T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html)> [ⓘ](https://doc.rust-lang.org)

Returns the two raw pointers spanning the slice.

The returned range is half-open, which means that the end pointer
points *one past* the last element of the slice. This way, an empty
slice is represented by two equal pointers, and the difference between
the two pointers represents the size of the slice.

See [ as_ptr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html#method.as_ptr) for warnings on using these pointers. The end pointer
requires extra caution, as it does not point to a valid element in the
slice.

This function is useful for interacting with foreign interfaces which use two pointers to refer to a range of elements in memory, as is common in C++.

It can also be useful to check if a pointer to an element refers to an element of this slice:

Swaps two elements in the slice, without doing bounds checking.

For a safe alternative see [ swap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html#method.swap).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#arguments-1)Arguments

- a - The index of the first element
- b - The index of the second element

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety-7)Safety

Calling this method with an out-of-bounds index is * undefined behavior*.
The caller has to ensure that

`a < self.len()` and `b < self.len()`.[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-89)Examples

Returns an iterator over all contiguous windows of length
`size`. The windows overlap. If the slice is shorter than
`size`, the iterator returns no values.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-21)Panics

Panics if `size` is zero.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-93)Examples

```
let slice = ['l', 'o', 'r', 'e', 'm'];
let mut iter = slice.windows(3);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &['l', 'o', 'r']);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &['o', 'r', 'e']);
assert_eq!(iter.next().unwrap(), &['r', 'e', 'm']);
assert!(iter.next().is_none());
```
If the slice is shorter than `size`:

Because the [Iterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/iter/trait.Iterator.html) trait cannot represent the required lifetimes,
there is no `windows_mut` analog to `windows`;
`[0,1,2].windows_mut(2).collect()` would violate [the rules of references](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch04-02-references-and-borrowing.html#the-rules-of-references)
(though a [LendingIterator](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2022/10/28/gats-stabilization.html) analog is possible). You can sometimes use
[ Cell::as_slice_of_cells](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cell/struct.Cell.html#method.as_slice_of_cells) in
conjunction with

`windows` instead:```
use std::cell::Cell;
let mut array = ['R', 'u', 's', 't', ' ', '2', '0', '1', '5'];
let slice = &mut array[..];
let slice_of_cells: &[Cell<char>] = Cell::from_mut(slice).as_slice_of_cells();
for w in slice_of_cells.windows(3) {
    Cell::swap(&w[0], &w[2]);
}
assert_eq!(array, ['s', 't', ' ', '2', '0', '1', '5', 'u', 'R']);
```
Returns an iterator over `chunk_size` elements of the slice at a time, starting at the
beginning of the slice.

The chunks are slices and do not overlap. If `chunk_size` does not divide the length of the
slice, then the last chunk will not have length `chunk_size`.

See [ chunks_exact](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html#method.chunks_exact) for a variant of this iterator that returns chunks of always exactly

`chunk_size` elements, and [for the same iterator but starting at the end of the slice.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html#method.rchunks)

`rchunks`If your `chunk_size` is a constant, consider using [ as_chunks](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.slice.html#method.as_chunks) instead, which will
give references to arrays of exactly that length, rather than slices.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-22)Panics

Panics if `chunk_size` is zero.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-94)Examples
