#### pub const fn [overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_add)(self, rhs: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html)) -> ([i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

Calculates `self` + `rhs` + `carry` and checks for overflow.

Performs “ternary addition” of two integer operands and a carry-in bit, and returns a tuple of the sum along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. On overflow, the wrapped value is returned.

This allows chaining together multiple additions to create a wider
addition, and can be useful for bignum addition. This method should
only be used for the most significant word; for the less significant
words the unsigned method
[ u32::carrying_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.carrying_add)
should be used.

The output boolean returned by this method is *not* a carry flag,
and should *not* be added to a more significant word.

If overflow occurred, the wrapped value is returned (negative if overflowed
above [ MAX](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html#associatedconstant.MAX), non-negative if below

[).](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html#associatedconstant.MIN)

`MIN`If the input carry is false, this method is equivalent to
[ overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html#method.overflowing_add).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-82)Examples

```
#![feature(signed_bigint_helpers)]
// Only the most significant word is signed.
//
//   10  MAX    (a = 10 × 2^32 + 2^32 - 1)
// + -5    9    (b = -5 × 2^32 + 9)
// ---------
//    6    8    (sum = 6 × 2^32 + 8)
let (a1, a0): (i32, u32) = (10, u32::MAX);
let (b1, b0): (i32, u32) = (-5, 9);
let carry0 = false;
// u32::carrying_add for the less significant words
let (sum0, carry1) = a0.carrying_add(b0, carry0);
assert_eq!(carry1, true);
// i32::carrying_add for the most significant word
let (sum1, overflow) = a1.carrying_add(b1, carry1);
assert_eq!(overflow, false);
assert_eq!((sum1, sum0), (6, 8));
```

without the possibility to overflow.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

Performs “long multiplication” which takes in an extra amount to add, and may return an additional amount of overflow. This allows for chaining together multiple multiplications to create “big integers” which represent larger values.

1.38.0 (const: 1.52.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#390-409)#### pub const fn [div_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.div_euclid)(self, rhs: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html)) -> [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#390-409)

#### pub const fn [div_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.div_euclid)(self, rhs: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html)) -> [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html)

Calculates the quotient of Euclidean division of `self` by `rhs`.

This computes the integer `q` such that `self = q * rhs + r`, with
`r = self.rem_euclid(rhs)` and `0 <= r < abs(rhs)`.

In other words, the result is `self / rhs` rounded to the integer `q`
such that `self >= q * rhs`.
If `self > 0`, this is equal to rounding towards zero (the default in Rust);
if `self < 0`, this is equal to rounding away from zero (towards +/- infinity).
If `rhs > 0`, this is equal to rounding towards -infinity;
if `rhs < 0`, this is equal to rounding towards +infinity.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-25)Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero or if `self` is `Self::MIN`
and `rhs` is -1. This behavior is not affected by the `overflow-checks` flag.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-102)Examples

1.38.0 (const: 1.52.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#390-409)#### pub const fn [rem_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.rem_euclid)(self, rhs: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html)) -> [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#390-409)

#### pub const fn [rem_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.rem_euclid)(self, rhs: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html)) -> [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html)

Calculates the least nonnegative remainder of `self` when
divided by `rhs`.

This is done as if by the Euclidean division algorithm – given
`r = self.rem_euclid(rhs)`, the result satisfies
`self = rhs * self.div_euclid(rhs) + r` and `0 <= r < abs(rhs)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-26)Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero or if `self` is `Self::MIN` and
`rhs` is -1. This behavior is not affected by the `overflow-checks` flag.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-103)Examples

```
let a: i32 = 7; // or any other integer type
let b = 4;
assert_eq!(a.rem_euclid(b), 3);
assert_eq!((-a).rem_euclid(b), 1);
assert_eq!(a.rem_euclid(-b), 3);
assert_eq!((-a).rem_euclid(-b), 1);
```
This will panic:

If `rhs` is positive, calculates the smallest value greater than or
equal to `self` that is a multiple of `rhs`. If `rhs` is negative,

multiple of `rhs`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#overflow-behavior-15)Overflow behavior

On overflow, this function will panic if overflow checks are enabled (default in debug mode) and wrap if overflow checks are disabled (default in release mode).

#![feature(int_roundings)]

assert_eq!(23_i32.next_multiple_of(8), 24);
assert_eq!(16_i32.next_multiple_of(-8), 16);
assert_eq!(23_i32.next_multiple_of(-8), 16);
assert_eq!((-16_i32).next_multiple_of(8), -16);
assert_eq!((-23_i32).next_multiple_of(8), -16);
assert_eq!((-16_i32).next_multiple_of(-8), -16);
assert_eq!((-23_i32).next_multiple_of(-8), -24);
```
[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#390-409)#### pub const fn [checked_next_multiple_of](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.checked_next_multiple_of)(self, rhs: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/option/enum.Option.html)<[i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html)>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#390-409)

#### pub const fn [checked_next_multiple_of](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.checked_next_multiple_of)(self, rhs: [i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/option/enum.Option.html)<[i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html)>

If `rhs` is positive, calculates the smallest value greater than or
equal to `self` that is a multiple of `rhs`. If `rhs` is negative,
calculates the largest value less than or equal to `self` that is a
multiple of `rhs`. Returns `None` if `rhs` is zero or the operation
would result in overflow.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-107)Examples

```
#![feature(int_roundings)]
assert_eq!(16_i32.checked_next_multiple_of(8), Some(16));
assert_eq!(23_i32.checked_next_multiple_of(8), Some(24));
assert_eq!(16_i32.checked_next_multiple_of(-8), Some(16));
assert_eq!(23_i32.checked_next_multiple_of(-8), Some(16));
assert_eq!((-16_i32).checked_next_multiple_of(8), Some(-16));
assert_eq!((-23_i32).checked_next_multiple_of(8), Some(-16));
assert_eq!((-16_i32).checked_next_multiple_of(-8), Some(-16));
assert_eq!((-23_i32).checked_next_multiple_of(-8), Some(-24));
assert_eq!(1_i32.checked_next_multiple_of(0), None);
assert_eq!(i32::MAX.checked_next_multiple_of(2), None);
```
Returns the logarithm of the number with respect to an arbitrary base, rounded down.

This method might not be optimized owing to implementation details;
`ilog2` can produce results more efficiently for base 2, and `ilog10`
can produce results more efficiently for base 10.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-30)Panics

This function will panic if `self` is less than or equal to zero,
or if `base` is less than 2.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-108)Examples

Returns `None` if the number is negative or zero, or if the base is not at least 2.

This method might not be optimized owing to implementation details;
`checked_ilog2` can produce results more efficiently for base 2, and
`checked_ilog10` can produce results more efficiently for base 10.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-110)Examples

Computes the absolute value of `self`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#overflow-behavior-16)Overflow behavior

The absolute value of
`i32::MIN`
cannot be represented as an
`i32`,
and attempting to calculate it will cause an overflow. This means
that code in debug mode will trigger a panic on this case and
optimized code will return
`i32::MIN`
without a panic. If you do not want this behavior, consider
using [ unsigned_abs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html#method.unsigned_abs) instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-112)Examples

Calculates the midpoint (average) between `self` and `rhs`.

`midpoint(a, b)` is `(a + b) / 2` as if it were performed in a
sufficiently-large signed integral type. This implies that the result is
always rounded towards zero and that no overflow will ever occur.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-128)Examples

Parses an integer from a string slice with digits in a given base.

The string is expected to be an optional
`+` or `-`
sign followed by only digits. Leading and trailing non-digit characters (including
whitespace) represent an error. Underscores (which are accepted in Rust literals)
also represent an error.

Digits are a subset of these characters, depending on `radix`:

- `0-9`
- `a-z`
- `A-Z`

1.0.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#414-433)#### pub const fn [rotate_left](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.rotate_left)(self, n: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#414-433)

#### pub const fn [rotate_left](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.rotate_left)(self, n: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)

Shifts the bits to the left by a specified amount, `n`,
wrapping the truncated bits to the end of the resulting integer.

`rotate_left(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_left(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn’t the same operation as the `<<` shifting operator!

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-14)Examples

#### pub const fn [reverse_bits](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.reverse_bits)(self) -> [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)

Swaps bytes of `self` on little endian targets.

On big endian this is a no-op.

The returned value has the same type as `self`, and will be interpreted
as (a potentially different) value of a native-endian
`i64`.

See [ to_be_bytes()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html#method.to_be_bytes) for a type-safe alternative.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-20)Examples

Swaps bytes of `self` on big endian targets.

On little endian this is a no-op.

The returned value has the same type as `self`, and will be interpreted
as (a potentially different) value of a native-endian
`i64`.

See [ to_le_bytes()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html#method.to_le_bytes) for a type-safe alternative.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-5)Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#overflow-behavior-5)Overflow behavior

This function will always panic on overflow, regardless of whether overflow checks are enabled.

The only case where such an overflow can occur is when one divides `MIN / -1` on a signed type (where
`MIN` is the negative minimal value for the type); this is equivalent to `-MIN`, a positive value
that is too large to represent in the type.

Unbounded shift left. Computes `self << rhs`, without bounding the value of `rhs`.

If `rhs` is larger or equal to the number of bits in `self`,
the entire value is shifted out, and `0` is returned.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-46)Examples

```
assert_eq!(0x1_i64.unbounded_shl(4), 0x10);
assert_eq!(0x1_i64.unbounded_shl(129), 0);
assert_eq!(0b101_i64.unbounded_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_i64.unbounded_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_i64.unbounded_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(42_i64.unbounded_shl(64), 0);
assert_eq!(42_i64.unbounded_shl(1).unbounded_shl(63), 0);
assert_eq!((-13_i64).unbounded_shl(64), 0);
assert_eq!((-13_i64).unbounded_shl(1).unbounded_shl(63), 0);
```
Exact shift left. Computes `self << rhs` as long as it can be reversed losslessly.

Returns `None` if any bits that would be shifted out differ from the resulting sign bit
or if `rhs` >=
`i64::BITS`.
Otherwise, returns `Some(self << rhs)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-47)Examples

```
#![feature(exact_bitshifts)]
assert_eq!(0x1i64.shl_exact(4), Some(0x10));
assert_eq!(0x1i64.shl_exact(i64::BITS - 2), Some(1 << i64::BITS - 2));
assert_eq!(0x1i64.shl_exact(i64::BITS - 1), None);
assert_eq!((-0x2i64).shl_exact(i64::BITS - 2), Some(-0x2 << i64::BITS - 2));
assert_eq!((-0x2i64).shl_exact(i64::BITS - 1), None);
```

1.2.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#414-433)#### pub const fn [wrapping_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#414-433)

#### pub const fn [wrapping_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)

Panic-free bitwise shift-left; yields `self << mask(rhs)`, where `mask` removes
any high-order bits of `rhs` that would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed.  The behaviour matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `<<` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it’s weird.  Consider, instead,
using [ Self::unbounded_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html#method.unbounded_shl) which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-left; the RHS of a wrapping shift-left is restricted to
the range of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS being returned to the other end.
The primitive integer types all implement a [ rotate_left](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html#method.rotate_left) function,
which may be what you want instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-76)Examples

1.7.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#414-433)#### pub const fn [overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_add)(self, rhs: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)) -> ([i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#414-433)

#### pub const fn [overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_add)(self, rhs: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)) -> ([i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

Calculates `self` + `rhs` + `carry` and checks for overflow.

Performs “ternary addition” of two integer operands and a carry-in bit, and returns a tuple of the sum along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. On overflow, the wrapped value is returned.

This allows chaining together multiple additions to create a wider
addition, and can be useful for bignum addition. This method should
only be used for the most significant word; for the less significant
words the unsigned method
[ u64::carrying_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.carrying_add)
should be used.

The output boolean returned by this method is *not* a carry flag,
and should *not* be added to a more significant word.

If overflow occurred, the wrapped value is returned (negative if overflowed
above [ MAX](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html#associatedconstant.MAX), non-negative if below

[).](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html#associatedconstant.MIN)

`MIN`If the input carry is false, this method is equivalent to
[ overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html#method.overflowing_add).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-82)Examples

```
#![feature(signed_bigint_helpers)]
// Only the most significant word is signed.
//
//   10  MAX    (a = 10 × 2^64 + 2^64 - 1)
// + -5    9    (b = -5 × 2^64 + 9)
// ---------
//    6    8    (sum = 6 × 2^64 + 8)
let (a1, a0): (i64, u64) = (10, u64::MAX);
let (b1, b0): (i64, u64) = (-5, 9);
let carry0 = false;
// u64::carrying_add for the less significant words
let (sum0, carry1) = a0.carrying_add(b0, carry0);
assert_eq!(carry1, true);
// i64::carrying_add for the most significant word
let (sum1, overflow) = a1.carrying_add(b1, carry1);
assert_eq!(overflow, false);
assert_eq!((sum1, sum0), (6, 8));
```

[ u64::borrowing_sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.borrowing_sub)
should be used.

The output boolean returned by this method is *not* a borrow flag,
and should *not* be subtracted from a more significant word.

If overflow occurred, the wrapped value is returned (negative if overflowed
above [ MAX](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html#associatedconstant.MAX), non-negative if below

[).](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html#associatedconstant.MIN)

`MIN`If the input borrow is false, this method is equivalent to
[ overflowing_sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html#method.overflowing_sub).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-85)Examples

//

// ---------
//   10  MAX    (diff = 10 × 2^64 + 2^64 - 1)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#414-433)#### pub const fn [widening_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.widening_mul)(self, rhs: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)) -> ([u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html), [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html))

#### pub const fn [widening_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.widening_mul)(self, rhs: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)) -> ([u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html), [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html))

Calculates the complete product `self * rhs` without the possibility to overflow.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

If you also need to add a carry to the wide result, then you want
[ Self::carrying_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html#method.carrying_mul) instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-88)Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `i32` is used.

Calculates the “full multiplication” `self * rhs + carry`
without the possibility to overflow.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

Performs “long multiplication” which takes in an extra amount to add, and may return an additional amount of overflow. This allows for chaining together multiple multiplications to create “big integers” which represent larger values.

If you don’t need the `carry`, then you can use [ Self::widening_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html#method.widening_mul) instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-89)Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `i32` is used.

```
#![feature(signed_bigint_helpers)]
assert_eq!(5i32.carrying_mul(-2, 0), (4294967286, -1));
assert_eq!(5i32.carrying_mul(-2, 10), (0, 0));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000i32.carrying_mul(-10, 0), (2884901888, -3));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000i32.carrying_mul(-10, 10), (2884901898, -3));
assert_eq!(i64::MAX.carrying_mul(i64::MAX, i64::MAX), (i64::MAX.unsigned_abs() + 1, i64::MAX / 2));
```
Calculates the “full multiplication” `self * rhs + carry + add`
without the possibility to overflow.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

Performs “long multiplication” which takes in an extra amount to add, and may return an additional amount of overflow. This allows for chaining together multiple multiplications to create “big integers” which represent larger values.

If you don’t need either `carry`, then you can use [ Self::widening_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html#method.widening_mul) instead,
and if you only need one

`carry`, then you can use [instead.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html#method.carrying_mul)

```
#![feature(signed_bigint_helpers)]

assert_eq!(5i32.carrying_mul_add(-2, 10, 10), (10, 0));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000i32.carrying_mul_add(-10, 0, 0), (2884901888, -3));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000i32.carrying_mul_add(-10, 10, 10), (2884901908, -3));
assert_eq!(i64::MAX.carrying_mul_add(i64::MAX, i64::MAX, i64::MAX), (u64::MAX, i64::MAX / 2));
```

1.38.0 (const: 1.52.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#414-433)#### pub const fn [div_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.div_euclid)(self, rhs: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)) -> [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#414-433)

#### pub const fn [div_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.div_euclid)(self, rhs: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)) -> [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)

Calculates the quotient of Euclidean division of `self` by `rhs`.

This computes the integer `q` such that `self = q * rhs + r`, with
`r = self.rem_euclid(rhs)` and `0 <= r < abs(rhs)`.

In other words, the result is `self / rhs` rounded to the integer `q`
such that `self >= q * rhs`.
If `self > 0`, this is equal to rounding towards zero (the default in Rust);
if `self < 0`, this is equal to rounding away from zero (towards +/- infinity).
If `rhs > 0`, this is equal to rounding towards -infinity;
if `rhs < 0`, this is equal to rounding towards +infinity.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-25)Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero or if `self` is `Self::MIN`
and `rhs` is -1. This behavior is not affected by the `overflow-checks` flag.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-102)Examples

1.38.0 (const: 1.52.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#414-433)#### pub const fn [rem_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.rem_euclid)(self, rhs: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)) -> [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#414-433)

#### pub const fn [rem_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.rem_euclid)(self, rhs: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)) -> [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i64.html)

Calculates the least nonnegative remainder of `self` when
divided by `rhs`.

This is done as if by the Euclidean division algorithm – given
`r = self.rem_euclid(rhs)`, the result satisfies
`self = rhs * self.div_euclid(rhs) + r` and `0 <= r < abs(rhs)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-26)Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero or if `self` is `Self::MIN` and
`rhs` is -1. This behavior is not affected by the `overflow-checks` flag.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-103)Examples

```
let a: i64 = 7; // or any other integer type
let b = 4;
assert_eq!(a.rem_euclid(b), 3);
assert_eq!((-a).rem_euclid(b), 1);
assert_eq!(a.rem_euclid(-b), 3);
assert_eq!((-a).rem_euclid(-b), 1);
```

`midpoint(a, b)` is `(a + b) / 2` as if it were performed in a
sufficiently-large signed integral type. This implies that the result is
always rounded towards zero and that no overflow will ever occur.

# i128 - Rust

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.i128.html

# Primitive Type i128

## Expand description

The 128-bit signed integer type.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#abi-compatibility)ABI compatibility

Rust’s `i128` is expected to be ABI-compatible with C’s `__int128` on platforms where the type
is available, which includes most 64-bit architectures. If any platforms that do not specify
`__int128` are updated to introduce it, the Rust `i128` ABI on relevant targets will be changed
to match.

It is important to note that in C, `__int128` is *not* the same as `_BitInt(128)`, and the two
types are allowed to have different ABIs. In particular, on x86, `__int128` and `_BitInt(128)`
do not use the same alignment. `i128` is intended to always match `__int128` and does not
attempt to match `_BitInt(128)` on platforms without `__int128`.

Shifts the bits to the left by a specified amount, `n`,
wrapping the truncated bits to the end of the resulting integer.

`rotate_left(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_left(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn’t the same operation as the `<<` shifting operator!

1.79.0 (const: 1.79.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#438-459)#### pub const unsafe fn [unchecked_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unchecked_add)(self, rhs: [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)) -> [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#438-459)

#### pub const unsafe fn [unchecked_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unchecked_add)(self, rhs: [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)) -> [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)

Unchecked integer addition. Computes `self + rhs`, assuming overflow
cannot occur.

Calling `x.unchecked_add(y)` is semantically equivalent to calling
`x.``checked_add``(y).``unwrap_unchecked``()`.

`None`.1.87.0 (const: 1.87.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#438-459)#### pub const fn [unbounded_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unbounded_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#438-459)

#### pub const fn [unbounded_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unbounded_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)

Unbounded shift left. Computes `self << rhs`, without bounding the value of `rhs`.

If `rhs` is larger or equal to the number of bits in `self`,
the entire value is shifted out, and `0` is returned.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-46)Examples

```
assert_eq!(0x1_i128.unbounded_shl(4), 0x10);
assert_eq!(0x1_i128.unbounded_shl(129), 0);
assert_eq!(0b101_i128.unbounded_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_i128.unbounded_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_i128.unbounded_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(42_i128.unbounded_shl(128), 0);
assert_eq!(42_i128.unbounded_shl(1).unbounded_shl(127), 0);
assert_eq!((-13_i128).unbounded_shl(128), 0);
assert_eq!((-13_i128).unbounded_shl(1).unbounded_shl(127), 0);
```
Exact shift left. Computes `self << rhs` as long as it can be reversed losslessly.

Returns `None` if any bits that would be shifted out differ from the resulting sign bit
or if `rhs` >=
`i128::BITS`.
Otherwise, returns `Some(self << rhs)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-47)Examples

```
#![feature(exact_bitshifts)]
assert_eq!(0x1i128.shl_exact(4), Some(0x10));
assert_eq!(0x1i128.shl_exact(i128::BITS - 2), Some(1 << i128::BITS - 2));

Unbounded shift right. Computes `self >> rhs`, without bounding the value of `rhs`.

If `rhs` is larger or equal to the number of bits in `self`,
the entire value is shifted out, which yields `0` for a positive number,
and `-1` for a negative number.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-50)Examples

```
assert_eq!(0x10_i128.unbounded_shr(4), 0x1);
assert_eq!(0x10_i128.unbounded_shr(129), 0);
assert_eq!(i128::MIN.unbounded_shr(129), -1);
assert_eq!(0b1010_i128.unbounded_shr(0), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b1010_i128.unbounded_shr(1), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b1010_i128.unbounded_shr(2), 0b10);
assert_eq!(42_i128.unbounded_shr(128), 0);
assert_eq!(42_i128.unbounded_shr(1).unbounded_shr(127), 0);
assert_eq!((-13_i128).unbounded_shr(128), -1);
assert_eq!((-13_i128).unbounded_shr(1).unbounded_shr(127), -1);
```
Exact shift right. Computes `self >> rhs` as long as it can be reversed losslessly.

Returns `None` if any non-zero bits would be shifted out or if `rhs` >=
`i128::BITS`.
Otherwise, returns `Some(self >> rhs)`.

Wrapping (modular) division. Computes `self / rhs`, wrapping around at the
boundary of the type.

The only case where such wrapping can occur is when one divides `MIN / -1` on a signed type (where
`MIN` is the negative minimal value for the type); this is equivalent to `-MIN`, a positive value
that is too large to represent in the type. In such a case, this function returns `MIN` itself.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-16)Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-71)Examples

#### pub const fn [wrapping_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)

Panic-free bitwise shift-left; yields `self << mask(rhs)`, where `mask` removes
any high-order bits of `rhs` that would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed.  The behaviour matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `<<` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it’s weird.  Consider, instead,
using [ Self::unbounded_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html#method.unbounded_shl) which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-left; the RHS of a wrapping shift-left is restricted to
the range of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS being returned to the other end.
The primitive integer types all implement a [ rotate_left](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html#method.rotate_left) function,
which may be what you want instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-76)Examples

Wrapping (modular) absolute value. Computes `self.abs()`, wrapping around at
the boundary of the type.

The only case where such wrapping can occur is when one takes the absolute value of the negative
minimal value for the type; this is a positive value that is too large to represent in the type. In
such a case, this function returns `MIN` itself.

1.7.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#438-459)#### pub const fn [overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_add)(self, rhs: [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)) -> ([i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#438-459)

#### pub const fn [overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_add)(self, rhs: [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)) -> ([i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

Calculates `self` + `rhs` + `carry` and checks for overflow.

Performs “ternary addition” of two integer operands and a carry-in bit, and returns a tuple of the sum along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. On overflow, the wrapped value is returned.

This allows chaining together multiple additions to create a wider
addition, and can be useful for bignum addition. This method should
only be used for the most significant word; for the less significant
words the unsigned method
[ u128::carrying_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html#method.carrying_add)
should be used.

The output boolean returned by this method is *not* a carry flag,
and should *not* be added to a more significant word.

If overflow occurred, the wrapped value is returned (negative if overflowed
above [ MAX](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html#associatedconstant.MAX), non-negative if below

[).](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html#associatedconstant.MIN)

`MIN`If the input carry is false, this method is equivalent to
[ overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html#method.overflowing_add).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-82)Examples

```
#![feature(signed_bigint_helpers)]
// Only the most significant word is signed.
//
//   10  MAX    (a = 10 × 2^128 + 2^128 - 1)
// + -5    9    (b = -5 × 2^128 + 9)
// ---------
//    6    8    (sum = 6 × 2^128 + 8)
let (a1, a0): (i128, u128) = (10, u128::MAX);
let (b1, b0): (i128, u128) = (-5, 9);
let carry0 = false;
// u128::carrying_add for the less significant words
let (sum0, carry1) = a0.carrying_add(b0, carry0);
assert_eq!(carry1, true);
// i128::carrying_add for the most significant word
let (sum1, overflow) = a1.carrying_add(b1, carry1);
assert_eq!(overflow, false);
assert_eq!((sum1, sum0), (6, 8));
```

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#438-459)

Calculates `self` − `rhs` − `borrow` and checks for
overflow.

Performs “ternary subtraction” by subtracting both an integer
operand and a borrow-in bit from `self`, and returns a tuple of the
difference along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic
overflow would occur. On overflow, the wrapped value is returned.

This allows chaining together multiple subtractions to create a
wider subtraction, and can be useful for bignum subtraction. This
method should only be used for the most significant word; for the
less significant words the unsigned method
[ u128::borrowing_sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html#method.borrowing_sub)
should be used.

The output boolean returned by this method is *not* a borrow flag,
and should *not* be subtracted from a more significant word.

If overflow occurred, the wrapped value is returned (negative if overflowed
above [ MAX](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html#associatedconstant.MAX), non-negative if below

[).](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html#associatedconstant.MIN)

`MIN`If the input borrow is false, this method is equivalent to
[ overflowing_sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html#method.overflowing_sub).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-85)Examples

```
#![feature(signed_bigint_helpers)]
// Only the most significant word is signed.
//
//    6    8    (a = 6 × 2^128 + 8)
// - -5    9    (b = -5 × 2^128 + 9)
// ---------
//   10  MAX    (diff = 10 × 2^128 + 2^128 - 1)

let (b1, b0): (i128, u128) = (-5, 9);

```

Calculates the complete product `self * rhs` without the possibility to overflow.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

If you also need to add a carry to the wide result, then you want
[ Self::carrying_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html#method.carrying_mul) instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-88)Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `i32` is used.

Calculates the “full multiplication” `self * rhs + carry`
without the possibility to overflow.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

Performs “long multiplication” which takes in an extra amount to add, and may return an additional amount of overflow. This allows for chaining together multiple multiplications to create “big integers” which represent larger values.

If you don’t need the `carry`, then you can use [ Self::widening_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html#method.widening_mul) instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-89)Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `i32` is used.

```
#![feature(signed_bigint_helpers)]
assert_eq!(5i32.carrying_mul(-2, 0), (4294967286, -1));
assert_eq!(5i32.carrying_mul(-2, 10), (0, 0));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000i32.carrying_mul(-10, 0), (2884901888, -3));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000i32.carrying_mul(-10, 10), (2884901898, -3));
assert_eq!(i128::MAX.carrying_mul(i128::MAX, i128::MAX), (i128::MAX.unsigned_abs() + 1, i128::MAX / 2));
```

1.38.0 (const: 1.52.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#438-459)#### pub const fn [div_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.div_euclid)(self, rhs: [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)) -> [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#438-459)

#### pub const fn [div_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.div_euclid)(self, rhs: [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)) -> [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)

Calculates the quotient of Euclidean division of `self` by `rhs`.

This computes the integer `q` such that `self = q * rhs + r`, with
`r = self.rem_euclid(rhs)` and `0 <= r < abs(rhs)`.

In other words, the result is `self / rhs` rounded to the integer `q`
such that `self >= q * rhs`.
If `self > 0`, this is equal to rounding towards zero (the default in Rust);
if `self < 0`, this is equal to rounding away from zero (towards +/- infinity).
If `rhs > 0`, this is equal to rounding towards -infinity;
if `rhs < 0`, this is equal to rounding towards +infinity.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-25)Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero or if `self` is `Self::MIN`
and `rhs` is -1. This behavior is not affected by the `overflow-checks` flag.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-102)Examples

1.38.0 (const: 1.52.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#438-459)#### pub const fn [rem_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.rem_euclid)(self, rhs: [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)) -> [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#438-459)

#### pub const fn [rem_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.rem_euclid)(self, rhs: [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)) -> [i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)

Calculates the least nonnegative remainder of `self` when
divided by `rhs`.

This is done as if by the Euclidean division algorithm – given
`r = self.rem_euclid(rhs)`, the result satisfies
`self = rhs * self.div_euclid(rhs) + r` and `0 <= r < abs(rhs)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-26)Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero or if `self` is `Self::MIN` and
`rhs` is -1. This behavior is not affected by the `overflow-checks` flag.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-103)Examples

```
let a: i128 = 7; // or any other integer type
let b = 4;
assert_eq!(a.rem_euclid(b), 3);
assert_eq!((-a).rem_euclid(b), 1);
assert_eq!(a.rem_euclid(-b), 3);
assert_eq!((-a).rem_euclid(-b), 1);
```

Computes the absolute value of `self`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#overflow-behavior-16)Overflow behavior

The absolute value of
`i128::MIN`
cannot be represented as an
`i128`,
and attempting to calculate it will cause an overflow. This means
that code in debug mode will trigger a panic on this case and
optimized code will return
`i128::MIN`
without a panic. If you do not want this behavior, consider
using [ unsigned_abs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html#method.unsigned_abs) instead.

Parses an integer from a string slice with digits in a given base.

The string is expected to be an optional
`+` or `-`
sign followed by only digits. Leading and trailing non-digit characters (including
whitespace) represent an error. Underscores (which are accepted in Rust literals)
also represent an error.

Digits are a subset of these characters, depending on `radix`:

- `0-9`
- `a-z`
- `A-Z`

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-33)Panics

This function panics if `radix` is not in the range from 2 to 36.

) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/result/enum.Result.html)<[i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html), [ParseIntError](https://doc.rust-lang.org/num/struct.ParseIntError.html)>

Parses an integer from an ASCII-byte slice with digits in a given base.

The characters are expected to be an optional
`+` or `-`
sign followed by only digits. Leading and trailing non-digit characters (including
whitespace) represent an error. Underscores (which are accepted in Rust literals)
also represent an error.

Digits are a subset of these characters, depending on `radix`:

- `0-9`
- `a-z`
- `A-Z`

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-34)Panics

This function panics if `radix` is not in the range from 2 to 36.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-131)Examples

Trailing space returns error:

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/fmt/num.rs.html#796)#### pub fn [format_into](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.format_into)(self, buf: &mut [NumBuffer](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/num_buffer/struct.NumBuffer.html)<[i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)>) -> &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/fmt/num.rs.html#796)

#### pub fn [format_into](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.format_into)(self, buf: &mut [NumBuffer](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/num_buffer/struct.NumBuffer.html)<[i128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i128.html)>) -> &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html)

Allows users to write an integer (in signed decimal format) into a variable `buf` of
type [ NumBuffer](https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/fmt/num_buffer/struct.NumBuffer.html) that is passed by the caller by mutable reference.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-132)Examples

```
#![feature(int_format_into)]
use core::fmt::NumBuffer;
let n = 0i128;
let mut buf = NumBuffer::new();
assert_eq!(n.format_into(&mut buf), "0");
let n1 = i128::MIN;
assert_eq!(n1.format_into(&mut buf), i128::MIN.to_string());
let n2 = i128::MAX;
assert_eq!(n2.format_into(&mut buf), i128::MAX.to_string());
```

# isize - Rust

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.isize.html

# Primitive Type isize

## Expand description

The pointer-sized signed integer type.

The size of this primitive is how many bytes it takes to reference any location in memory. For example, on a 32 bit target, this is 4 bytes and on a 64 bit target, this is 8 bytes.

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#515-534)

#### pub const fn [rotate_left](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.rotate_left)(self, n: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)

**64-bit**only.

Shifts the bits to the left by a specified amount, `n`,
wrapping the truncated bits to the end of the resulting integer.

`rotate_left(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_left(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn’t the same operation as the `<<` shifting operator!

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-14)Examples

**64-bit**only.

Swaps bytes of `self` on little endian targets.

On big endian this is a no-op.

The returned value has the same type as `self`, and will be interpreted
as (a potentially different) value of a native-endian
`isize`.

See [ to_be_bytes()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html#method.to_be_bytes) for a type-safe alternative.

**64-bit**only.

Unchecked integer addition. Computes `self + rhs`, assuming overflow
cannot occur.

Calling `x.unchecked_add(y)` is semantically equivalent to calling
`x.``checked_add``(y).``unwrap_unchecked``()`.

If you’re just trying to avoid the panic in debug mode, then **do not**
use this.  Instead, you’re looking for [ wrapping_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html#method.wrapping_add).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety)Safety

This results in undefined behavior when
`self + rhs > isize::MAX` or `self + rhs < isize::MIN`,
i.e. when [ checked_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html#method.checked_add) would return

**64-bit**only.

Unbounded shift left. Computes `self << rhs`, without bounding the value of `rhs`.

If `rhs` is larger or equal to the number of bits in `self`,
the entire value is shifted out, and `0` is returned.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-46)Examples

```
assert_eq!(0x1_isize.unbounded_shl(4), 0x10);
assert_eq!(0x1_isize.unbounded_shl(129), 0);
assert_eq!(0b101_isize.unbounded_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_isize.unbounded_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_isize.unbounded_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(42_isize.unbounded_shl(64), 0);
assert_eq!(42_isize.unbounded_shl(1).unbounded_shl(63), 0);
assert_eq!((-13_isize).unbounded_shl(64), 0);
assert_eq!((-13_isize).unbounded_shl(1).unbounded_shl(63), 0);
```
Exact shift left. Computes `self << rhs` as long as it can be reversed losslessly.

Returns `None` if any bits that would be shifted out differ from the resulting sign bit
or if `rhs` >=
`isize::BITS`.
Otherwise, returns `Some(self << rhs)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-47)Examples

```
#![feature(exact_bitshifts)]
assert_eq!(0x1isize.shl_exact(4), Some(0x10));
assert_eq!(0x1isize.shl_exact(isize::BITS - 2), Some(1 << isize::BITS - 2));
assert_eq!(0x1isize.shl_exact(isize::BITS - 1), None);
assert_eq!((-0x2isize).shl_exact(isize::BITS - 2), Some(-0x2 << isize::BITS - 2));
assert_eq!((-0x2isize).shl_exact(isize::BITS - 1), None);
```
[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#515-534)#### pub const unsafe fn [unchecked_shl_exact](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unchecked_shl_exact)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)

**64-bit** only.

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#515-534)

#### pub const unsafe fn [unchecked_shl_exact](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unchecked_shl_exact)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)

**64-bit**only.

Unchecked exact shift left. Computes `self << rhs`, assuming the operation can be
losslessly reversed and `rhs` cannot be larger than
`isize::BITS`.

#### pub const fn [unbounded_shr](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unbounded_shr)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)

**64-bit**only.

Unbounded shift right. Computes `self >> rhs`, without bounding the value of `rhs`.

If `rhs` is larger or equal to the number of bits in `self`,
the entire value is shifted out, which yields `0` for a positive number,
and `-1` for a negative number.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-50)Examples

```
assert_eq!(0x10_isize.unbounded_shr(4), 0x1);
assert_eq!(0x10_isize.unbounded_shr(129), 0);
assert_eq!(isize::MIN.unbounded_shr(129), -1);
assert_eq!(0b1010_isize.unbounded_shr(0), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b1010_isize.unbounded_shr(1), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b1010_isize.unbounded_shr(2), 0b10);
assert_eq!(42_isize.unbounded_shr(64), 0);
assert_eq!(42_isize.unbounded_shr(1).unbounded_shr(63), 0);
assert_eq!((-13_isize).unbounded_shr(64), -1);
assert_eq!((-13_isize).unbounded_shr(1).unbounded_shr(63), -1);
```
Exact shift right. Computes `self >> rhs` as long as it can be reversed losslessly.

Returns `None` if any non-zero bits would be shifted out or if `rhs` >=
`isize::BITS`.
Otherwise, returns `Some(self >> rhs)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-51)Examples

**64-bit**only.

Wrapping (modular) division. Computes `self / rhs`, wrapping around at the
boundary of the type.

The only case where such wrapping can occur is when one divides `MIN / -1` on a signed type (where
`MIN` is the negative minimal value for the type); this is equivalent to `-MIN`, a positive value
that is too large to represent in the type. In such a case, this function returns `MIN` itself.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-16)Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-71)Examples

1.2.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#515-534)#### pub const fn [wrapping_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)

 Available on **64-bit** only.

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#515-534)

#### pub const fn [wrapping_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)

**64-bit**only.

Panic-free bitwise shift-left; yields `self << mask(rhs)`, where `mask` removes
any high-order bits of `rhs` that would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed.  The behaviour matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `<<` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it’s weird.  Consider, instead,
using [ Self::unbounded_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html#method.unbounded_shl) which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-left; the RHS of a wrapping shift-left is restricted to
the range of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS being returned to the other end.
The primitive integer types all implement a [ rotate_left](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html#method.rotate_left) function,
which may be what you want instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-76)Examples

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#515-534)#### pub const fn [carrying_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.carrying_add)(self, rhs: [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html), carry: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html)) -> ([isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

**64-bit** only.

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#515-534)

#### pub const fn [carrying_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.carrying_add)(self, rhs: [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html), carry: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html)) -> ([isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

**64-bit**only.

Calculates `self` + `rhs` + `carry` and checks for overflow.

Performs “ternary addition” of two integer operands and a carry-in bit, and returns a tuple of the sum along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. On overflow, the wrapped value is returned.

This allows chaining together multiple additions to create a wider
addition, and can be useful for bignum addition. This method should
only be used for the most significant word; for the less significant
words the unsigned method
[ usize::carrying_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html#method.carrying_add)
should be used.

The output boolean returned by this method is *not* a carry flag,
and should *not* be added to a more significant word.

If overflow occurred, the wrapped value is returned (negative if overflowed
above [ MAX](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html#associatedconstant.MAX), non-negative if below

[).](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html#associatedconstant.MIN)

`MIN`If the input carry is false, this method is equivalent to
[ overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html#method.overflowing_add).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-82)Examples

```
#![feature(signed_bigint_helpers)]
// Only the most significant word is signed.
//
//   10  MAX    (a = 10 × 2^64 + 2^64 - 1)
// + -5    9    (b = -5 × 2^64 + 9)
// ---------
//    6    8    (sum = 6 × 2^64 + 8)
let (a1, a0): (isize, usize) = (10, usize::MAX);
let (b1, b0): (isize, usize) = (-5, 9);
let carry0 = false;
// usize::carrying_add for the less significant words
let (sum0, carry1) = a0.carrying_add(b0, carry0);
assert_eq!(carry1, true);
// isize::carrying_add for the most significant word
let (sum1, overflow) = a1.carrying_add(b1, carry1);
assert_eq!(overflow, false);
assert_eq!((sum1, sum0), (6, 8));
```

[ usize::borrowing_sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html#method.borrowing_sub)

and should *not* be subtracted from a more significant word.

above [ MAX](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html#associatedconstant.MAX), non-negative if below

[).](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html#associatedconstant.MIN)

`MIN`If the input borrow is false, this method is equivalent to

**64-bit**only.

Calculates the “full multiplication” `self * rhs + carry`
without the possibility to overflow.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

Performs “long multiplication” which takes in an extra amount to add, and may return an additional amount of overflow. This allows for chaining together multiple multiplications to create “big integers” which represent larger values.

If you don’t need the `carry`, then you can use [ Self::widening_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html#method.widening_mul) instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-89)Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `i32` is used.

```
#![feature(signed_bigint_helpers)]
assert_eq!(5i32.carrying_mul(-2, 0), (4294967286, -1));
assert_eq!(5i32.carrying_mul(-2, 10), (0, 0));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000i32.carrying_mul(-10, 0), (2884901888, -3));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000i32.carrying_mul(-10, 10), (2884901898, -3));
assert_eq!(isize::MAX.carrying_mul(isize::MAX, isize::MAX), (isize::MAX.unsigned_abs() + 1, isize::MAX / 2));
```

1.38.0 (const: 1.52.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#515-534)#### pub const fn [div_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.div_euclid)(self, rhs: [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)) -> [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)

 Available on **64-bit** only.

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#515-534)

#### pub const fn [div_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.div_euclid)(self, rhs: [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)) -> [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)

**64-bit**only.

Calculates the quotient of Euclidean division of `self` by `rhs`.

This computes the integer `q` such that `self = q * rhs + r`, with
`r = self.rem_euclid(rhs)` and `0 <= r < abs(rhs)`.

In other words, the result is `self / rhs` rounded to the integer `q`
such that `self >= q * rhs`.
If `self > 0`, this is equal to rounding towards zero (the default in Rust);
if `self < 0`, this is equal to rounding away from zero (towards +/- infinity).
If `rhs > 0`, this is equal to rounding towards -infinity;
if `rhs < 0`, this is equal to rounding towards +infinity.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-25)Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero or if `self` is `Self::MIN`
and `rhs` is -1. This behavior is not affected by the `overflow-checks` flag.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-102)Examples

1.38.0 (const: 1.52.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#515-534)#### pub const fn [rem_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.rem_euclid)(self, rhs: [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)) -> [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)

 Available on **64-bit** only.

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#515-534)

#### pub const fn [rem_euclid](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.rem_euclid)(self, rhs: [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)) -> [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)

**64-bit**only.

Calculates the least nonnegative remainder of `self` when
divided by `rhs`.

This is done as if by the Euclidean division algorithm – given
`r = self.rem_euclid(rhs)`, the result satisfies
`self = rhs * self.div_euclid(rhs) + r` and `0 <= r < abs(rhs)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-26)Panics

This function will panic if `rhs` is zero or if `self` is `Self::MIN` and
`rhs` is -1. This behavior is not affected by the `overflow-checks` flag.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-103)Examples

```
let a: isize = 7; // or any other integer type
let b = 4;
assert_eq!(a.rem_euclid(b), 3);
assert_eq!((-a).rem_euclid(b), 1);
assert_eq!(a.rem_euclid(-b), 3);
assert_eq!((-a).rem_euclid(-b), 1);
```
This will panic:

**Note**: This function takes an array of length 2, 4 or 8 bytes
depending on the target pointer size.

# pointer - Rust

Source: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.pointer.html

# Primitive Type pointer

## Expand description

Raw, unsafe pointers, `*const T`, and `*mut T`.

Working with raw pointers in Rust is uncommon, typically limited to a few patterns. Raw pointers
can be out-of-bounds, unaligned, or [ null](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/fn.null.html). However, when loading from or storing to a raw
pointer, it must be

[valid](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/index.html#safety)for the given access and aligned. When using a field expression, tuple index expression, or array/slice index expression on a raw pointer, it follows the rules of

[in-bounds pointer arithmetic](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html#method.offset).

Storing through a raw pointer using `*ptr = data` calls `drop` on the old value, so
[ write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/fn.write.html) must be used if the type has drop glue and memory is not already
initialized - otherwise

`drop` would be called on the uninitialized memory.Use the [ null](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/fn.null.html) and

[functions to create null pointers, and the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/fn.null_mut.html)

`null_mut`[method of the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html#method.is_null)

`is_null``*const T` and `*mut T` types to check for null.
The `*const T` and `*mut T` types also define the [method, for pointer math.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html#method.offset)

`offset`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#common-ways-to-create-raw-pointers)Common ways to create raw pointers

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#1-coerce-a-reference-t-or-mutable-reference-mut-t)1. Coerce a reference (`&T`) or mutable reference (`&mut T`).

```
let my_num: i32 = 10;
let my_num_ptr: *const i32 = &my_num;
let mut my_speed: i32 = 88;
let my_speed_ptr: *mut i32 = &mut my_speed;
```
To get a pointer to a boxed value, dereference the box:

```
let my_num: Box<i32> = Box::new(10);
let my_num_ptr: *const i32 = &*my_num;
let mut my_speed: Box<i32> = Box::new(88);
let my_speed_ptr: *mut i32 = &mut *my_speed;
```
This does not take ownership of the original allocation and requires no resource management later, but you must not use the pointer after its lifetime.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#2-consume-a-box-boxt)2. Consume a box (`Box<T>`).

The [ into_raw](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/boxed/struct.Box.html#method.into_raw) function consumes a box and returns
the raw pointer. It doesn’t destroy

`T` or deallocate any memory.```
let my_speed: Box<i32> = Box::new(88);
let my_speed: *mut i32 = Box::into_raw(my_speed);
// By taking ownership of the original `Box<T>` though
// we are obligated to put it together later to be destroyed.
unsafe {
    drop(Box::from_raw(my_speed));
}
```
Note that here the call to [ drop](https://doc.rust-lang.org/mem/fn.drop.html) is for clarity - it indicates
that we are done with the given value and it should be destroyed.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#3-create-it-using-raw)3. Create it using `&raw`

Instead of coercing a reference to a raw pointer, you can use the raw borrow
operators `&raw const` (for `*const T`) and `&raw mut` (for `*mut T`).
These operators allow you to create raw pointers to fields to which you cannot
create a reference (without causing undefined behavior), such as an
unaligned field. This might be necessary if packed structs or uninitialized
memory is involved.

```
#[derive(Debug, Default, Copy, Clone)]
#[repr(C, packed)]
struct S {
    aligned: u8,
    unaligned: u32,
}
let s = S::default();
let p = &raw const s.unaligned; // not allowed with coercion
```
[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#4-get-it-from-c)4. Get it from C.

```
#[allow(unused_extern_crates)]
extern crate libc;
unsafe {
    let my_num: *mut i32 = libc::malloc(size_of::<i32>()) as *mut i32;
    if my_num.is_null() {
        panic!("failed to allocate memory");
    }
    libc::free(my_num as *mut core::ffi::c_void);
}
```
Usually you wouldn’t literally use `malloc` and `free` from Rust,
but C APIs hand out a lot of pointers generally, so are a common source
of raw pointers in Rust.

## Implementations[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#implementations)

Returns `true` if the pointer is null.

Note that unsized types have many possible null pointers, as only the raw data pointer is considered, not their length, vtable, etc. Therefore, two pointers that are null may still not compare equal to each other.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-during-const-evaluation)Panics during const evaluation

If this method is used during const evaluation, and `self` is a pointer
that is offset beyond the bounds of the memory it initially pointed to,
then there might not be enough information to determine whether the
pointer is null. This is because the absolute address in memory is not
known at compile time. If the nullness of the pointer cannot be
determined, this method will panic.

In-bounds pointers are never null, so the method will never panic for such pointers.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples)Examples

Casts to a pointer of another type.

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/ptr/const_ptr.rs.html#74)#### pub fn [try_cast_aligned](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.try_cast_aligned)<U>(self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/option/enum.Option.html)<[*const U](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html)>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/ptr/const_ptr.rs.html#74)

#### pub fn [try_cast_aligned](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.try_cast_aligned)<U>(self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/option/enum.Option.html)<[*const U](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html)>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/ptr/const_ptr.rs.html#130-132)#### pub const fn [with_metadata_of](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.with_metadata_of)<U>(self, meta: [*const U](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html)) -> [*const U](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/ptr/const_ptr.rs.html#130-132)

#### pub const fn [with_metadata_of](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.with_metadata_of)<U>(self, meta: [*const U](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html)) -> [*const U](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html)

Uses the address value in a new pointer of another type.

This operation will ignore the address part of its `meta` operand and discard existing
metadata of `self`. For pointers to a sized types (thin pointers), this has the same effect
as a simple cast. For pointers to an unsized type (fat pointers) this recombines the address
with new metadata such as slice lengths or `dyn`-vtable.

The resulting pointer will have provenance of `self`. This operation is semantically the
same as creating a new pointer with the data pointer value of `self` but the metadata of
`meta`, being fat or thin depending on the `meta` operand.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-2)Examples

This function is primarily useful for enabling pointer arithmetic on potentially fat pointers. The pointer is cast to a sized pointee to utilize offset operations and then recombined with its own original metadata.

```
#![feature(set_ptr_value)]
let arr: [i32; 3] = [1, 2, 3];
let mut ptr = arr.as_ptr() as *const dyn Debug;
let thin = ptr as *const u8;
unsafe {
    ptr = thin.add(8).with_metadata_of(ptr);
    println!("{:?}", &*ptr); // will print "3"
}
```
[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#incorrect-usage)*Incorrect* usage

The provenance from pointers is *not* combined. The result must only be used to refer to the
address allowed by `self`.

```
#![feature(set_ptr_value)]
let x = 0u32;
let y = 1u32;
let x = (&x) as *const u32;
let y = (&y) as *const u32;
let offset = (x as usize - y as usize) / 4;
let bad = x.wrapping_add(offset).with_metadata_of(y);
// This dereference is UB. The pointer only has provenance for `x` but points to `y`.
println!("{:?}", unsafe { &*bad });
```
Changes constness without changing the type.

This is a bit safer than `as` because it wouldn’t silently change the type if the code is
refactored.

Gets the “address” portion of the pointer.

This is similar to `self as usize`, except that the [provenance](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/index.html#provenance) of
the pointer is discarded and not [exposed](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/index.html#exposed-provenance). This means that
casting the returned address back to a pointer yields a [pointer without
provenance](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/fn.without_provenance.html), which is undefined behavior to dereference. To properly
restore the lost information and obtain a dereferenceable pointer, use
[ with_addr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html#method.with_addr) or

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html#method.map_addr)

`map_addr`If using those APIs is not possible because there is no way to preserve a pointer with the
required provenance, then Strict Provenance might not be for you. Use pointer-integer casts
or [ expose_provenance](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html#method.expose_provenance) and

[instead. However, note that this makes your code less portable and less amenable to tools that check for compliance with the Rust memory model.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/fn.with_exposed_provenance.html)

`with_exposed_provenance`On most platforms this will produce a value with the same bytes as the original pointer, because all the bytes are dedicated to describing the address. Platforms which need to store additional information in the pointer may perform a change of representation to produce a value containing only the address portion of the pointer. What that means is up to the platform to define.

This is a [Strict Provenance](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/index.html#strict-provenance) API.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-during-const-evaluation-2)Panics during const evaluation

This method will panic during const evaluation if the pointer cannot be
determined to be null or not. See [ is_null](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.is_null) for more information.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-5)Examples

Adds a signed offset to a pointer.

`count` is in units of T; e.g., a `count` of 3 represents a pointer
offset of `3 * size_of::<T>()` bytes.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety-3)Safety

If any of the following conditions are violated, the result is Undefined Behavior:

-
The offset in bytes, `count * size_of::<T>()`, computed on mathematical integers (without “wrapping around”), must fit in an`isize`.
-
If the computed offset is non-zero, then `self`must be[derived from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/index.html#provenance)a pointer to some[allocation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/index.html#allocation), and the entire memory range between`self`and the result must be in bounds of that allocation. In particular, this range must not “wrap around” the edge of the address space. Note that “range” here refers to a half-open range as usual in Rust, i.e.,`self..result`for non-negative offsets and`result..self`for negative offsets.

Allocations can never be larger than `isize::MAX` bytes, so if the computed offset
stays in bounds of the allocation, it is guaranteed to satisfy the first requirement.
This implies, for instance, that `vec.as_ptr().add(vec.len())` (for `vec: Vec<T>`) is always
safe.

Consider using [ wrapping_offset](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_offset) instead if these constraints are
difficult to satisfy. The only advantage of this method is that it
enables more aggressive compiler optimizations.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-6)Examples

1.16.0 (const: 1.61.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/ptr/const_ptr.rs.html#463-465)#### pub const fn [wrapping_offset](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_offset)(self, count: [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)) -> [*const T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/ptr/const_ptr.rs.html#463-465)

#### pub const fn [wrapping_offset](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_offset)(self, count: [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)) -> [*const T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html)

Adds a signed offset to a pointer using wrapping arithmetic.

`count` is in units of T; e.g., a `count` of 3 represents a pointer
offset of `3 * size_of::<T>()` bytes.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety-4)Safety

This operation itself is always safe, but using the resulting pointer is not.

The resulting pointer “remembers” the [allocation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/index.html#allocation) that `self` points to
(this is called “[Provenance](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/index.html#provenance)”).
The pointer must not be used to read or write other allocations.

In other words, `let z = x.wrapping_offset((y as isize) - (x as isize))` does *not* make `z`
the same as `y` even if we assume `T` has size `1` and there is no overflow: `z` is still
attached to the object `x` is attached to, and dereferencing it is Undefined Behavior unless
`x` and `y` point into the same allocation.

Compared to [ offset](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.offset), this method basically delays the requirement of staying within the
same allocation:

[is immediate Undefined Behavior when crossing object boundaries;](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.offset)

`offset``wrapping_offset` produces a pointer but still leads to Undefined Behavior if a
pointer is dereferenced when it is out-of-bounds of the object it is attached to. [can be optimized better and is thus preferable in performance-sensitive code.](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.offset)

`offset`The delayed check only considers the value of the pointer that was dereferenced, not the
intermediate values used during the computation of the final result. For example,
`x.wrapping_offset(o).wrapping_offset(o.wrapping_neg())` is always the same as `x`. In other
words, leaving the allocation and then re-entering it later is permitted.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-7)Examples

```
// Iterate using a raw pointer in increments of two elements
let data = [1u8, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let mut ptr: *const u8 = data.as_ptr();
let step = 2;
let end_rounded_up = ptr.wrapping_offset(6);
let mut out = String::new();
while ptr != end_rounded_up {
    unsafe {
        write!(&mut out, "{}, ", *ptr)?;
    }
    ptr = ptr.wrapping_offset(step);
}
assert_eq!(out.as_str(), "1, 3, 5, ");
```

This is purely a convenience for casting to a `u8` pointer and

Masks out bits of the pointer according to a mask.

This is convenience for `ptr.map_addr(|a| a & mask)`.

For non-`Sized` pointees this operation changes only the data pointer,
leaving the metadata untouched.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-8)Examples

```
#![feature(ptr_mask)]
let v = 17_u32;
let ptr: *const u32 = &v;
// `u32` is 4 bytes aligned,
// which means that lower 2 bits are always 0.
let tag_mask = 0b11;
let ptr_mask = !tag_mask;
// We can store something in these lower bits
let tagged_ptr = ptr.map_addr(|a| a | 0b10);
// Get the "tag" back
let tag = tagged_ptr.addr() & tag_mask;
assert_eq!(tag, 0b10);
// Note that `tagged_ptr` is unaligned, it's UB to read from it.
// To get original pointer `mask` can be used:
let masked_ptr = tagged_ptr.mask(ptr_mask);
assert_eq!(unsafe { *masked_ptr }, 17);
```
1.47.0 (const: 1.65.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/ptr/const_ptr.rs.html#612-614)#### pub const unsafe fn [offset_from](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.offset_from)(self, origin: [*const T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html)) -> [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/ptr/const_ptr.rs.html#612-614)

#### pub const unsafe fn [offset_from](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.offset_from)(self, origin: [*const T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html)) -> [isize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.isize.html)

Calculates the distance between two pointers within the same allocation. The returned value is in
units of T: the distance in bytes divided by `size_of::<T>()`.

This is equivalent to `(self as isize - origin as isize) / (size_of::<T>() as isize)`,
except that it has a lot more opportunities for UB, in exchange for the compiler
better understanding what you are doing.

The primary motivation of this method is for computing the `len` of an array/slice
of `T` that you are currently representing as a “start” and “end” pointer
(and “end” is “one past the end” of the array).
In that case, `end.offset_from(start)` gets you the length of the array.

All of the following safety requirements are trivially satisfied for this usecase.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety-5)Safety

If any of the following conditions are violated, the result is Undefined Behavior:

-
`self`and`origin`must either- point to the same address, or
- both be [derived from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/index.html#provenance)a pointer to the same[allocation](https://doc.rust-lang.org/ptr/index.html#allocation), and the memory range between the two pointers must be in bounds of that object. (See below for an example.)

-
The distance between the pointers, in bytes, must be an exact multiple of the size of `T`.

As a consequence, the absolute distance between the pointers, in bytes, computed on
mathematical integers (without “wrapping around”), cannot overflow an `isize`. This is
implied by the in-bounds requirement, and the fact that no allocation can be larger
than `isize::MAX` bytes.

The requirement for pointers to be derived from the same allocation is primarily
needed for `const`-compatibility: the distance between pointers into *different* allocated
objects is not known at compile-time. However, the requirement also exists at
runtime and may be exploited by optimizations. If you wish to compute the difference between
pointers that are not guaranteed to be from the same allocation, use `(self as isize - origin as isize) / size_of::<T>()`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics)Panics

This function panics if `T` is a Zero-Sized Type (“ZST”).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-9)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let a = [0; 5];
let ptr1: *const i32 = &a[1];
let ptr2: *const i32 = &a[3];
unsafe {
    assert_eq!(ptr2.offset_from(ptr1), 2);
    assert_eq!(ptr1.offset_from(ptr2), -2);
    assert_eq!(ptr1.offset(2), ptr2);
    assert_eq!(ptr2.offset(-2), ptr1);
}
```
*Incorrect* usage:

```
let ptr1 = Box::into_raw(Box::new(0u8)) as *const u8;
let ptr2 = Box::into_raw(Box::new(1u8)) as *const u8;
let diff = (ptr2 as isize).wrapping_sub(ptr1 as isize);
// Make ptr2_other an "alias" of ptr2.add(1), but derived from ptr1.
let ptr2_other = (ptr1 as *const u8).wrapping_offset(diff).wrapping_offset(1);
assert_eq!(ptr2 as usize, ptr2_other as usize);
// Since ptr2_other and ptr2 are derived from pointers to different objects,
// computing their offset is undefined behavior, even though
// they point to addresses that are in-bounds of the same object!
unsafe {
    let one = ptr2_other.offset_from(ptr2); // Undefined Behavior! ⚠️
}
```

1.87.0 (const: 1.87.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/ptr/const_ptr.rs.html#701-703)#### pub const unsafe fn [offset_from_unsigned](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.offset_from_unsigned)(self, origin: [*const T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html)) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/ptr/const_ptr.rs.html#701-703)

#### pub const unsafe fn [offset_from_unsigned](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.offset_from_unsigned)(self, origin: [*const T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.pointer.html)) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.usize.html)

Calculates the distance between two pointers within the same allocation, *where it’s known that
 self is equal to or greater than origin*. The returned value is in
units of T: the distance in bytes is divided by

`size_of::<T>()`.This computes the same value that [ offset_from](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.offset_from)
would compute, but with the added precondition that the offset is
guaranteed to be non-negative.  This method is equivalent to

`usize::try_from(self.offset_from(origin)).unwrap_unchecked()`,
but it provides slightly more information to the optimizer, which can
sometimes allow it to optimize slightly better with some backends.This method can be thought of as recovering the `count` that was passed
to [ add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.add) (or, with the parameters in the other order,
to

[). The following are all equivalent, assuming that their safety preconditions are met:](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.sub)

`sub`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety-6)Safety

-
The distance between the pointers must be non-negative ( `self >= origin`)
-
*All*the safety conditions of`offset_from`

Importantly, despite the return type of this method being able to represent
a larger offset, it’s still *not permitted* to pass pointers which differ
by more than `isize::MAX` *bytes*.  As such, the result of this method will
always be less than or equal to `isize::MAX as usize`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-1)Panics

This function panics if `T` is a Zero-Sized Type (“ZST”).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-10)Examples

    assert_eq!(ptr2.offset_from_unsigned(ptr1), 2);
    assert_eq!(ptr1.add(2), ptr2);
    assert_eq!(ptr2.sub(2), ptr1);
    assert_eq!(ptr2.offset_from_unsigned(ptr2), 0);
}
// This would be incorrect, as the pointers are not correctly ordered:
// ptr1.offset_from_unsigned(ptr2)
