[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1184-1208)#### pub const unsafe fn [unchecked_disjoint_bitor](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unchecked_disjoint_bitor)(self, other: [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)) -> [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1184-1208)

#### pub const unsafe fn [unchecked_disjoint_bitor](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unchecked_disjoint_bitor)(self, other: [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)) -> [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)

Same value as `self | other`, but UB if any bit position is set in both inputs.

This is a situational micro-optimization for places where you’d rather
use addition on some platforms and bitwise or on other platforms, based
on exactly which instructions combine better with whatever else you’re
doing.  Note that there’s no reason to bother using this for places
where it’s clear from the operations involved that they can’t overlap.
For example, if you’re combining `u16`s into a `u32` with
`((a as u32) << 16) | (b as u32)`, that’s fine, as the backend will
know those sides of the `|` are disjoint without needing help.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-47)Examples

```
#![feature(disjoint_bitor)]
// SAFETY: `1` and `4` have no bits in common.
unsafe {
    assert_eq!(1_u16.unchecked_disjoint_bitor(4), 5);
}
```
[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety-6)Safety

Requires that `(self & other) == 0`, otherwise it’s immediate UB.

Equivalently, requires that `(self | other) == (self + other)`.

Returns the logarithm of the number with respect to an arbitrary base, rounded down.

This method might not be optimized owing to implementation details;
`ilog2` can produce results more efficiently for base 2, and `ilog10`
can produce results more efficiently for base 10.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-12)Panics

This function will panic if `self` is zero, or if `base` is less than 2.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-48)Examples

Unbounded shift left. Computes `self << rhs`, without bounding the value of `rhs`.

If `rhs` is larger or equal to the number of bits in `self`,
the entire value is shifted out, and `0` is returned.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-57)Examples

```
assert_eq!(0x1_u16.unbounded_shl(4), 0x10);
assert_eq!(0x1_u16.unbounded_shl(129), 0);
assert_eq!(0b101_u16.unbounded_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_u16.unbounded_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_u16.unbounded_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(42_u16.unbounded_shl(16), 0);
assert_eq!(42_u16.unbounded_shl(1).unbounded_shl(15), 0);
let start : u16 = 13;
let mut running = start;
for i in 0..160 {
    // The unbounded shift left by i is the same as `<< 1` i times
    assert_eq!(running, start.unbounded_shl(i));
    // Which is not always the case for a wrapping shift
    assert_eq!(running == start.wrapping_shl(i), i < 16);
    running <<= 1;
}
```
Exact shift left. Computes `self << rhs` as long as it can be reversed losslessly.

Returns `None` if any non-zero bits would be shifted out or if `rhs` >=
`u16::BITS`.
Otherwise, returns `Some(self << rhs)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-58)Examples

1.2.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1184-1208)#### pub const fn [wrapping_neg](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_neg)(self) -> [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1184-1208)

#### pub const fn [wrapping_neg](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_neg)(self) -> [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)

Wrapping (modular) negation. Computes `-self`,
wrapping around at the boundary of the type.

Since unsigned types do not have negative equivalents
all applications of this function will wrap (except for `-0`).
For values smaller than the corresponding signed type’s maximum
the result is the same as casting the corresponding signed value.
Any larger values are equivalent to `MAX + 1 - (val - MAX - 1)` where
`MAX` is the corresponding signed type’s maximum.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-81)Examples

1.2.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1184-1208)#### pub const fn [wrapping_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1184-1208)

#### pub const fn [wrapping_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)

Panic-free bitwise shift-left; yields `self << mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed.  The behaviour matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `<<` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it’s weird.  Consider, instead,
using [ Self::unbounded_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html#method.unbounded_shl) which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-left; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-left is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a [ rotate_left](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html#method.rotate_left) function,
which may be what you want instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-82)Examples

```
assert_eq!(1_u16.wrapping_shl(7), 128);
assert_eq!(0b101_u16.wrapping_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_u16.wrapping_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_u16.wrapping_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(u16::MAX.wrapping_shl(2), u16::MAX - 3);
assert_eq!(42_u16.wrapping_shl(16), 42);
assert_eq!(42_u16.wrapping_shl(1).wrapping_shl(15), 0);
assert_eq!(1_u16.wrapping_shl(128), 1);
assert_eq!(5_u16.wrapping_shl(1025), 10);
```

1.7.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1184-1208)#### pub const fn [overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_add)(self, rhs: [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)) -> ([u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1184-1208)

#### pub const fn [overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_add)(self, rhs: [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)) -> ([u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

Calculates `self` + `rhs`.

Returns a tuple of the addition along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. If an overflow would have occurred then the wrapped value is returned.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-85)Examples

Calculates `self` + `rhs` + `carry` and returns a tuple containing
the sum and the output carry (in that order).

Performs “ternary addition” of two integer operands and a carry-in bit, and returns an output integer and a carry-out bit. This allows chaining together multiple additions to create a wider addition, and can be useful for bignum addition.

This can be thought of as a 16-bit “full adder”, in the electronics sense.

If the input carry is false, this method is equivalent to
[ overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html#method.overflowing_add), and the output carry is
equal to the overflow flag. Note that although carry and overflow
flags are similar for unsigned integers, they are different for
signed integers.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-86)Examples

```
//    3  MAX    (a = 3 × 2^16 + 2^16 - 1)
// +  5    7    (b = 5 × 2^16 + 7)
// ---------
//    9    6    (sum = 9 × 2^16 + 6)
let (a1, a0): (u16, u16) = (3, u16::MAX);
let (b1, b0): (u16, u16) = (5, 7);
let carry0 = false;
let (sum0, carry1) = a0.carrying_add(b0, carry0);
assert_eq!(carry1, true);
let (sum1, carry2) = a1.carrying_add(b1, carry1);
assert_eq!(carry2, false);
assert_eq!((sum1, sum0), (9, 6));
```

Calculates `self` - `rhs`.

Returns a tuple of the subtraction along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. If an overflow would have occurred then the wrapped value is returned.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-88)Examples

Calculates `self` − `rhs` − `borrow` and returns a tuple
containing the difference and the output borrow.

Performs “ternary subtraction” by subtracting both an integer
operand and a borrow-in bit from `self`, and returns an output
integer and a borrow-out bit. This allows chaining together multiple
subtractions to create a wider subtraction, and can be useful for
bignum subtraction.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-89)Examples

```
//    9    6    (a = 9 × 2^16 + 6)
// -  5    7    (b = 5 × 2^16 + 7)
// ---------
//    3  MAX    (diff = 3 × 2^16 + 2^16 - 1)
let (a1, a0): (u16, u16) = (9, 6);
let (b1, b0): (u16, u16) = (5, 7);
let borrow0 = false;
let (diff0, borrow1) = a0.borrowing_sub(b0, borrow0);
assert_eq!(borrow1, true);
let (diff1, borrow2) = a1.borrowing_sub(b1, borrow1);
assert_eq!(borrow2, false);
assert_eq!((diff1, diff0), (3, u16::MAX));
```

1.7.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1184-1208)#### pub const fn [overflowing_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_mul)(self, rhs: [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)) -> ([u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

Calculates the multiplication of `self` and `rhs`.

Returns a tuple of the multiplication along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. If an overflow would have occurred then the wrapped value is returned.

If you want the *value* of the overflow, rather than just *whether*
an overflow occurred, see [ Self::carrying_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html#method.carrying_mul).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-92)Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u32` is used.

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1184-1208)#### pub const fn [widening_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.widening_mul)(self, rhs: [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)) -> ([u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html), [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html))

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1184-1208)

#### pub const fn [widening_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.widening_mul)(self, rhs: [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html)) -> ([u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html), [u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html))

Calculates the complete double-width product `self * rhs`.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits
of the result as two separate values, in that order. As such,
`a.widening_mul(b).0` produces the same result as `a.wrapping_mul(b)`.

If you also need to add a value and carry to the wide result, then you want
[ Self::carrying_mul_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html#method.carrying_mul_add) instead.

If you also need to add a carry to the wide result, then you want
[ Self::carrying_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html#method.carrying_mul) instead.

If you just want to know *whether* the multiplication overflowed, then you
want [ Self::overflowing_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html#method.overflowing_mul) instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-93)Examples

```
#![feature(widening_mul)]
assert_eq!(5_u16.widening_mul(7), (35, 0));
assert_eq!(u16::MAX.widening_mul(u16::MAX), (1, u16::MAX - 1));
```
Compared to other `*_mul` methods:

```
#![feature(widening_mul)]
assert_eq!(u16::widening_mul(1 << 15, 6), (0, 3));
assert_eq!(u16::overflowing_mul(1 << 15, 6), (0, true));
assert_eq!(u16::wrapping_mul(1 << 15, 6), 0);
assert_eq!(u16::checked_mul(1 << 15, 6), None);
```
Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u32` is used.

Calculates the “full multiplication” `self * rhs + carry`
without the possibility to overflow.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

Performs “long multiplication” which takes in an extra amount to add, and may return an additional amount of overflow. This allows for chaining together multiple multiplications to create “big integers” which represent larger values.

If you also need to add a value, then use [ Self::carrying_mul_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html#method.carrying_mul_add).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-94)Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u32` is used.

```
assert_eq!(5u32.carrying_mul(2, 0), (10, 0));
assert_eq!(5u32.carrying_mul(2, 10), (20, 0));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000u32.carrying_mul(10, 0), (1410065408, 2));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000u32.carrying_mul(10, 10), (1410065418, 2));
assert_eq!(u16::MAX.carrying_mul(u16::MAX, u16::MAX), (0, u16::MAX));
```
This is the core operation needed for scalar multiplication when implementing it for wider-than-native types.

```
fn scalar_mul_eq(little_endian_digits: &mut Vec<u16>, multiplicand: u16) {
    let mut carry = 0;
    for d in little_endian_digits.iter_mut() {
        (*d, carry) = d.carrying_mul(multiplicand, carry);
    }
    if carry != 0 {
        little_endian_digits.push(carry);
    }
}
let mut v = vec![10, 20];
scalar_mul_eq(&mut v, 3);
assert_eq!(v, [30, 60]);
assert_eq!(0x87654321_u64 * 0xFEED, 0x86D3D159E38D);
let mut v = vec![0x4321, 0x8765];
scalar_mul_eq(&mut v, 0xFEED);
assert_eq!(v, [0xE38D, 0xD159, 0x86D3]);
```
If `carry` is zero, this is similar to [ overflowing_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html#method.overflowing_mul),
except that it gives the value of the overflow instead of just whether one happened:

```
#![feature(const_unsigned_bigint_helpers)]
let r = u8::carrying_mul(7, 13, 0);
assert_eq!((r.0, r.1 != 0), u8::overflowing_mul(7, 13));
let r = u8::carrying_mul(13, 42, 0);
assert_eq!((r.0, r.1 != 0), u8::overflowing_mul(13, 42));
```
The value of the first field in the returned tuple matches what you’d get
by combining the [ wrapping_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html#method.wrapping_mul) and

[methods:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html#method.wrapping_add)

`wrapping_add`1.91.0 (const: [unstable](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/152015)) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1184-1208)

[unstable](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/152015)) ·

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1184-1208)

Calculates the “full multiplication” `self * rhs + carry + add`.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

This cannot overflow, as the double-width result has exactly enough space for the largest possible result. This is equivalent to how, in decimal, 9 × 9 + 9 + 9 = 81 + 18 = 99 = 9×10⁰ + 9×10¹ = 10² - 1.

Performs “long multiplication” which takes in an extra amount to add, and may return an additional amount of overflow. This allows for chaining together multiple multiplications to create “big integers” which represent larger values.

If you don’t need the `add` part, then you can use [ Self::carrying_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html#method.carrying_mul) instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-95)Examples

Please note that this example is shared between integer types,
which explains why `u32` is used here.

```
assert_eq!(5u32.carrying_mul_add(2, 0, 0), (10, 0));
assert_eq!(5u32.carrying_mul_add(2, 10, 10), (30, 0));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000u32.carrying_mul_add(10, 0, 0), (1410065408, 2));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000u32.carrying_mul_add(10, 10, 10), (1410065428, 2));
assert_eq!(u16::MAX.carrying_mul_add(u16::MAX, u16::MAX, u16::MAX), (u16::MAX, u16::MAX));
```
This is the core per-digit operation for “grade school” O(n²) multiplication.

Please note that this example is shared between integer types,
using `u8` for simplicity of the demonstration.

```
fn quadratic_mul<const N: usize>(a: [u8; N], b: [u8; N]) -> [u8; N] {
    let mut out = [0; N];
    for j in 0..N {
        let mut carry = 0;
        for i in 0..(N - j) {
            (out[j + i], carry) = u8::carrying_mul_add(a[i], b[j], out[j + i], carry);
        }
    }
    out
}
// -1 * -1 == 1
assert_eq!(quadratic_mul([0xFF; 3], [0xFF; 3]), [1, 0, 0]);
assert_eq!(u32::wrapping_mul(0x9e3779b9, 0x7f4a7c15), 0xcffc982d);
assert_eq!(
    quadratic_mul(u32::to_le_bytes(0x9e3779b9), u32::to_le_bytes(0x7f4a7c15)),
    u32::to_le_bytes(0xcffc982d)
);
```

Creates a native endian integer value from its memory representation as a byte array in native endianness.

As the target platform’s native endianness is used, portable code
likely wants to use [ from_be_bytes](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html#method.from_be_bytes) or

[, as appropriate instead.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u16.html#method.from_le_bytes)

`from_le_bytes`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-122)Examples

```
let value = u16::from_ne_bytes(if cfg!(target_endian = "big") {
    [0x12, 0x34]
} else {
    [0x34, 0x12]
});
assert_eq!(value, 0x1234);
```

#### pub const fn [checked_truncate](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.checked_truncate)<Target>(self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/option/enum.Option.html)<Target>

Calculates the midpoint (average) between `self` and `rhs`.

`midpoint(a, b)` is `(a + b) / 2` as if it were performed in a
sufficiently-large unsigned integral type. This implies that the result is
always rounded towards zero and that no overflow will ever occur.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-127)Examples

Calculates the “full carryless multiplication” without the possibility to overflow.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-129)Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u8` is used.

```
#![feature(uint_carryless_mul)]
assert_eq!(0b1000_0000u8.carrying_carryless_mul(0b1000_0000, 0b0000), (0, 0b0100_0000));
assert_eq!(0b1000_0000u8.carrying_carryless_mul(0b1000_0000, 0b1111), (0b1111, 0b0100_0000));
assert_eq!(u16::MAX.carrying_carryless_mul(u16::MAX, u16::MAX), (!(u16::MAX / 3), u16::MAX / 3));
```

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-130)Examples

```
#![feature(utf16_extra)]
let low_non_surrogate = 0xA000u16;
let low_surrogate = 0xD800u16;
let high_surrogate = 0xDC00u16;
let high_non_surrogate = 0xE000u16;
assert!(!low_non_surrogate.is_utf16_surrogate());
assert!(low_surrogate.is_utf16_surrogate());
assert!(high_surrogate.is_utf16_surrogate());
assert!(!high_non_surrogate.is_utf16_surrogate());
```

Parses an integer from a string slice with digits in a given base.

The string is expected to be an optional
`+`
sign followed by only digits. Leading and trailing non-digit characters (including
whitespace) represent an error. Underscores (which are accepted in Rust literals)
also represent an error.

Digits are a subset of these characters, depending on `radix`:

- `0-9`
- `a-z`
- `A-Z`

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-33)Panics

This function panics if `radix` is not in the range from 2 to 36.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#see-also)See also

Maps a `char` with a code point from U+0000 to U+FFFF (inclusive) to a `u16` in `0x0000..=0xFFFF`
with the same value, failing if the code point is greater than U+FFFF.

This corresponds to the UCS-2 encoding, as specified in ISO/IEC 10646:2003.

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)

#### pub const fn [count_zeros](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.count_zeros)(self) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)

Returns the number of zeros in the binary representation of `self`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-4)Examples

```
let zero = 0u32;
assert_eq!(zero.count_zeros(), 32);
let max = u32::MAX;
assert_eq!(max.count_zeros(), 0);
```
This is heavily dependent on the width of the type, and thus might give surprising results depending on type inference:

```
let lucky = 7;
foo(lucky);
assert_eq!(lucky.count_zeros(), 5);
assert_eq!(lucky.count_ones(), 3);
let lucky = 7;
bar(lucky);
assert_eq!(lucky.count_zeros(), 13);
assert_eq!(lucky.count_ones(), 3);
```
You might want to use [ Self::count_ones](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.count_ones) instead, or emphasize
the type you’re using in the call rather than method syntax:

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)

#### pub const fn [rotate_left](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.rotate_left)(self, n: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)

Shifts the bits to the left by a specified amount, `n`,
wrapping the truncated bits to the end of the resulting integer.

`rotate_left(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_left(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn’t the same operation as the `<<` shifting operator!

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-15)Examples

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)#### pub const fn [carryless_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.carryless_mul)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)

#### pub const fn [carryless_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.carryless_mul)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)

Performs a carry-less multiplication, returning the lower bits.

This operation is similar to long multiplication in base 2, except that exclusive or is used instead of addition. The implementation is equivalent to:

```
pub fn carryless_mul(lhs: u32, rhs: u32) -> u32{
    let mut retval = 0;
    for i in 0..u32::BITS {
        if (rhs >> i) & 1 != 0 {
            // long multiplication would use +=
            retval ^= lhs << i;
        }
    }
    retval
}
```
The actual implementation is more efficient, and on some platforms lowers directly to a dedicated instruction.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#uses)Uses

Carryless multiplication can be used to turn a bitmask of quote characters into a bit mask of characters surrounded by quotes:

```
r#"abc xxx "foobar" zzz "a"!"#; // input string
 0b0000000010000001000001010; // quote_mask
 0b0000000001111110000000100; // quote_mask.carryless_mul(!0) & !quote_mask
```
Another use is in cryptography, where carryless multiplication allows for efficient
implementations of polynomial multiplication in `GF(2)[X]`, the polynomial ring
over `GF(2)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-19)Examples

Calling `x.unchecked_add(y)` is semantically equivalent to calling
`x.``checked_add``(y).``unwrap_unchecked``()`.

If you’re just trying to avoid the panic in debug mode, then **do not**
use this.  Instead, you’re looking for [ wrapping_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.wrapping_add).

If you’re just trying to avoid the panic in debug mode, then **do not**
use this.  Instead, you’re looking for [ wrapping_sub](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.wrapping_sub).

If you find yourself writing code like this:

```
if foo >= bar {
    // SAFETY: just checked it will not overflow
    let diff = unsafe { foo.unchecked_sub(bar) };
    // ... use diff ...
}
```
Consider changing it to

As that does exactly the same thing – including telling the optimizer
that the subtraction cannot overflow – but avoids needing `unsafe`.

Checked integer subtraction. Computes `self - rhs` and checks if the result fits into an [ i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.i32.html), returning

`None` if overflow occurred.[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-34)Examples

```
assert_eq!(10u32.checked_signed_diff(2), Some(8));
assert_eq!(2u32.checked_signed_diff(10), Some(-8));
assert_eq!(u32::MAX.checked_signed_diff(i32::MAX as u32), None);
assert_eq!((i32::MAX as u32).checked_signed_diff(u32::MAX), Some(i32::MIN));
assert_eq!((i32::MAX as u32 + 1).checked_signed_diff(0), None);
assert_eq!(u32::MAX.checked_signed_diff(u32::MAX), Some(0));
```

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)#### pub const unsafe fn [unchecked_disjoint_bitor](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unchecked_disjoint_bitor)(self, other: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)

#### pub const unsafe fn [unchecked_disjoint_bitor](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unchecked_disjoint_bitor)(self, other: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)

Same value as `self | other`, but UB if any bit position is set in both inputs.

This is a situational micro-optimization for places where you’d rather
use addition on some platforms and bitwise or on other platforms, based
on exactly which instructions combine better with whatever else you’re
doing.  Note that there’s no reason to bother using this for places
where it’s clear from the operations involved that they can’t overlap.
For example, if you’re combining `u16`s into a `u32` with
`((a as u32) << 16) | (b as u32)`, that’s fine, as the backend will
know those sides of the `|` are disjoint without needing help.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-47)Examples

```
#![feature(disjoint_bitor)]
// SAFETY: `1` and `4` have no bits in common.
unsafe {
    assert_eq!(1_u32.unchecked_disjoint_bitor(4), 5);
}
```
[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety-6)Safety

Requires that `(self & other) == 0`, otherwise it’s immediate UB.

Equivalently, requires that `(self | other) == (self + other)`.

Returns the logarithm of the number with respect to an arbitrary base, rounded down.

This method might not be optimized owing to implementation details;
`ilog2` can produce results more efficiently for base 2, and `ilog10`
can produce results more efficiently for base 10.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-12)Panics

This function will panic if `self` is zero, or if `base` is less than 2.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-48)Examples

#### pub const fn [unbounded_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unbounded_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)

Unbounded shift left. Computes `self << rhs`, without bounding the value of `rhs`.

If `rhs` is larger or equal to the number of bits in `self`,
the entire value is shifted out, and `0` is returned.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-57)Examples

```
assert_eq!(0x1_u32.unbounded_shl(4), 0x10);
assert_eq!(0x1_u32.unbounded_shl(129), 0);
assert_eq!(0b101_u32.unbounded_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_u32.unbounded_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_u32.unbounded_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(42_u32.unbounded_shl(32), 0);
assert_eq!(42_u32.unbounded_shl(1).unbounded_shl(31), 0);
let start : u32 = 13;
let mut running = start;
for i in 0..160 {
    // The unbounded shift left by i is the same as `<< 1` i times
    assert_eq!(running, start.unbounded_shl(i));
    // Which is not always the case for a wrapping shift
    assert_eq!(running == start.wrapping_shl(i), i < 32);
    running <<= 1;
}
```
Exact shift left. Computes `self << rhs` as long as it can be reversed losslessly.

Returns `None` if any non-zero bits would be shifted out or if `rhs` >=
`u32::BITS`.
Otherwise, returns `Some(self << rhs)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-58)Examples

1.2.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)#### pub const fn [wrapping_neg](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_neg)(self) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)

#### pub const fn [wrapping_neg](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_neg)(self) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)

Wrapping (modular) negation. Computes `-self`,
wrapping around at the boundary of the type.

Since unsigned types do not have negative equivalents
all applications of this function will wrap (except for `-0`).
For values smaller than the corresponding signed type’s maximum
the result is the same as casting the corresponding signed value.
Any larger values are equivalent to `MAX + 1 - (val - MAX - 1)` where
`MAX` is the corresponding signed type’s maximum.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-81)Examples

1.2.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)#### pub const fn [wrapping_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)

#### pub const fn [wrapping_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)

Panic-free bitwise shift-left; yields `self << mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed.  The behaviour matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `<<` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it’s weird.  Consider, instead,
using [ Self::unbounded_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.unbounded_shl) which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-left; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-left is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a [ rotate_left](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.rotate_left) function,
which may be what you want instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-82)Examples

```
assert_eq!(1_u32.wrapping_shl(7), 128);
assert_eq!(0b101_u32.wrapping_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_u32.wrapping_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_u32.wrapping_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(u32::MAX.wrapping_shl(2), u32::MAX - 3);
assert_eq!(42_u32.wrapping_shl(32), 42);
assert_eq!(42_u32.wrapping_shl(1).wrapping_shl(31), 0);
assert_eq!(1_u32.wrapping_shl(128), 1);
assert_eq!(5_u32.wrapping_shl(1025), 10);
```

1.7.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)#### pub const fn [overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_add)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> ([u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)

#### pub const fn [overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_add)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> ([u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

Calculates `self` + `rhs`.

Returns a tuple of the addition along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. If an overflow would have occurred then the wrapped value is returned.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-85)Examples

Calculates `self` + `rhs` + `carry` and returns a tuple containing
the sum and the output carry (in that order).

Performs “ternary addition” of two integer operands and a carry-in bit, and returns an output integer and a carry-out bit. This allows chaining together multiple additions to create a wider addition, and can be useful for bignum addition.

This can be thought of as a 32-bit “full adder”, in the electronics sense.

If the input carry is false, this method is equivalent to
[ overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.overflowing_add), and the output carry is
equal to the overflow flag. Note that although carry and overflow
flags are similar for unsigned integers, they are different for
signed integers.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-86)Examples

```
//    3  MAX    (a = 3 × 2^32 + 2^32 - 1)
// +  5    7    (b = 5 × 2^32 + 7)
// ---------
//    9    6    (sum = 9 × 2^32 + 6)
let (a1, a0): (u32, u32) = (3, u32::MAX);
let (b1, b0): (u32, u32) = (5, 7);
let carry0 = false;
let (sum0, carry1) = a0.carrying_add(b0, carry0);
assert_eq!(carry1, true);
let (sum1, carry2) = a1.carrying_add(b1, carry1);
assert_eq!(carry2, false);
assert_eq!((sum1, sum0), (9, 6));
```

Returns a tuple of the subtraction along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. If an overflow would have occurred then the wrapped value is returned.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-88)Examples

Calculates `self` − `rhs` − `borrow` and returns a tuple
containing the difference and the output borrow.

Performs “ternary subtraction” by subtracting both an integer
operand and a borrow-in bit from `self`, and returns an output
integer and a borrow-out bit. This allows chaining together multiple
subtractions to create a wider subtraction, and can be useful for
bignum subtraction.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-89)Examples

```
//    9    6    (a = 9 × 2^32 + 6)
// -  5    7    (b = 5 × 2^32 + 7)
// ---------
//    3  MAX    (diff = 3 × 2^32 + 2^32 - 1)
let (a1, a0): (u32, u32) = (9, 6);
let (b1, b0): (u32, u32) = (5, 7);
let borrow0 = false;
let (diff0, borrow1) = a0.borrowing_sub(b0, borrow0);
assert_eq!(borrow1, true);
let (diff1, borrow2) = a1.borrowing_sub(b1, borrow1);
assert_eq!(borrow2, false);
assert_eq!((diff1, diff0), (3, u32::MAX));
```

1.7.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)#### pub const fn [overflowing_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_mul)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> ([u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

Calculates the multiplication of `self` and `rhs`.

Returns a tuple of the multiplication along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. If an overflow would have occurred then the wrapped value is returned.

If you want the *value* of the overflow, rather than just *whether*
an overflow occurred, see [ Self::carrying_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.carrying_mul).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-92)Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u32` is used.

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)#### pub const fn [widening_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.widening_mul)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> ([u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html), [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html))

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)

#### pub const fn [widening_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.widening_mul)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> ([u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html), [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html))

Calculates the complete double-width product `self * rhs`.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits
of the result as two separate values, in that order. As such,
`a.widening_mul(b).0` produces the same result as `a.wrapping_mul(b)`.

If you also need to add a value and carry to the wide result, then you want
[ Self::carrying_mul_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.carrying_mul_add) instead.

If you also need to add a carry to the wide result, then you want
[ Self::carrying_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.carrying_mul) instead.

If you just want to know *whether* the multiplication overflowed, then you
want [ Self::overflowing_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.overflowing_mul) instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-93)Examples

```
#![feature(widening_mul)]
assert_eq!(5_u32.widening_mul(7), (35, 0));
assert_eq!(u32::MAX.widening_mul(u32::MAX), (1, u32::MAX - 1));
```
Compared to other `*_mul` methods:

```
#![feature(widening_mul)]
assert_eq!(u32::widening_mul(1 << 31, 6), (0, 3));
assert_eq!(u32::overflowing_mul(1 << 31, 6), (0, true));
assert_eq!(u32::wrapping_mul(1 << 31, 6), 0);
assert_eq!(u32::checked_mul(1 << 31, 6), None);
```
Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u32` is used.

Calculates the “full multiplication” `self * rhs + carry`
without the possibility to overflow.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

Performs “long multiplication” which takes in an extra amount to add, and may return an additional amount of overflow. This allows for chaining together multiple multiplications to create “big integers” which represent larger values.

If you also need to add a value, then use [ Self::carrying_mul_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.carrying_mul_add).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-94)Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u32` is used.

```
assert_eq!(5u32.carrying_mul(2, 0), (10, 0));
assert_eq!(5u32.carrying_mul(2, 10), (20, 0));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000u32.carrying_mul(10, 0), (1410065408, 2));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000u32.carrying_mul(10, 10), (1410065418, 2));
assert_eq!(u32::MAX.carrying_mul(u32::MAX, u32::MAX), (0, u32::MAX));
```
This is the core operation needed for scalar multiplication when implementing it for wider-than-native types.

```
fn scalar_mul_eq(little_endian_digits: &mut Vec<u16>, multiplicand: u16) {
    let mut carry = 0;
    for d in little_endian_digits.iter_mut() {
        (*d, carry) = d.carrying_mul(multiplicand, carry);
    }
    if carry != 0 {
        little_endian_digits.push(carry);
    }
}
let mut v = vec![10, 20];
scalar_mul_eq(&mut v, 3);
assert_eq!(v, [30, 60]);
assert_eq!(0x87654321_u64 * 0xFEED, 0x86D3D159E38D);
let mut v = vec![0x4321, 0x8765];
scalar_mul_eq(&mut v, 0xFEED);
assert_eq!(v, [0xE38D, 0xD159, 0x86D3]);
```
If `carry` is zero, this is similar to [ overflowing_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.overflowing_mul),
except that it gives the value of the overflow instead of just whether one happened:

```
#![feature(const_unsigned_bigint_helpers)]
let r = u8::carrying_mul(7, 13, 0);
assert_eq!((r.0, r.1 != 0), u8::overflowing_mul(7, 13));
let r = u8::carrying_mul(13, 42, 0);
assert_eq!((r.0, r.1 != 0), u8::overflowing_mul(13, 42));
```
The value of the first field in the returned tuple matches what you’d get
by combining the [ wrapping_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.wrapping_mul) and

[methods:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.wrapping_add)

`wrapping_add`1.91.0 (const: [unstable](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/152015)) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)

[unstable](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/152015)) ·

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1239-1263)

Calculates the “full multiplication” `self * rhs + carry + add`.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

This cannot overflow, as the double-width result has exactly enough space for the largest possible result. This is equivalent to how, in decimal, 9 × 9 + 9 + 9 = 81 + 18 = 99 = 9×10⁰ + 9×10¹ = 10² - 1.

Performs “long multiplication” which takes in an extra amount to add, and may return an additional amount of overflow. This allows for chaining together multiple multiplications to create “big integers” which represent larger values.

If you don’t need the `add` part, then you can use [ Self::carrying_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.carrying_mul) instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-95)Examples

Please note that this example is shared between integer types,
which explains why `u32` is used here.

```
assert_eq!(5u32.carrying_mul_add(2, 0, 0), (10, 0));
assert_eq!(5u32.carrying_mul_add(2, 10, 10), (30, 0));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000u32.carrying_mul_add(10, 0, 0), (1410065408, 2));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000u32.carrying_mul_add(10, 10, 10), (1410065428, 2));
assert_eq!(u32::MAX.carrying_mul_add(u32::MAX, u32::MAX, u32::MAX), (u32::MAX, u32::MAX));
```
This is the core per-digit operation for “grade school” O(n²) multiplication.

Please note that this example is shared between integer types,
using `u8` for simplicity of the demonstration.

```
fn quadratic_mul<const N: usize>(a: [u8; N], b: [u8; N]) -> [u8; N] {
    let mut out = [0; N];
    for j in 0..N {
        let mut carry = 0;
        for i in 0..(N - j) {
            (out[j + i], carry) = u8::carrying_mul_add(a[i], b[j], out[j + i], carry);
        }
    }
    out
}
// -1 * -1 == 1
assert_eq!(quadratic_mul([0xFF; 3], [0xFF; 3]), [1, 0, 0]);
assert_eq!(u32::wrapping_mul(0x9e3779b9, 0x7f4a7c15), 0xcffc982d);
assert_eq!(
    quadratic_mul(u32::to_le_bytes(0x9e3779b9), u32::to_le_bytes(0x7f4a7c15)),
    u32::to_le_bytes(0xcffc982d)
);
```

Creates a native endian integer value from its memory representation as a byte array in native endianness.

As the target platform’s native endianness is used, portable code
likely wants to use [ from_be_bytes](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.from_be_bytes) or

[, as appropriate instead.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html#method.from_le_bytes)

`from_le_bytes`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-122)Examples

```
let value = u32::from_ne_bytes(if cfg!(target_endian = "big") {
    [0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x78]
} else {
    [0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12]
});
assert_eq!(value, 0x12345678);
```
When starting from a slice rather than an array, fallible conversion APIs can be used:

#### pub const fn [checked_truncate](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.checked_truncate)<Target>(self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/option/enum.Option.html)<Target>

Calculates the midpoint (average) between `self` and `rhs`.

`midpoint(a, b)` is `(a + b) / 2` as if it were performed in a
sufficiently-large unsigned integral type. This implies that the result is
always rounded towards zero and that no overflow will ever occur.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-127)Examples

Calculates the “full carryless multiplication” without the possibility to overflow.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-129)Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u8` is used.

```
#![feature(uint_carryless_mul)]
assert_eq!(0b1000_0000u8.carrying_carryless_mul(0b1000_0000, 0b0000), (0, 0b0100_0000));
assert_eq!(0b1000_0000u8.carrying_carryless_mul(0b1000_0000, 0b1111), (0b1111, 0b0100_0000));
assert_eq!(u32::MAX.carrying_carryless_mul(u32::MAX, u32::MAX), (!(u32::MAX / 3), u32::MAX / 3));
```

#### pub const fn [from_str_radix](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.from_str_radix)(src: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html), radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/result/enum.Result.html)<[u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html), [ParseIntError](https://doc.rust-lang.org/num/struct.ParseIntError.html)>

Parses an integer from a string slice with digits in a given base.

The string is expected to be an optional
`+`
sign followed by only digits. Leading and trailing non-digit characters (including
whitespace) represent an error. Underscores (which are accepted in Rust literals)
also represent an error.

Digits are a subset of these characters, depending on `radix`:

- `0-9`
- `a-z`
- `A-Z`

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-33)Panics

This function panics if `radix` is not in the range from 2 to 36.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#see-also)See also

If the string to be parsed is in base 10 (decimal),
[ from_str](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.from_str) or

[can also be used.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html#method.parse)

#### pub const fn [count_zeros](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.count_zeros)(self) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)

Returns the number of zeros in the binary representation of `self`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-4)Examples

```
let zero = 0u64;
assert_eq!(zero.count_zeros(), 64);
let max = u64::MAX;
assert_eq!(max.count_zeros(), 0);
```
This is heavily dependent on the width of the type, and thus might give surprising results depending on type inference:

```
let lucky = 7;
foo(lucky);
assert_eq!(lucky.count_zeros(), 5);
assert_eq!(lucky.count_ones(), 3);
let lucky = 7;
bar(lucky);
assert_eq!(lucky.count_zeros(), 13);
assert_eq!(lucky.count_ones(), 3);
```
You might want to use [ Self::count_ones](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.count_ones) instead, or emphasize
the type you’re using in the call rather than method syntax:

Shifts the bits to the left by a specified amount, `n`,
wrapping the truncated bits to the end of the resulting integer.

`rotate_left(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_left(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn’t the same operation as the `<<` shifting operator!

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-15)Examples

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)#### pub const fn [carryless_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.carryless_mul)(self, rhs: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)

#### pub const fn [carryless_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.carryless_mul)(self, rhs: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)

Performs a carry-less multiplication, returning the lower bits.

This operation is similar to long multiplication in base 2, except that exclusive or is used instead of addition. The implementation is equivalent to:

```
pub fn carryless_mul(lhs: u64, rhs: u64) -> u64{
    let mut retval = 0;
    for i in 0..u64::BITS {
        if (rhs >> i) & 1 != 0 {
            // long multiplication would use +=
            retval ^= lhs << i;
        }
    }
    retval
}
```
The actual implementation is more efficient, and on some platforms lowers directly to a dedicated instruction.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#uses)Uses

Carryless multiplication can be used to turn a bitmask of quote characters into a bit mask of characters surrounded by quotes:

```
r#"abc xxx "foobar" zzz "a"!"#; // input string
 0b0000000010000001000001010; // quote_mask
 0b0000000001111110000000100; // quote_mask.carryless_mul(!0) & !quote_mask
```
Another use is in cryptography, where carryless multiplication allows for efficient
implementations of polynomial multiplication in `GF(2)[X]`, the polynomial ring
over `GF(2)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-19)Examples

`None` if overflow occurred.[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-34)Examples

```
assert_eq!(10u64.checked_signed_diff(2), Some(8));
assert_eq!(2u64.checked_signed_diff(10), Some(-8));
assert_eq!(u64::MAX.checked_signed_diff(i64::MAX as u64), None);
assert_eq!((i64::MAX as u64).checked_signed_diff(u64::MAX), Some(i64::MIN));
assert_eq!((i64::MAX as u64 + 1).checked_signed_diff(0), None);
assert_eq!(u64::MAX.checked_signed_diff(u64::MAX), Some(0));
```

Strict division on unsigned types is just normal division. There’s no

positive integers, all common definitions of division are equal, this
is exactly equal to `self.strict_div(rhs)`.

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)#### pub const unsafe fn [unchecked_disjoint_bitor](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unchecked_disjoint_bitor)(self, other: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)

#### pub const unsafe fn [unchecked_disjoint_bitor](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unchecked_disjoint_bitor)(self, other: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)

Same value as `self | other`, but UB if any bit position is set in both inputs.

This is a situational micro-optimization for places where you’d rather
use addition on some platforms and bitwise or on other platforms, based
on exactly which instructions combine better with whatever else you’re
doing.  Note that there’s no reason to bother using this for places
where it’s clear from the operations involved that they can’t overlap.
For example, if you’re combining `u16`s into a `u32` with
`((a as u32) << 16) | (b as u32)`, that’s fine, as the backend will
know those sides of the `|` are disjoint without needing help.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-47)Examples

```
#![feature(disjoint_bitor)]
// SAFETY: `1` and `4` have no bits in common.
unsafe {
    assert_eq!(1_u64.unchecked_disjoint_bitor(4), 5);
}
```
[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety-6)Safety

Requires that `(self & other) == 0`, otherwise it’s immediate UB.

Equivalently, requires that `(self | other) == (self + other)`.

Returns the logarithm of the number with respect to an arbitrary base, rounded down.

This method might not be optimized owing to implementation details;
`ilog2` can produce results more efficiently for base 2, and `ilog10`
can produce results more efficiently for base 10.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-12)Panics

This function will panic if `self` is zero, or if `base` is less than 2.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-48)Examples

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)

#### pub const fn [unbounded_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unbounded_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)

Unbounded shift left. Computes `self << rhs`, without bounding the value of `rhs`.

If `rhs` is larger or equal to the number of bits in `self`,
the entire value is shifted out, and `0` is returned.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-57)Examples

```
assert_eq!(0x1_u64.unbounded_shl(4), 0x10);
assert_eq!(0x1_u64.unbounded_shl(129), 0);
assert_eq!(0b101_u64.unbounded_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_u64.unbounded_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_u64.unbounded_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(42_u64.unbounded_shl(64), 0);
assert_eq!(42_u64.unbounded_shl(1).unbounded_shl(63), 0);
let start : u64 = 13;
let mut running = start;
for i in 0..160 {
    // The unbounded shift left by i is the same as `<< 1` i times
    assert_eq!(running, start.unbounded_shl(i));
    // Which is not always the case for a wrapping shift
    assert_eq!(running == start.wrapping_shl(i), i < 64);
    running <<= 1;
}
```
Exact shift left. Computes `self << rhs` as long as it can be reversed losslessly.

Returns `None` if any non-zero bits would be shifted out or if `rhs` >=
`u64::BITS`.
Otherwise, returns `Some(self << rhs)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-58)Examples

#### pub const fn [wrapping_neg](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_neg)(self) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)

Wrapping (modular) negation. Computes `-self`,
wrapping around at the boundary of the type.

Since unsigned types do not have negative equivalents
all applications of this function will wrap (except for `-0`).
For values smaller than the corresponding signed type’s maximum
the result is the same as casting the corresponding signed value.
Any larger values are equivalent to `MAX + 1 - (val - MAX - 1)` where
`MAX` is the corresponding signed type’s maximum.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-81)Examples

1.2.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)#### pub const fn [wrapping_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)

#### pub const fn [wrapping_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)

Panic-free bitwise shift-left; yields `self << mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed.  The behaviour matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `<<` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it’s weird.  Consider, instead,
using [ Self::unbounded_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.unbounded_shl) which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-left; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-left is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a [ rotate_left](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.rotate_left) function,
which may be what you want instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-82)Examples

```
assert_eq!(1_u64.wrapping_shl(7), 128);
assert_eq!(0b101_u64.wrapping_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_u64.wrapping_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_u64.wrapping_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(u64::MAX.wrapping_shl(2), u64::MAX - 3);
assert_eq!(42_u64.wrapping_shl(64), 42);
assert_eq!(42_u64.wrapping_shl(1).wrapping_shl(63), 0);
assert_eq!(1_u64.wrapping_shl(128), 1);
assert_eq!(5_u64.wrapping_shl(1025), 10);
```

1.7.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)#### pub const fn [overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_add)(self, rhs: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)) -> ([u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)

#### pub const fn [overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_add)(self, rhs: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)) -> ([u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

Calculates `self` + `rhs`.

Returns a tuple of the addition along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. If an overflow would have occurred then the wrapped value is returned.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-85)Examples

Calculates `self` + `rhs` + `carry` and returns a tuple containing
the sum and the output carry (in that order).

Performs “ternary addition” of two integer operands and a carry-in bit, and returns an output integer and a carry-out bit. This allows chaining together multiple additions to create a wider addition, and can be useful for bignum addition.

This can be thought of as a 64-bit “full adder”, in the electronics sense.

If the input carry is false, this method is equivalent to
[ overflowing_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.overflowing_add), and the output carry is
equal to the overflow flag. Note that although carry and overflow
flags are similar for unsigned integers, they are different for
signed integers.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-86)Examples

```
//    3  MAX    (a = 3 × 2^64 + 2^64 - 1)
// +  5    7    (b = 5 × 2^64 + 7)
// ---------
//    9    6    (sum = 9 × 2^64 + 6)
let (a1, a0): (u64, u64) = (3, u64::MAX);
let (b1, b0): (u64, u64) = (5, 7);
let carry0 = false;
let (sum0, carry1) = a0.carrying_add(b0, carry0);
assert_eq!(carry1, true);
let (sum1, carry2) = a1.carrying_add(b1, carry1);
assert_eq!(carry2, false);
assert_eq!((sum1, sum0), (9, 6));
```

Performs “ternary subtraction” by subtracting both an integer
operand and a borrow-in bit from `self`, and returns an output
integer and a borrow-out bit. This allows chaining together multiple
subtractions to create a wider subtraction, and can be useful for
bignum subtraction.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-89)Examples

```
//    9    6    (a = 9 × 2^64 + 6)
// -  5    7    (b = 5 × 2^64 + 7)
// ---------
//    3  MAX    (diff = 3 × 2^64 + 2^64 - 1)
let (a1, a0): (u64, u64) = (9, 6);
let (b1, b0): (u64, u64) = (5, 7);

let (diff0, borrow1) = a0.borrowing_sub(b0, borrow0);
assert_eq!(borrow1, true);

assert_eq!(borrow2, false);

1.7.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)#### pub const fn [overflowing_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_mul)(self, rhs: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)) -> ([u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)

#### pub const fn [overflowing_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.overflowing_mul)(self, rhs: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)) -> ([u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html), [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.bool.html))

Calculates the multiplication of `self` and `rhs`.

Returns a tuple of the multiplication along with a boolean indicating whether an arithmetic overflow would occur. If an overflow would have occurred then the wrapped value is returned.

If you want the *value* of the overflow, rather than just *whether*
an overflow occurred, see [ Self::carrying_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.carrying_mul).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-92)Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u32` is used.

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)#### pub const fn [widening_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.widening_mul)(self, rhs: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)) -> ([u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html), [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html))

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)

#### pub const fn [widening_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.widening_mul)(self, rhs: [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html)) -> ([u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html), [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html))

Calculates the complete double-width product `self * rhs`.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits
of the result as two separate values, in that order. As such,
`a.widening_mul(b).0` produces the same result as `a.wrapping_mul(b)`.

If you also need to add a value and carry to the wide result, then you want
[ Self::carrying_mul_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.carrying_mul_add) instead.

If you also need to add a carry to the wide result, then you want
[ Self::carrying_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.carrying_mul) instead.

If you just want to know *whether* the multiplication overflowed, then you
want [ Self::overflowing_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.overflowing_mul) instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-93)Examples

```
#![feature(widening_mul)]
assert_eq!(5_u64.widening_mul(7), (35, 0));
assert_eq!(u64::MAX.widening_mul(u64::MAX), (1, u64::MAX - 1));
```
Compared to other `*_mul` methods:

```
#![feature(widening_mul)]
assert_eq!(u64::widening_mul(1 << 63, 6), (0, 3));
assert_eq!(u64::overflowing_mul(1 << 63, 6), (0, true));
assert_eq!(u64::wrapping_mul(1 << 63, 6), 0);
assert_eq!(u64::checked_mul(1 << 63, 6), None);
```
Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u32` is used.

Calculates the “full multiplication” `self * rhs + carry`
without the possibility to overflow.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

Performs “long multiplication” which takes in an extra amount to add, and may return an additional amount of overflow. This allows for chaining together multiple multiplications to create “big integers” which represent larger values.

If you also need to add a value, then use [ Self::carrying_mul_add](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.carrying_mul_add).

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-94)Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u32` is used.

```
assert_eq!(5u32.carrying_mul(2, 0), (10, 0));
assert_eq!(5u32.carrying_mul(2, 10), (20, 0));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000u32.carrying_mul(10, 0), (1410065408, 2));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000u32.carrying_mul(10, 10), (1410065418, 2));
assert_eq!(u64::MAX.carrying_mul(u64::MAX, u64::MAX), (0, u64::MAX));
```
This is the core operation needed for scalar multiplication when implementing it for wider-than-native types.

```
fn scalar_mul_eq(little_endian_digits: &mut Vec<u16>, multiplicand: u16) {
    let mut carry = 0;
    for d in little_endian_digits.iter_mut() {
        (*d, carry) = d.carrying_mul(multiplicand, carry);
    }
    if carry != 0 {
        little_endian_digits.push(carry);
    }
}
let mut v = vec![10, 20];
scalar_mul_eq(&mut v, 3);
assert_eq!(v, [30, 60]);
assert_eq!(0x87654321_u64 * 0xFEED, 0x86D3D159E38D);
let mut v = vec![0x4321, 0x8765];
scalar_mul_eq(&mut v, 0xFEED);
assert_eq!(v, [0xE38D, 0xD159, 0x86D3]);
```
If `carry` is zero, this is similar to [ overflowing_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.overflowing_mul),
except that it gives the value of the overflow instead of just whether one happened:

```
#![feature(const_unsigned_bigint_helpers)]
let r = u8::carrying_mul(7, 13, 0);
assert_eq!((r.0, r.1 != 0), u8::overflowing_mul(7, 13));
let r = u8::carrying_mul(13, 42, 0);
assert_eq!((r.0, r.1 != 0), u8::overflowing_mul(13, 42));
```
The value of the first field in the returned tuple matches what you’d get
by combining the [ wrapping_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.wrapping_mul) and

[methods:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.wrapping_add)

`wrapping_add`1.91.0 (const: [unstable](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/152015)) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)

[unstable](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/152015)) ·

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1270-1294)

Calculates the “full multiplication” `self * rhs + carry + add`.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

This cannot overflow, as the double-width result has exactly enough space for the largest possible result. This is equivalent to how, in decimal, 9 × 9 + 9 + 9 = 81 + 18 = 99 = 9×10⁰ + 9×10¹ = 10² - 1.

Performs “long multiplication” which takes in an extra amount to add, and may return an additional amount of overflow. This allows for chaining together multiple multiplications to create “big integers” which represent larger values.

If you don’t need the `add` part, then you can use [ Self::carrying_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.carrying_mul) instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-95)Examples

Please note that this example is shared between integer types,
which explains why `u32` is used here.

```
assert_eq!(5u32.carrying_mul_add(2, 0, 0), (10, 0));
assert_eq!(5u32.carrying_mul_add(2, 10, 10), (30, 0));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000u32.carrying_mul_add(10, 0, 0), (1410065408, 2));
assert_eq!(1_000_000_000u32.carrying_mul_add(10, 10, 10), (1410065428, 2));
assert_eq!(u64::MAX.carrying_mul_add(u64::MAX, u64::MAX, u64::MAX), (u64::MAX, u64::MAX));
```
This is the core per-digit operation for “grade school” O(n²) multiplication.

Please note that this example is shared between integer types,
using `u8` for simplicity of the demonstration.

```
fn quadratic_mul<const N: usize>(a: [u8; N], b: [u8; N]) -> [u8; N] {
    let mut out = [0; N];
    for j in 0..N {
        let mut carry = 0;
        for i in 0..(N - j) {
            (out[j + i], carry) = u8::carrying_mul_add(a[i], b[j], out[j + i], carry);
        }
    }
    out
}
// -1 * -1 == 1
assert_eq!(quadratic_mul([0xFF; 3], [0xFF; 3]), [1, 0, 0]);
assert_eq!(u32::wrapping_mul(0x9e3779b9, 0x7f4a7c15), 0xcffc982d);
assert_eq!(
    quadratic_mul(u32::to_le_bytes(0x9e3779b9), u32::to_le_bytes(0x7f4a7c15)),
    u32::to_le_bytes(0xcffc982d)
);
```

This function is equivalent to `self % rhs == 0`, except that it will not panic
for `rhs == 0`. Instead, `0.is_multiple_of(0) == true`, and for any non-zero `n`,
`n.is_multiple_of(0) == false`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-121)Examples

```

```

Creates a native endian integer value from its memory representation as a byte array in native endianness.

As the target platform’s native endianness is used, portable code
likely wants to use [ from_be_bytes](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.from_be_bytes) or

[, as appropriate instead.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html#method.from_le_bytes)

`from_le_bytes`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-122)Examples

```
let value = u64::from_ne_bytes(if cfg!(target_endian = "big") {
    [0x12, 0x34, 0x56, 0x78, 0x90, 0x12, 0x34, 0x56]
} else {
    [0x56, 0x34, 0x12, 0x90, 0x78, 0x56, 0x34, 0x12]
});
assert_eq!(value, 0x1234567890123456);
```

#### pub const fn [checked_truncate](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.checked_truncate)<Target>(self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/option/enum.Option.html)<Target>

Calculates the midpoint (average) between `self` and `rhs`.

`midpoint(a, b)` is `(a + b) / 2` as if it were performed in a
sufficiently-large unsigned integral type. This implies that the result is
always rounded towards zero and that no overflow will ever occur.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-127)Examples

Calculates the “full carryless multiplication” without the possibility to overflow.

This returns the low-order (wrapping) bits and the high-order (overflow) bits of the result as two separate values, in that order.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-129)Examples

Please note that this example is shared among integer types, which is why `u8` is used.

```
#![feature(uint_carryless_mul)]
assert_eq!(0b1000_0000u8.carrying_carryless_mul(0b1000_0000, 0b0000), (0, 0b0100_0000));
assert_eq!(0b1000_0000u8.carrying_carryless_mul(0b1000_0000, 0b1111), (0b1111, 0b0100_0000));
assert_eq!(u64::MAX.carrying_carryless_mul(u64::MAX, u64::MAX), (!(u64::MAX / 3), u64::MAX / 3));
```

#### pub const fn [from_str_radix](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.from_str_radix)(src: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html), radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/result/enum.Result.html)<[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u64.html), [ParseIntError](https://doc.rust-lang.org/num/struct.ParseIntError.html)>

Parses an integer from a string slice with digits in a given base.

The string is expected to be an optional
`+`
sign followed by only digits. Leading and trailing non-digit characters (including
whitespace) represent an error. Underscores (which are accepted in Rust literals)
also represent an error.

Digits are a subset of these characters, depending on `radix`:

- `0-9`
- `a-z`
- `A-Z`

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-33)Panics

This function panics if `radix` is not in the range from 2 to 36.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#see-also)See also

If the string to be parsed is in base 10 (decimal),
[ from_str](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.from_str) or

[can also be used.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.str.html#method.parse)

`str::parse`[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-130)Examples

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1301-1327)

#### pub const fn [count_zeros](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.count_zeros)(self) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)

Returns the number of zeros in the binary representation of `self`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-4)Examples

```
let zero = 0u128;
assert_eq!(zero.count_zeros(), 128);
let max = u128::MAX;
assert_eq!(max.count_zeros(), 0);
```
This is heavily dependent on the width of the type, and thus might give surprising results depending on type inference:

```
let lucky = 7;
foo(lucky);
assert_eq!(lucky.count_zeros(), 5);
assert_eq!(lucky.count_ones(), 3);
let lucky = 7;
bar(lucky);
assert_eq!(lucky.count_zeros(), 13);
assert_eq!(lucky.count_ones(), 3);
```
You might want to use [ Self::count_ones](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html#method.count_ones) instead, or emphasize
the type you’re using in the call rather than method syntax:

#### pub const fn [rotate_left](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.rotate_left)(self, n: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)

Shifts the bits to the left by a specified amount, `n`,
wrapping the truncated bits to the end of the resulting integer.

`rotate_left(n)` is equivalent to applying `rotate_left(1)` a total of `n` times. In
particular, a rotation by the number of bits in `self` returns the input value
unchanged.

Please note this isn’t the same operation as the `<<` shifting operator!

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-15)Examples

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1301-1327)#### pub const fn [carryless_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.carryless_mul)(self, rhs: [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)) -> [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1301-1327)

#### pub const fn [carryless_mul](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.carryless_mul)(self, rhs: [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)) -> [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)

Performs a carry-less multiplication, returning the lower bits.

This operation is similar to long multiplication in base 2, except that exclusive or is used instead of addition. The implementation is equivalent to:

```
pub fn carryless_mul(lhs: u128, rhs: u128) -> u128{
    let mut retval = 0;
    for i in 0..u128::BITS {
        if (rhs >> i) & 1 != 0 {
            // long multiplication would use +=
            retval ^= lhs << i;
        }
    }
    retval
}
```
The actual implementation is more efficient, and on some platforms lowers directly to a dedicated instruction.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#uses)Uses

Carryless multiplication can be used to turn a bitmask of quote characters into a bit mask of characters surrounded by quotes:

```
r#"abc xxx "foobar" zzz "a"!"#; // input string
 0b0000000010000001000001010; // quote_mask
 0b0000000001111110000000100; // quote_mask.carryless_mul(!0) & !quote_mask
```
Another use is in cryptography, where carryless multiplication allows for efficient
implementations of polynomial multiplication in `GF(2)[X]`, the polynomial ring
over `GF(2)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-19)Examples

`None` if overflow occurred.[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-34)Examples

```
assert_eq!(10u128.checked_signed_diff(2), Some(8));
assert_eq!(2u128.checked_signed_diff(10), Some(-8));
assert_eq!(u128::MAX.checked_signed_diff(i128::MAX as u128), None);
assert_eq!((i128::MAX as u128).checked_signed_diff(u128::MAX), Some(i128::MIN));
assert_eq!((i128::MAX as u128 + 1).checked_signed_diff(0), None);
assert_eq!(u128::MAX.checked_signed_diff(u128::MAX), Some(0));
```

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1301-1327)#### pub const unsafe fn [unchecked_disjoint_bitor](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unchecked_disjoint_bitor)(self, other: [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)) -> [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1301-1327)

#### pub const unsafe fn [unchecked_disjoint_bitor](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unchecked_disjoint_bitor)(self, other: [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)) -> [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)

Same value as `self | other`, but UB if any bit position is set in both inputs.

This is a situational micro-optimization for places where you’d rather
use addition on some platforms and bitwise or on other platforms, based
on exactly which instructions combine better with whatever else you’re
doing.  Note that there’s no reason to bother using this for places
where it’s clear from the operations involved that they can’t overlap.
For example, if you’re combining `u16`s into a `u32` with
`((a as u32) << 16) | (b as u32)`, that’s fine, as the backend will
know those sides of the `|` are disjoint without needing help.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-47)Examples

```
#![feature(disjoint_bitor)]
// SAFETY: `1` and `4` have no bits in common.
unsafe {
    assert_eq!(1_u128.unchecked_disjoint_bitor(4), 5);
}
```
[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#safety-6)Safety

Requires that `(self & other) == 0`, otherwise it’s immediate UB.

Equivalently, requires that `(self | other) == (self + other)`.

Returns the logarithm of the number with respect to an arbitrary base, rounded down.

This method might not be optimized owing to implementation details;
`ilog2` can produce results more efficiently for base 2, and `ilog10`
can produce results more efficiently for base 10.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#panics-12)Panics

This function will panic if `self` is zero, or if `base` is less than 2.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-48)Examples

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1301-1327)

#### pub const fn [unbounded_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.unbounded_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)

Unbounded shift left. Computes `self << rhs`, without bounding the value of `rhs`.

If `rhs` is larger or equal to the number of bits in `self`,
the entire value is shifted out, and `0` is returned.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-57)Examples

```
assert_eq!(0x1_u128.unbounded_shl(4), 0x10);
assert_eq!(0x1_u128.unbounded_shl(129), 0);
assert_eq!(0b101_u128.unbounded_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_u128.unbounded_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_u128.unbounded_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(42_u128.unbounded_shl(128), 0);
assert_eq!(42_u128.unbounded_shl(1).unbounded_shl(127), 0);
let start : u128 = 13;
let mut running = start;
for i in 0..160 {
    // The unbounded shift left by i is the same as `<< 1` i times
    assert_eq!(running, start.unbounded_shl(i));
    // Which is not always the case for a wrapping shift
    assert_eq!(running == start.wrapping_shl(i), i < 128);
    running <<= 1;
}
```
Exact shift left. Computes `self << rhs` as long as it can be reversed losslessly.

Returns `None` if any non-zero bits would be shifted out or if `rhs` >=
`u128::BITS`.
Otherwise, returns `Some(self << rhs)`.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-58)Examples

1.2.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1301-1327)#### pub const fn [wrapping_neg](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_neg)(self) -> [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)

#### pub const fn [wrapping_neg](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_neg)(self) -> [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)

Wrapping (modular) negation. Computes `-self`,
wrapping around at the boundary of the type.

Since unsigned types do not have negative equivalents
all applications of this function will wrap (except for `-0`).
For values smaller than the corresponding signed type’s maximum
the result is the same as casting the corresponding signed value.
Any larger values are equivalent to `MAX + 1 - (val - MAX - 1)` where
`MAX` is the corresponding signed type’s maximum.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-81)Examples

1.2.0 (const: 1.32.0) · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1301-1327)#### pub const fn [wrapping_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/src/core/num/mod.rs.html#1301-1327)

#### pub const fn [wrapping_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org#method.wrapping_shl)(self, rhs: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u32.html)) -> [u128](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html)

Panic-free bitwise shift-left; yields `self << mask(rhs)`,
where `mask` removes any high-order bits of `rhs` that
would cause the shift to exceed the bitwidth of the type.

Beware that, unlike most other `wrapping_*` methods on integers, this
does *not* give the same result as doing the shift in infinite precision
then truncating as needed.  The behaviour matches what shift instructions
do on many processors, and is what the `<<` operator does when overflow
checks are disabled, but numerically it’s weird.  Consider, instead,
using [ Self::unbounded_shl](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html#method.unbounded_shl) which has nicer behaviour.

Note that this is *not* the same as a rotate-left; the
RHS of a wrapping shift-left is restricted to the range
of the type, rather than the bits shifted out of the LHS
being returned to the other end. The primitive integer
types all implement a [ rotate_left](https://doc.rust-lang.org/primitive.u128.html#method.rotate_left) function,
which may be what you want instead.

[§](https://doc.rust-lang.org#examples-82)Examples

```
assert_eq!(1_u128.wrapping_shl(7), 128);
assert_eq!(0b101_u128.wrapping_shl(0), 0b101);
assert_eq!(0b101_u128.wrapping_shl(1), 0b1010);
assert_eq!(0b101_u128.wrapping_shl(2), 0b10100);
assert_eq!(u128::MAX.wrapping_shl(2), u128::MAX - 3);
assert_eq!(42_u128.wrapping_shl(128), 42);
assert_eq!(42_u128.wrapping_shl(1).wrapping_shl(127), 0);
assert_eq!(1_u128.wrapping_shl(128), 1);
assert_eq!(5_u128.wrapping_shl(1025), 10);
```
